# 1.1 Sets and Venn Diagrams

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a set is

A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right. The objects that make up a set are its **elements**, also called its **members**. A set that does not contain any elements is the **empty set**, or **null set**, written $\emptyset$.

Because a set is itself an object, sets can be compared, combined and taken apart, and that is what the rest of this lesson is about.

## Membership, subsets and size

| Symbol | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x \in A$ | Element | $x$ is an element of $A$ |
| $x \notin A$ | Not an element | $x$ is not an element of $A$ |
| $A \subset B$, $A \subseteq B$ | Subset | Every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| $B \supset A$, $B \supseteq A$ | Superset | Every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| $\lvert A \rvert$ | Cardinality | The number of elements in the set $A$ |

The two subset symbols are not interchangeable. $A \subset B$ means $A$ is a **proper subset** of $B$ — $B$ has elements that are not in $A$. $A \subseteq B$ can also mean that $A$ equals $B$.

A **superset** is simply the other side of the same relation: $B \supset A$ says that the second set named is a subset of the first, and not the other way around.

## Operations on sets

The **intersection** $A \cap B$ is the set containing the elements common to both $A$ and $B$. The **union** $A \cup B$ is the set containing all elements of $A$ and $B$.

The **complement** of $A$, denoted $A'$, is the set of elements in the universal set that are not in $A$. Textbooks usually print this as a bar over the name of the set, $\overline{A}$; the prime is the same thing written in a form a computer can type.

The **difference** of $A$ and $B$, denoted $A - B$, is the set of all elements which are in $A$ but not in $B$. Written as a condition on membership, $C = A - B$ when for every $n \in C$ we have $n \in A$ and $n \notin B$, that is

$$C = \{\, n \mid n \in A,\ n \notin B \,\}$$

## The laws of sets

For sets $A$, $B$ and $C$ inside a universal set $U$:

| # | Law | Union form | Intersection form |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Commutative | $A \cup B = B \cup A$ | $A \cap B = B \cap A$ |
| 2 | Associative | $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ | $(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)$ |
| 3 | Distributive | $A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$ | $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$ |
| 4 | Identity | $A \cup \emptyset = A$ | $A \cap U = A$ |
| 5 | Complement | $A \cup A' = U$ | $A \cap A' = \emptyset$ |
| 6 | Idempotent | $A \cup A = A$ | $A \cap A = A$ |
| 7 | Null | $A \cup U = U$ | $A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset$ |
| 8 | Absorption | $A \cup (A \cap B) = A$ | $A \cap (A \cup B) = A$ |
| 9 | Difference | $A - B = A \cap B'$ | |
| 10 | De Morgan | $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ | $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$ |

The names carry the reasoning. The empty set is the identity element for union, because adding nothing changes nothing; the universal set is the identity for intersection, because everything is already inside it. Correspondingly, a union with the universal set is the universal set, and an intersection with the empty set is empty.

Law 9 restates difference in terms of the two basic operations: taking $A$ but not $B$ is the same as taking what is both in $A$ and outside $B$.

**De Morgan's laws are the ones to know cold.** They say that complementing a union turns it into an intersection of complements, and complementing an intersection turns it into a union of complements — the operation flips when the bar goes on.

## Venn diagrams

A **Venn diagram** is a diagram that shows all possible logical relations between a finite collection of different sets. Each set is represented by a **circle**, usually drawn inside a rectangular field which stands for the universal set. Regions of overlap are exactly the intersections, so a Venn diagram turns the laws above into pictures.

## Counting with Venn diagrams

Two counting formulas follow from the picture:

$$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$$

$$n(A') = n(U) - n(A)$$

The subtraction in the first is necessary because the elements lying in both sets sit in the overlap and are therefore counted once in $n(A)$ and again in $n(B)$; removing $n(A \cap B)$ corrects the double count. The second says the number of elements not in $A$ is everything in the universal set minus what is in $A$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Set** | A collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right |
| **Element (member)** | An object that makes up the set |
| **Empty set (null set)** | A set that does not contain any elements |
| **Intersection $\cap$** | $A \cap B$ is the set containing elements common to both set $A$ and set $B$ |
| **Union $\cup$** | $A \cup B$ is the set containing all elements of $A$ and $B$ |
| **Cardinality $\lvert A \rvert$** | Number of elements in the set $A$ |
| **Element of $\in$** | If set $A$ contains a certain element, it is symbolised $x \in A$, read "$x$ is an element of $A$" |
| **Not an element $\notin$** | If set $A$ does not contain a certain element, it is symbolised $x \notin A$ |
| **Subset $\subset$, $\subseteq$** | A set $A$ is a subset of set $B$ if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| **Proper subset** | $A \subset B$: $A$ is a subset of $B$ and $B$ has elements not in $A$ |
| **Superset $\supset$, $\supseteq$** | A set $B$ is a superset of set $A$ if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| **Complement $A'$** | The set of elements in the universal set that are not in $A$ |
| **Difference $A - B$** | The set of all elements which are in $A$ but not in $B$ |
| **Venn diagram** | A diagram that shows all possible logical relations between a finite collection of different sets |
| **Circle** | Each set is represented by a circle, usually inside a rectangular field (the universal set) |

# 1.2 Inductive and Deductive Reasoning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two directions of argument

Mathematical arguments run in one of two directions, and the difference is which end you start from.

**Inductive reasoning** is a type of logical thinking that involves forming generalisations based on specific incidents you have experienced, observations you have made, or facts you know to be true or false. It works upwards: several particular cases suggest a rule that covers them all.

**Deductive reasoning** is a type of logical thinking where you start with a general fact, rule, or premise and then deduce or infer certain specific details or conclusions. It works downwards: an accepted rule is applied to a particular case.

## Comparing the two

| | Inductive reasoning | Deductive reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | Specific incidents, observations, or known facts | A general fact, rule, or premise |
| Direction | From particular cases to a generalisation | From the general rule to specific details |
| Result | A generalisation | A conclusion inferred about the particular case |

Because inductive reasoning generalises from cases you happen to have seen, its conclusion goes beyond the evidence used to reach it. Deductive reasoning does not: the specific conclusion is already contained in the general premise you started from, and drawing it out is what "deduce" means.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inductive reasoning** | A type of logical thinking that involves forming generalisations based on specific incidents you've experienced, observations you've made, or facts you know to be true or false |
| **Deductive reasoning** | A type of logical thinking where you start with a general fact, rule, or premise and then deduce or infer certain specific details or conclusions |

# 1.3 Logic Statements

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Propositions

A **proposition**, also known as a statement, is a declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both. That restriction is what makes a proposition usable in logic: every proposition has exactly one truth value to work with.

A **compound proposition** is a combination of two or more propositions using logical operators. The operators are conjunction, disjunction, implication and biconditional, and each has its own rule for when the compound comes out true.

## The logical operators

- **Conjunction** — a compound proposition that uses the logical operator AND. For the conjunction $p \wedge q$ to be true, both $p$ and $q$ must be true.
- **Disjunction** — a compound proposition that uses the logical operator OR. For the disjunction $p \vee q$, it is enough for either $p$ or $q$ to be true for the entire disjunction to be true.
- **Negation** — the negation of a proposition $p$ is "not $p$", denoted $\sim p$ or $\neg p$. If $p$ is true, then $\sim p$ is false, and vice versa.
- **Conditional statement (implication)** — a compound proposition of the form "if $p$ then $q$", represented as $p \to q$. It is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false; otherwise it is true.
- **Biconditional statement** — a statement of the form "$p$ if and only if $q$", true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth values and false when they are different. It is represented as $p \leftrightarrow q$ or $p \equiv q$.

Setting those rules side by side gives the truth values of every compound:

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \wedge q$ | $p \vee q$ | $p \to q$ | $p \leftrightarrow q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | F | T | T | F |
| F | F | F | F | T | T |

The conditional row worth pausing on is the third: $p$ false, $q$ true still gives a true implication, because the only way to break "if $p$ then $q$" is to have the hypothesis hold and the conclusion fail.

## Contradiction and contingency

A **contradiction** is a compound proposition that is always false regardless of the truth values of the individual propositions that constitute it. A **contingency** is a compound proposition that could be either true or false depending on the truth values of its constituent propositions.

## Sufficient and necessary

These two words describe the two roles in a conditional.

- **Sufficient**: when given $A$, we can know $B$; then $A$ is sufficient for $B$.
- **Necessary**: when given $A$, we can know $B$; then $B$ is necessary for $A$.

The same single implication supports both readings — the hypothesis is the sufficient condition, the conclusion is the necessary one.

## Converse, inverse and contrapositive

In a conditional statement of the form "if $p$ then $q$", also written $p \to q$, different forms are created by switching or negating the hypothesis and the conclusion.

| Form | Statement | Symbols | Built by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original | if $p$ then $q$ | $p \to q$ | — |
| **Converse** | if $q$ then $p$ | $q \to p$ | Switching the hypothesis and the conclusion |
| **Inverse** | if not $p$ then not $q$ | $\neg p \to \neg q$ | Negating both the hypothesis and the conclusion |
| **Contrapositive** | if not $q$ then not $p$ | $\neg q \to \neg p$ | Both switching and negating the hypothesis and the conclusion |

## Logical equivalence

In terms of truth values, certain relationships always hold:

- A statement and its contrapositive are **logically equivalent**. This means they are both either true or false. If "if $p$ then $q$" is true, then "if not $q$ then not $p$" is also true, and vice versa.
- Similarly, a converse and an inverse are logically equivalent. If "if $q$ then $p$" is true, then "if not $p$ then not $q$" is also true, and vice versa.

Notice what these pairings do *not* say. The original and its converse are not paired, and the original and its inverse are not paired; proving $p \to q$ therefore tells you nothing about whether $q \to p$ holds.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Proposition** | A declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both |
| **Compound proposition** | A combination of two or more propositions using logical operators |
| **Conjunction** | A compound proposition using AND; $p \wedge q$ is true only when both $p$ and $q$ are true |
| **Disjunction** | A compound proposition using OR; $p \vee q$ is true when either $p$ or $q$ is true |
| **Negation** | "Not $p$", denoted $\sim p$ or $\neg p$; false when $p$ is true and true when $p$ is false |
| **Conditional statement (implication)** | "If $p$ then $q$", written $p \to q$; false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false |
| **Biconditional statement** | "$p$ if and only if $q$", written $p \leftrightarrow q$ or $p \equiv q$; true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth values |
| **Contradiction** | A compound proposition that is always false regardless of the truth values of its constituent propositions |
| **Contingency** | A compound proposition that could be either true or false depending on the truth values of its constituent propositions |
| **Sufficient** | When given $A$ we can know $B$, then $A$ is sufficient for $B$ |
| **Necessary** | When given $A$ we can know $B$, then $B$ is necessary for $A$ |
| **Converse** | The converse of "if $p$ then $q$" is "if $q$ then $p$" |
| **Inverse** | The inverse of "if $p$ then $q$" is "if not $p$ then not $q$" |
| **Contrapositive** | The contrapositive of "if $p$ then $q$" is "if not $q$ then not $p$" |

# 1.4 Geometric Theorems and Postulates

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Postulates that set up measurement

Before anything can be proved about a figure, the figure has to be measurable. Two postulates do that work.

The **Ruler Postulate** states that the points on a line can be paired with the real numbers in such a way that any given point can always be paired with zero and any other with a positive number. This is what licenses talking about the length of a segment at all: once points carry numbers, distance is a difference of numbers.

The **Protractor Postulate** states that, taking $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ to be opposite rays in a plane, we can measure angles $\angle AOB$ for every rotation about point $O$. It is the angular counterpart of the Ruler Postulate.

## Adding angles

The **Angle Addition Postulate**: if point $B$ lies in the interior of $\angle AOC$, then

$$m\angle AOB + m\angle BOC = m\angle AOC$$

The condition matters — $B$ must lie *in the interior* of the angle, otherwise the two smaller angles do not partition the larger one.

## The Parallel Postulate

In Euclidean geometry, the **Parallel Postulate** states that given a line and a point not on the line, there is exactly one line through the point that is parallel to the given line. "Exactly one" is doing two jobs: at least one such line exists, and no second one does.

## Angle relationships

| Name | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Linear Pair Postulate** | If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary (their sum is $180°$) |
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the pairs of corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the alternate interior angles are congruent |

The last two are the working tools for any diagram containing a transversal: knowing the lines are parallel turns a pair of angles in different places into a pair of equal measures.

## A triangle theorem

The **Isosceles Triangle Theorem**: if two sides of a triangle are congruent — that is, the triangle is isosceles — then the angles opposite those sides are congruent.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ruler Postulate** | The points on a line can be paired with the real numbers so that any given point can be paired with zero and any other with a positive number |
| **Protractor Postulate** | With $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ opposite rays in a plane, angles $\angle AOB$ can be measured for every rotation about point $O$ |
| **Angle Addition Postulate** | If point $B$ lies in the interior of $\angle AOC$, then $\angle AOB + \angle BOC = \angle AOC$ |
| **Parallel Postulate** | Given a line and a point not on the line, there is exactly one line through the point parallel to the given line |
| **Linear Pair Postulate** | If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary (their sum is $180°$) |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the alternate interior angles are congruent |
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the pairs of corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent |

# 2.1 Isosceles Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The parts of an isosceles triangle

An isosceles triangle has two congruent sides, and its parts are named around that fact.

| Part | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Leg** | Either of the congruent sides of an isosceles triangle |
| **Base** | The third side |
| **Vertex angle** | The angle formed by the two congruent sides |
| **Base angle** | Either of the other two angles |

So a leg is a side, the base is the odd side out, the vertex angle sits between the legs, and the base angles sit at the ends of the base.

## The Isosceles Triangle Theorem and its converse

**Isosceles Triangle Theorem:** if two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent.

$$\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC} \implies \angle B \cong \angle C$$

**Converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem:** if two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite the angles are congruent.

$$\angle B \cong \angle C \implies \overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$$

Because both directions hold, congruent legs and congruent base angles are interchangeable pieces of evidence: in a triangle, whichever you are given, you may conclude the other.

## The bisector of the vertex angle

The bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is the perpendicular bisector of the base.

This is a strong statement, because one line is doing three jobs at once. Drawn from the vertex angle, it bisects that angle, it meets the base at right angles, and it cuts the base into two congruent halves.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Leg** | The congruent sides of an isosceles triangle |
| **Base** | The third side of an isosceles triangle |
| **Vertex angle** | The angle formed by the two congruent sides |
| **Base angle** | Either of the two angles other than the vertex angle |
| **Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent |
| **Converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite the angles are congruent |

markdown:
# 2.2 Equilateral Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## From equilateral to equiangular

If a triangle is equilateral, then the triangle is **equiangular**.

The reason is already available from the isosceles case. An equilateral triangle has three congruent sides, so it is isosceles in three different ways at once — any pair of its sides can be taken as the legs. Applying the Isosceles Triangle Theorem to one pair gives one pair of congruent angles; applying it to a second pair gives another. Between them, all three angles are forced to be congruent, which is what equiangular means.

$$\overline{AB} \cong \overline{BC} \cong \overline{CA} \implies \angle A \cong \angle B \cong \angle C$$

## Working with the result

Because an equilateral triangle is isosceles on every side, everything established for isosceles triangles applies to it from any vertex. In particular, the bisector of the angle at any vertex is the perpendicular bisector of the opposite side, since that vertex angle is the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle whose base is that opposite side.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Equilateral triangle** | A triangle whose sides are all congruent |
| **Equiangular** | Having all angles congruent; if a triangle is equilateral, then the triangle is equiangular |

# 2.3 Inequalities in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The exterior angle inequality

The measure of an **exterior angle** of a triangle is greater than the measure of each of its **remote interior angles**. Labelling the exterior angle $\angle 1$ and the two remote interior angles $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$:

$$m\angle 1 > m\angle 2 \quad \text{and} \quad m\angle 1 > m\angle 3$$

Note that the comparison is with *each* remote interior angle separately, not with their sum.

## Sides against angles

The next two theorems are converses of one another, and they are the reason a triangle's shape can be read off from either its sides or its angles.

| Theorem | Statement | Mnemonic |
|---|---|---|
| **Theorem 5-10** | If two sides of a triangle are not congruent, then the larger angle lies opposite the longer side | 大边对大角 |
| **Theorem 5-11** | If two angles of a triangle are not congruent, then the longer side lies opposite the larger angle | 大角对大边 |

Read together: in any triangle, longest side and largest angle face each other, and shortest side and smallest angle face each other. Given the three side lengths you can rank the angles without measuring any of them, and given the three angles you can rank the sides.

## The Triangle Inequality

**Theorem 5-12:** the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side.

$$a + b > c, \qquad b + c > a, \qquad a + c > b$$

The word *any* means all three comparisons have to hold, so testing whether three given lengths can form a triangle means checking each pair in turn.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Exterior angle** | An angle of a triangle whose measure is greater than the measure of each of its remote interior angles |
| **Theorem 5-10** | If two sides of a triangle are not congruent, then the larger angle lies opposite the longer side |
| **Theorem 5-11** | If two angles of a triangle are not congruent, then the longer side lies opposite the larger angle |
| **Theorem 5-12 (Triangle Inequality)** | The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side |

# 2.4 Bisectors in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The perpendicular bisector

The **perpendicular bisector** of a segment is the line perpendicular to it at its midpoint. Both conditions are part of the definition: right angles alone are not enough, and cutting the segment in half is not enough either.

**Perpendicular Bisector Theorem:** if a point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment, then it is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment.

**Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem:** if a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

Taken together the two statements say that the perpendicular bisector *is* the set of points equidistant from the two endpoints — nothing else qualifies, and nothing that qualifies is left out.

$$P \text{ on the perpendicular bisector of } \overline{AB} \iff PA = PB$$

## The angle bisector

**Angle Bisector Theorem:** if a point is on the bisector of an angle, then the point is equidistant from the sides of the angle.

**Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem:** if a point in the interior of an angle is equidistant from the sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector.

The converse carries an extra condition the forward theorem does not need: the point must lie *in the interior* of the angle.

Note also what "distance from a side" means here. The sides of an angle are lines, so the distance meant is the perpendicular distance to each side, and the theorem says the bisector is where those two perpendicular distances are equal.

## The pattern

Both pairs follow the same shape. A bisector is characterised by an equal-distance property, and the property runs in both directions, so it can be used either to deduce equal distances from a known bisector or to prove a point lies on a bisector from known equal distances.

| Bisector | Equidistant from | Forward direction | Converse direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Perpendicular bisector of a segment | The endpoints of the segment | On the bisector $\Rightarrow$ equidistant | Equidistant $\Rightarrow$ on the bisector |
| Bisector of an angle | The sides of the angle | On the bisector $\Rightarrow$ equidistant | Equidistant and in the interior $\Rightarrow$ on the bisector |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Perpendicular bisector** | A line that is perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint |
| **Perpendicular Bisector Theorem** | If a point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment, then it is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment |
| **Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem** | If a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment |
| **Angle Bisector Theorem** | If a point is on the bisector of an angle, then the point is equidistant from the sides of the angle |
| **Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem** | If a point in the interior of an angle is equidistant from the sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector |

# 2.5 Concurrent Lines, Medians, and Altitudes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Concurrency

When three or more lines intersect in one point, they are **concurrent**. The point at which they intersect is the **point of concurrency**.

Three arbitrary lines in a plane will normally meet in three different points, so concurrency is a special condition. The theorems below say that four different sets of lines built from a triangle are concurrent every time.

## Four sets of lines in a triangle

| Lines | Point of concurrency | Theorem |
|---|---|---|
| Perpendicular bisectors of the sides | **Circumcentre** | Theorem 5-6 |
| Bisectors of the angles | **Incentre** | Theorem 5-7 |
| Medians | — | Theorem 5-8 |
| Lines containing the altitudes | **Orthocentre** | Theorem 5-9 |

A **median** of a triangle is a segment whose endpoints are a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side. An **altitude** of a triangle is the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side.

## The theorems

**Theorem 5-6:** the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the vertices. That point is the circumcentre.

**Theorem 5-7:** the bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the sides. That point is the incentre.

The distance properties in these two are not coincidental. A point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from that side's two endpoints, so a point on all three perpendicular bisectors is equidistant from all three vertices. Likewise a point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from that angle's two sides, so a point on all three angle bisectors is equidistant from all three sides.

**Theorem 5-8:** the medians of a triangle are concurrent at a point that is two thirds the distance from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. If the median from vertex $A$ meets the opposite side at midpoint $M$, and the point of concurrency is $P$, then

$$AP = \tfrac{2}{3}\,AM$$

**Theorem 5-9:** the lines that contain the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent. Their point of concurrency is the orthocentre.

## A caution about altitudes

Unlike angle bisectors and medians, an altitude of a triangle can be a side of the triangle, or it may lie outside the triangle. This is why Theorem 5-9 is phrased in terms of the *lines containing* the altitudes rather than the altitude segments themselves — in an obtuse triangle the segments themselves need not meet inside the figure at all.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Concurrent** | Three or more lines that intersect in one point |
| **Point of concurrency** | The point at which concurrent lines intersect |
| **Circumcentre** | The point of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle |
| **Incentre** | The point of concurrency of the angle bisectors of a triangle |
| **Median** | A segment whose endpoints are a vertex of a triangle and the midpoint of the opposite side |
| **Altitude** | The perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side |
| **Orthocentre** | The point of concurrency of the lines containing the altitudes of a triangle |
| **Theorem 5-6** | The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the vertices |
| **Theorem 5-7** | The bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the sides |
| **Theorem 5-8** | The medians of a triangle are concurrent at a point that is two thirds the distance from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side |
| **Theorem 5-9** | The lines that contain the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent |

title: Isometries
summary: A transformation of a geometric figure is a change in its position, shape, or size. The original figure is the preimage; the resulting figure is the image, and the preimage and image must be similar.
markdown:
# 5.1 Isometries

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Transformations, preimages and images

A **transformation** of a geometric figure is a change in its position, shape, or size. The original figure is the **preimage**; the resulting figure is the **image**, and the preimage and image must be similar.

An **isometry** is a transformation in which the preimage and image are congruent. Isometries are therefore the transformations that move a figure without altering it: position may change, size and shape may not.

## Notation

A transformation maps a figure onto its image and may be described with arrow notation, $\triangle ABC \longrightarrow \triangle A'B'C'$. Prime notation is sometimes used to identify image points, so the image of $A$ is written $A'$.

Notice that you list corresponding points of the preimage and image in the same order, as you do for corresponding points of congruent or similar figures. Getting that order right is what makes the statement say which point went where.

## Translations

A **translation**, or slide, is an isometry that maps all points of a figure the same distance in the same direction. Both conditions are required — every point moves, and every point moves identically.

A **composition** of translations is a combination of two or more transformations. In a composition, each transformation is performed on the image of the preceding transformation, so the order in which they are carried out is part of the description.

## Reflections

A **reflection**, or flip, is an isometry in which a figure and its image have opposite orientations. This is why a reflected image in a mirror appears "backwards".

You can use the following two rules to reflect a figure across a line $r$:

- If a point $A$ is on line $r$, then the image of $A$ is $A$ itself, that is $A' = A$.
- If a point $B$ is not on line $r$, then $r$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{BB'}$.

The second rule is the working construction: drop a perpendicular from $B$ to $r$ and continue the same distance beyond it.

## Rotations

To describe a rotation you need to know three things: the **centre of rotation** (a point), the **angle of rotation** (a positive number of degrees), and whether the rotation is clockwise or counterclockwise. Unless stated otherwise, rotations here are counterclockwise.

You can use the following two rules to rotate a figure through $x°$ about a point $R$:

- The image of $R$ is itself, that is $R' = R$.
- For any point $V$, $RV' = RV$ and $m\angle VRV' = x$.

The first rule identifies the one fixed point; the second says every other point keeps its distance from the centre and turns through the same angle.

## Rotating regular polygons

A regular polygon has a centre that is equidistant from its vertices. Segments that connect the centre to the vertices divide the polygon into congruent triangles, and this fact can be used to find rotation images of regular polygons: rotating by the angle that carries one of those congruent triangles onto the next carries the whole polygon onto itself.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Transformation** | A change in the position, shape, or size of a geometric figure |
| **Preimage** | The original figure |
| **Image** | The resulting figure |
| **Isometry** | A transformation in which the preimage and image are congruent |
| **Translation (slide)** | An isometry that maps all points of a figure the same distance in the same direction |
| **Composition** | A combination of two or more transformations, each performed on the image of the preceding transformation |
| **Reflection (flip)** | An isometry in which a figure and its image have opposite orientations |
| **Centre of rotation** | The point about which a rotation turns a figure |
| **Angle of rotation** | The positive number of degrees through which a rotation turns a figure |

# 5.2 Compositions of Reflections

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a composition is

A **composition** is a combination of two or more transformations. In a composition, each transformation is performed on the image of the preceding transformation — the output of one becomes the input of the next.

Because reflections are isometries, any composition of reflections is again a transformation that preserves congruence: each step leaves the figure congruent to what it received, so the final image is congruent to the original preimage.

## Glide reflections

If two figures are congruent and have opposite orientations, but are not simply reflections of each other, then there is a slide and a reflection that will map one onto the other. That combination of a translation with a reflection is a **glide reflection**.

The description tells you when to reach for one. Opposite orientations rule out a translation or a rotation on its own, since those preserve orientation. But if a single reflection does not do the job either — the figures are turned the right way round yet displaced along the mirror line — then the missing ingredient is the slide, and the pair of moves together completes the map.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Composition** | A combination of two or more transformations, in which each transformation is performed on the image of the preceding transformation |
| **Glide reflection** | The slide and reflection that map one figure onto another when the two are congruent with opposite orientations but are not simply reflections of each other |

# 5.3 Symmetry

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Symmetry as self-mapping

A figure has **symmetry** if there is an isometry that maps the figure onto itself. The definition is worth reading carefully: symmetry is not a property of how a figure looks but a statement that some motion leaves it apparently unchanged.

## Reflectional symmetry

**Reflectional symmetry** is the case where the isometry that maps the figure onto itself is a reflection. The line of that reflection is a line across which the figure matches itself point for point.

## Rotational symmetry

A figure that has **rotational symmetry** is its own image for some rotation of $180°$ or less.

A square has $90°$ and $180°$ rotational symmetry with the centre of rotation at the centre of the square. Because it has $180°$ rotational symmetry, a square also has **point symmetry**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Symmetry** | A figure has symmetry if there is an isometry that maps the figure onto itself |
| **Reflectional symmetry** | Symmetry in which the isometry mapping the figure onto itself is a reflection |
| **Rotational symmetry** | A figure has rotational symmetry if it is its own image for some rotation of $180°$ or less |
| **Point symmetry** | The symmetry a figure has when it is its own image under a $180°$ rotation |

# 5.4 Dilations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## A transformation that changes size

A **dilation** is a transformation whose preimage and image are similar. A dilation is therefore a similarity transformation, and it is not, in general, an isometry — an isometry requires the preimage and image to be congruent, while a dilation only requires them to be similar.

## Centre and scale factor

Every dilation has a **centre** $C$ and a **scale factor** $n$, with $n > 0$. The scale factor describes the size change from the original figure to the image.

The rule for locating image points is:

$$\text{For any point } R,\ R' \text{ is on } \overrightarrow{CR} \quad \text{and} \quad CR' = n \cdot CR$$

Each image point lies on the ray from the centre through the original point, so the direction from the centre is preserved; only the distance from the centre is multiplied.

## Enlargements and reductions

| Scale factor | Name | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| $n > 1$ | **Enlargement** | The image is larger than the preimage |
| $0 < n < 1$ | **Reduction** | The image is smaller than the preimage |

The dividing line is $n = 1$, which would multiply every distance from the centre by one and leave the figure where it is.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dilation** | A transformation whose preimage and image are similar; a similarity transformation, and not in general an isometry |
| **Centre of a dilation** | The fixed point $C$ from which distances are measured, with $R'$ on $\overrightarrow{CR}$ and $CR' = n \cdot CR$ |
| **Scale factor $n$** | The positive number describing the size change from the original figure to the image |
| **Enlargement** | A dilation whose scale factor is greater than $1$ |
| **Reduction** | A dilation whose scale factor is between $0$ and $1$ |

# 6.1 Circles and Arcs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The circle and its parts

A **circle** is the set of all points equidistant from a given point called the **centre**. Every other definition in this lesson is built on that one.

A **radius** is a segment that has one endpoint at the centre and the other endpoint on the circle. Because every point of the circle is the same distance from the centre, all radii of a circle are congruent, and **congruent circles have congruent radii**.

A **diameter** is a segment that contains the centre of a circle and has both endpoints on the circle. A **central angle** is an angle whose vertex is the centre of the circle.

In a circle with centre $P$ and points $A$, $B$, $C$ on the circle where $\overline{AB}$ passes through $P$: $\overline{PC}$, $\overline{PA}$ and $\overline{PB}$ are radii, $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, and $\angle CPA$ is a central angle.

**Concentric circles** are circles that lie in the same plane and have the same centre. They share a centre but not a radius, so they never intersect.

## Arcs

An **arc** is a part of a circle. Arcs are classified by size against the half-circle:

| Arc | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Semicircle** | Half of a circle |
| **Minor arc** | Smaller than a semicircle |
| **Major arc** | Greater than a semicircle |

**Adjacent arcs** are arcs of the same circle that have exactly one point in common. The "exactly one" is what makes them adjacent rather than overlapping: they meet end to end at a single shared endpoint.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Circle** | The set of all points equidistant from a given point called the centre |
| **Radius** | A segment that has one endpoint at the centre and the other endpoint on the circle |
| **Congruent circles** | Circles that have congruent radii |
| **Diameter** | A segment that contains the centre of a circle and has both endpoints on the circle |
| **Central angle** | An angle whose vertex is the centre of the circle |
| **Concentric circles** | Circles that lie in the same plane and have the same centre |
| **Arc** | A part of a circle |
| **Semicircle** | Half of a circle |
| **Minor arc** | An arc smaller than a semicircle |
| **Major arc** | An arc greater than a semicircle |
| **Adjacent arcs** | Arcs of the same circle that have exactly one point in common |

markdown:
# 6.2 Circumference, Area, Sectors, and Segments

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Circumference and $\pi$

The **circumference** of a circle is the distance around the circle. The number $\pi$ is the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter:

$$\pi = \frac{C}{d}$$

Rearranging that definition gives the circumference itself, and since a diameter is two radii,

$$C = \pi d = 2\pi r$$

The definition of $\pi$ as a *ratio* is what makes this work for every circle at once: the ratio is the same number whatever the size of the circle, so one constant serves them all.

## Area of a circle

$$A = \pi r^2$$

## Sectors

A **sector** of a circle is a region bounded by an arc of the circle and the two radii to the arc's endpoints. A sector is a slice of the whole disc, and the fraction of the disc it takes up is the fraction of the full turn that its arc subtends at the centre:

$$\text{area of sector} = \frac{m\overset{\frown}{AB}}{360} \cdot \pi r^2$$

## Segments

A part of a circle bounded by an arc and the segment joining its endpoints is a **segment** of a circle. A segment is what is left of a sector once the straight-sided piece is removed.

To find the area of a segment for a minor arc, draw the radii to form a sector. Then

$$\text{area of segment} = \text{area of sector} - \text{area of the triangle formed}$$

The triangle in question is the one whose vertices are the centre and the two endpoints of the arc — the two radii you drew plus the chord joining them.

## Comparing the two regions

| Region | Bounded by |
|---|---|
| Sector | An arc and the two radii to the arc's endpoints |
| Segment | An arc and the segment joining its endpoints |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Circumference** | The distance around the circle |
| **$\pi$** | The ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter |
| **Sector** | A region of a circle bounded by an arc of the circle and the two radii to the arc's endpoints |
| **Segment of a circle** | A part of a circle bounded by an arc and the segment joining its endpoints |

# 6.3 Tangents and Chords

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Tangents

A **tangent** to a circle is a line in the plane of the circle that intersects the circle in exactly one point. The point where a circle and a tangent intersect is the **point of tangency**.

"Exactly one point" is the whole of the definition. A line in the plane of a circle meets it twice, once, or not at all, and the tangent is the middle case.

## Chords

A segment whose endpoints are on a circle is called a **chord**. A diameter is therefore the special chord that also passes through the centre.

## Circles and triangles

If a circle is **circumscribed** about a triangle, the triangle is **inscribed** in the circle — the vertices of the triangle lie on the circle. Similarly, when a circle is inscribed in a triangle, the triangle is circumscribed about the circle.

The two phrasings describe the same picture from opposite sides; which word you use depends on which figure is on the outside.

When a circle is inscribed in a triangle, each side of the triangle is tangent to the circle. That makes each side touch the circle at exactly one point, and it gives the following result: **the tangent segments from each vertex are congruent.** From a vertex, the two sides of the triangle leaving it are both tangent to the circle, and the segments from that vertex to the two points of tangency have equal length.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Tangent** | A line in the plane of a circle that intersects the circle in exactly one point |
| **Point of tangency** | The point where a circle and a tangent intersect |
| **Chord** | A segment whose endpoints are on a circle |
| **Circumscribed circle** | A circle drawn about a triangle, so that the triangle is inscribed in the circle |
| **Inscribed circle** | A circle drawn inside a triangle, so that the triangle is circumscribed about the circle and each side of the triangle is tangent to the circle |

# 6.4 Inscribed Angles and Secants

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Inscribed angles and intercepted arcs

An **inscribed angle** is an angle whose vertex is on the circle and whose sides contain chords of the circle. It is the counterpart of the central angle, which has its vertex at the centre; moving the vertex out to the circle itself is what makes the angle inscribed.

The **intercepted arc** of an inscribed angle is the arc that lies in the interior of the angle, with its endpoints on the sides of the angle. Every inscribed angle picks out exactly one such arc, which is why the two are always discussed together: the angle is described by what it cuts off.

## Secants

A **secant** is a line that intersects a circle in two points. Set alongside the other lines and segments already defined, it completes a small family:

| Figure | Relationship to the circle |
|---|---|
| **Chord** | A segment whose endpoints are on the circle |
| **Secant** | A line that intersects the circle in two points |
| **Tangent** | A line in the plane of the circle that intersects the circle in exactly one point |

A chord and a secant describe the same two points of intersection; the difference is that the chord stops at the circle while the secant runs on past it in both directions. A tangent, by contrast, meets the circle only once, so no chord lies along it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inscribed angle** | An angle whose vertex is on the circle and whose sides contain chords of the circle |
| **Intercepted arc** | The arc lying in the interior of an inscribed angle, with its endpoints on the sides of the angle |
| **Secant** | A line that intersects a circle in two points |

# 6.5 Cyclic Quadrilaterals and Locus

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Cyclic quadrilaterals

A quadrilateral is said to be a **cyclic quadrilateral** if a circle can be drawn that passes through all four of its vertices. Points that lie on a common circle in this way are called **concyclic**.

Not every quadrilateral is cyclic. Three points that are not collinear always determine a circle, but the fourth vertex has to land on that same circle, and in general it will not.

## The test for concyclic points

To determine whether four points are concyclic, use this: **the opposite angles of the quadrilateral are supplementary.**

$$m\angle A + m\angle C = 180° \qquad m\angle B + m\angle D = 180°$$

This is the result to reach for whenever a question asks whether four given points lie on one circle. Work out the angles of the quadrilateral they form and check the two opposite pairs.

## Locus

A **locus** is the set of all points that satisfy a given condition. Describing a locus means describing the whole figure traced out by every point meeting the condition, and nothing that fails it.

One caution about dimension: if the locus is in **space**, it should be a three-dimensional figure. The same condition gives different answers depending on where you are allowed to look — a condition that produces a curve in the plane will generally produce a surface in space — so read the question for which setting is meant before describing the answer.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Cyclic quadrilateral** | A quadrilateral for which a circle can be drawn passing through all four of its vertices |
| **Concyclic** | Describing points that all lie on the same circle |
| **Locus** | The set of all points that satisfy a given condition; if the locus is in space, it should be a three-dimensional figure |

# 7.1 The Coordinate Plane and Linear Equations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Coordinate geometry

There is a **one-to-one correspondence** between the set of real numbers and the set of points on the number line: every real number is matched with exactly one point, and every point with exactly one real number.

Extending this concept, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the set of points on the plane and the set of ordered pairs of real numbers. This is the idea the whole of coordinate geometry rests on — because the matching is one-to-one in both directions, a geometric question about points can be turned into an algebraic question about numbers and back again without loss.

## The coordinate plane

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **$x$-axis** | One horizontal number line |
| **$y$-axis** | One vertical number line, perpendicular to the $x$-axis |
| **Coordinate axes** | The $x$- and $y$-axes together |
| **Quadrants** | The four parts that are formed by dividing the coordinate plane with the coordinate axes |

## Graphs

Given a set $S$ of ordered pairs of numbers, each element of the set can be represented by a point in the plane. The **graph** of $S$ is the set of all such points.

The **$y$-intercept** is the $y$-coordinate of the point where the graph of an equation intersects the $y$-axis. Note the definition names a single coordinate, not a point.

## Linear equations

A **linear equation** has the form

$$Ax + By = C$$

where $A$ and $B$ are not both zero. Its graph is a line.

The condition on $A$ and $B$ is what keeps the equation genuinely about the plane: if both were zero the left-hand side would vanish and no line would be described.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **One-to-one correspondence** | The pairing between the set of real numbers and the points on a number line, extended to the pairing between points in the plane and ordered pairs of real numbers |
| **$x$-axis** | One horizontal number line |
| **$y$-axis** | One vertical number line perpendicular to the $x$-axis |
| **Coordinate axes** | The $x$- and $y$-axes together |
| **Quadrants** | The four parts formed by dividing the coordinate plane with the coordinate axes |
| **Graph of $S$** | The set of all points representing the elements of a set $S$ of ordered pairs |
| **$y$-intercept** | The $y$-coordinate of the point where the graph of an equation intersects the $y$-axis |
| **Linear equation** | An equation $Ax + By = C$ with $A$ and $B$ not both zero; its graph is a line |

summary: The steepness, or slope, of a nonvertical line is defined as the ratio of the change in the vertical distance (the rise) to the change in the horizontal distance (the run) between any two points on th
markdown:
# 7.2 Slopes and Equations of Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Slope

The steepness, or **slope**, of a nonvertical line is defined as the ratio of the change in the vertical distance (the **rise**) to the change in the horizontal distance (the **run**) between any two points on the line.

$$m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$$

Two parts of the definition are doing work. *Nonvertical* is required because a vertical line has a run of zero between any two of its points, and the ratio would have zero in the denominator. *Any two points* is what makes slope a property of the line rather than of the pair of points chosen: whichever two you take, the ratio comes out the same.

## Parallel and perpendicular lines

| Relationship | Slopes |
|---|---|
| Parallel lines | Have the same slope |
| Perpendicular lines | Have negative reciprocal slopes |

So if one line has slope $m$, a line parallel to it also has slope $m$, and a line perpendicular to it has slope $-\dfrac{1}{m}$.

## Finding equations of lines

Three forms are used to write the equation of a line, and which one to reach for depends on what you have been given.

| Form | Equation | Use it when you know |
|---|---|---|
| **Point-slope form** | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ | A point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the line and the slope |
| **Slope-intercept form** | $y = mx + b$ | The slope and the $y$-intercept |
| **Standard form** | $Ax + By = C$ | — |

Point-slope form is the most direct translation of the slope definition: it says that between the known point and any other point on the line, the rise over the run equals $m$. Slope-intercept form displays the two numbers that determine the line — its steepness $m$ and where it crosses the $y$-axis at $b$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Slope** | The steepness of a nonvertical line, the ratio of the change in the vertical distance to the change in the horizontal distance between any two points on the line |
| **Rise** | The change in the vertical distance between two points on a line |
| **Run** | The change in the horizontal distance between two points on a line |
| **Point-slope form** | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ |
| **Slope-intercept form** | $y = mx + b$ |
| **Standard form** | $Ax + By = C$ |

markdown:
# 8.1 Solving Quadratic Equations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Solutions and roots

A **solution**, or **root**, of an equation is a value for which substituting that solution makes the equation true. That is the definition to fall back on whenever an answer needs checking: put it in and see whether the two sides agree.

A quadratic equation can have zero, one, or two real solutions.

## Solving by factoring

**Factoring** rests on a single fact: whenever the product of two factors is zero, at least one of the factors must be zero.

So once a quadratic is arranged with zero on one side and written as a product, each factor can be set equal to zero in turn and solved separately. The reason this works is exactly the fact above — a product cannot be zero unless something in it is.

## The quadratic formula

For a quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with $a \neq 0$,

$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$

## The discriminant

The **discriminant** is the quantity under the radical:

$$\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$$

Its sign settles how many real solutions there are before any of them is calculated, because it is the thing being square-rooted.

| Discriminant | Number of solutions |
|---|---|
| $b^2 - 4ac > 0$ | The equation has two different real solutions |
| $b^2 - 4ac = 0$ | The equation has one real solution (a **double root**) |
| $b^2 - 4ac < 0$ | The equation has zero real solutions; the solutions are imaginary numbers |

## Losing or gaining a root

Some legal-looking algebraic moves change the solution set, and this is a standard source of lost marks.

| Move | Effect |
|---|---|
| Dividing both sides of an equation by a common factor | **Lose** a root |
| Squaring both sides of an equation, or multiplying both sides by an expression | **Gain** a root |

A gained root is called an **extraneous root**. The two entries are mirror images: dividing by a factor throws away the case in which that factor is itself zero, while multiplying by an expression introduces the case in which that expression is zero. Because gained roots satisfy the altered equation but not the original one, every candidate must be substituted back into the original equation.

## Maximum and minimum

The value of the function at the vertex is an extreme value, and which one it is depends on the sign of $a$:

- If $a > 0$: the value of the function at the vertex is the **minimum**.
- If $a < 0$: the value of the function at the vertex is the **maximum**.

## Steepness

The bigger $\lvert a \rvert$ is, the narrower the parabola is.

## Zeros of a function

The $x$-intercepts are called the real **zeros** of the function. They are the same numbers as the real solutions of the corresponding equation, seen from the graph instead of the algebra: an $x$-intercept is a point where the function's value is zero.

## Graphs as transformations

The graph of a quadratic function can be interpreted as a series of transformations of the squaring function. For a function in the form

$$y = a(x - h)^2 + k$$

| Parameter | Effect |
|---|---|
| $a$ | Determines the dilation of the parabola |
| $k$ | Determines the vertical shift |
| $h$ | Determines the horizontal shift |
| $a < 0$ | The parabola is reflected in the $x$-axis |

Read together with the section above, $a$ is doing two jobs at once — its size sets how narrow the parabola is, and its sign sets whether the parabola opens upwards to a minimum or is reflected in the $x$-axis and opens downwards to a maximum.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Solution (root)** | A value for which substituting it makes the equation true |
| **Factoring** | A solving method resting on the fact that whenever the product of two factors is zero, at least one of the factors must be zero |
| **Quadratic formula** | $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ |
| **Discriminant** | $b^2 - 4ac$, whose sign gives the number of real solutions |
| **Double root** | The single real solution obtained when the discriminant is zero |
| **Extraneous root** | A gained root, produced by squaring both sides or multiplying both sides by an expression |
| **Zeros of a function** | The $x$-intercepts, the real values at which the function is zero |

# 8.2 Statistics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Variables

The characteristics recorded about each individual are called **variables**. Statistics begins by sorting them into two kinds, because the kind decides what displays and summaries are available.

| Kind | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Categorical variable** | Variables that name categories and answer questions about how cases fall into those categories |
| **Quantitative variable** | Measured variables that answer questions about the quantity of what is measured |

## Tabular display

Building a frequency table from quantitative data goes in three steps:

1. Determine the number of nonoverlapping classes.
2. Find the approximate class width, $\text{approximate class width} = \dfrac{\text{largest value} - \text{smallest value}}{\text{number of classes}}$.
3. Determine the class limits.

The classes must be nonoverlapping so that every observation falls into exactly one of them.

## Graphical displays

| Display | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dot plot** | A simple graphical summary of data with a horizontal axis showing the range for the data and dots showing frequency |
| **Histogram** | A common graphical display of quantitative data, with ranges of values instead of values as the horizontal axis |
| **Stem-and-leaf plot** | A graphical display used to show simultaneously the rank order and the shape of a distribution of data |
| **Boxplot** | A graphic displaying the 5-number summary as a central box with whiskers that extend to the non-outlying data values |

The histogram is the display that follows on from the tabular display above: its horizontal axis carries the classes, which is what "ranges of values instead of values" means.

## Reading a boxplot

The ends of the box are located at the first and third quartile, and a segment is drawn in the box at the location of the median.

The whiskers and the outlier marks are set using the **interquartile range**, a measure of variability that overcomes the dependency on extreme values:

$$\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$$

The limits are located at $1.5(\text{IQR})$ below $Q_1$ and $1.5(\text{IQR})$ above $Q_3$.

**Whiskers** are horizontal lines extending from each end of the box, drawn from the ends of the box to the smallest and largest values inside the limits. The location of each outlier is shown with a small asterisk.

So the whiskers stop at real data values, not at the limits themselves — the limits only decide which values count as non-outlying.

## Measures of centre and position

The **median** is a measure of central location: the value in the middle when the data is arranged in ascending order.

**Quartiles** divide the data set into four parts, with each part containing approximately one-fourth of the observations. Just as the median divides a set of data into two equal parts, a quartile divides each part in half.

## Measures of spread

The **range** is the difference between the maximum and minimum values.

The **variance** is a measure of variability that utilises all the data, based on the difference between the value of each observation $x_i$ and the mean:

$$\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \mu)^2}{N} \qquad \text{(population variance)}$$

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1} \qquad \text{(sample variance)}$$

The **standard deviation** is the positive square root of the variance.

Note the contrast with the range and the IQR. The range uses only the two extreme values; the IQR is chosen precisely because it overcomes the dependency on extreme values; the variance, by design, utilises all the data.

## Describing a distribution

A distribution is described by three things, in this order:

1. Shape
2. Centre
3. Spread

## Two quantitative variables

When two quantitative variables are measured on the same individuals, they take different roles. The **response variable** is the variable of interest; the **predictor** or **explanatory variable** is the other variable.

A **scatterplot** shows the relationship between two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals. Its overall pattern is described by five things:

1. Direction
2. Form
3. Strength
4. Outliers
5. Correlation

**Correlation** is the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables. The word *linear* limits it: correlation measures one particular form of relationship, which is why form is listed separately from strength.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Variables** | Characteristics recorded about each individual |
| **Categorical variable** | Variables that name categories and answer questions about how cases fall into those categories |
| **Quantitative variable** | Measured variables that answer questions about the quantity of what is measured |
| **Dot plot** | A simple graphical summary of data with a horizontal axis showing the range for the data and dots showing frequency |
| **Histogram** | A common graphical display of quantitative data, with ranges of values instead of values as the horizontal axis |
| **Stem-and-leaf plot** | A graphical display used to show simultaneously the rank order and shape of a distribution of data |
| **Boxplot** | A graphic displaying the 5-number summary as a central box with whiskers that extend to the non-outlying data values |
| **Interquartile range (IQR)** | A measure of variability that overcomes the dependency on extreme values; $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$ |
| **Whiskers** | Horizontal lines extending from each end of the box to the smallest and largest values inside the limits |
| **Median** | A measure of central location; the value in the middle when the data is arranged in ascending order |
| **Quartile** | A division of the data into four parts, each containing approximately one-fourth of the observations |
| **Range** | The difference between the maximum and minimum values |
| **Variance** | A measure of variability that utilises all the data, based on the difference between the value of each observation and the mean |
| **Standard deviation** | The positive square root of the variance |
| **Response variable** | The variable of interest |
| **Predictor (explanatory) variable** | The other variable in a two-variable analysis |
| **Scatterplot** | A display showing the relationship between two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals |
| **Correlation** | The direction and strength of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables |

# 8.3 Drawings, Nets, and Other Models

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Representing a solid on paper

A three-dimensional figure has to be flattened before it can be drawn, and there are several ways of doing it. Each keeps different information.

| Model | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Isometric drawing** | A drawing of a figure from a corner view |
| **Orthographic drawing** | A drawing showing a front, right, and top view |
| **Foundation drawing** | A drawing showing the layout of the structure and the dimensions of each part |
| **Net** | A two-dimensional shape that you can fold to form a three-dimensional figure |

## What each one is for

The isometric drawing is the one that looks like the object: taken from a corner, it shows three faces at once.

The orthographic drawing gives up that single picture in exchange for accuracy, splitting the figure into three straight-on views. Nothing is foreshortened in any of them, so measurements can be read off directly.

The foundation drawing records the plan of the structure together with the dimensions of each part, so it carries the numbers rather than the appearance.

A net is different in kind from the other three. It is not a view of the figure but the figure unrolled — a flat shape that folds up into the solid — which is what makes nets the natural tool for surface area, since the surface of the solid is laid out flat with no piece hidden.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Isometric drawing** | A drawing of a figure from a corner view |
| **Orthographic drawing** | A drawing showing a front, right, and top view |
| **Foundation drawing** | A drawing showing the layout of the structure and the dimensions of each part |
| **Net** | A two-dimensional shape that you can fold to form a 3D figure |

# 8.4 Space Figures and Cross Sections

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Polyhedra

A **polyhedron** is a three-dimensional figure whose surfaces are polygons. Each polygon is a **face** of the polyhedron.

An **edge** is a segment that is formed by the intersection of two faces. A **vertex** is a point where three or more edges intersect.

The three terms sit in a hierarchy: faces are the flat pieces, edges are where two faces meet, and vertices are where edges meet.

## Euler's Formula

The numbers of faces $F$, vertices $V$, and edges $E$ of a polyhedron are related by

$$F + V = E + 2$$

In two dimensions, Euler's Formula reduces to

$$F + V = E + 1$$

## Cross sections

A **cross section** is the intersection of a solid and a plane. Because it is an intersection, the cross section is a plane figure, and which figure it is depends on where and at what angle the plane cuts the solid.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polyhedron** | A 3-dimensional figure where surfaces are polygons |
| **Face** | Each polygon making up the surface of a polyhedron |
| **Edge** | A segment that is formed by the intersection of two faces |
| **Vertex** | A point where 3 or more edges intersect |
| **Euler's Formula** | $F + V = E + 2$ for a polyhedron; in two dimensions it reduces to $F + V = E + 1$ |
| **Cross section** | The intersection of a solid and a plane |

# 8.5 Surface Areas of Prisms and Cylinders

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Prisms

A **prism** is a polyhedron with exactly two congruent, parallel faces, called **bases**. The other faces are **lateral faces**. Prisms are named by the shape of their bases, so a prism with triangular bases is a triangular prism.

The **lateral area** of a prism is the sum of the areas of the lateral faces. The **surface area** is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the two bases.

## Cylinders

A **cylinder** has two congruent parallel bases, which are circles. Unrolling the curved face results in the lateral area, and the surface area is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the two circular bases.

The word "unrolling" is the key to the formula below. Flattened out, the curved face becomes a rectangle whose one side is the height and whose other side is the circumference of the base.

## Altitude and height

An **altitude** of a prism or of a cylinder is a perpendicular segment that joins the planes of the bases. The **height** $h$ of the prism or cylinder is the length of an altitude.

## The formulas

For a **right prism**, the lateral area is the product of the perimeter of the base and the height, and the surface area is the sum of the lateral area and the areas of the bases:

$$L.A. = ph$$

$$S.A. = L.A. + 2B$$

For a **right cylinder**, the lateral area is the product of the circumference of the base and the height, and the surface area is the sum of the lateral area and the areas of the two bases:

$$L.A. = \pi d h = 2\pi r h$$

$$S.A. = 2B + L.A.$$

The two are the same formula in different clothing. In each case the lateral area is (distance round the base) $\times$ (height) — perimeter for a prism, circumference for a cylinder — and in each case the $2B$ accounts for the two bases the solid has.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Prism** | A polyhedron with exactly two congruent, parallel faces, called bases |
| **Lateral face** | A face of a prism other than a base |
| **Lateral area of a prism** | The sum of the areas of the lateral faces |
| **Surface area** | The sum of the lateral area and the area of the bases |
| **Cylinder** | A solid with two congruent parallel bases, which are circles |
| **Altitude of a prism or cylinder** | A perpendicular segment that joins the planes of the bases |
| **Height $h$** | The length of an altitude |

# 8.6 Surface Areas of Pyramids and Cones

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Pyramids

A **pyramid** is a polyhedron in which the base can be any polygon and the other faces are triangles that meet at a common vertex.

The **altitude** is the perpendicular segment from the vertex to the plane of the base, and the length of the altitude is the **height** $h$. The **slant height** $l$ is the length of the altitude of a lateral face of a pyramid.

These two lengths are easy to confuse. The height runs from the apex straight down to the plane of the base, inside the solid; the slant height runs from the apex down the middle of a triangular face to the edge of the base.

A **regular pyramid** is a pyramid whose base is a regular polygon and whose lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles. The congruence of the lateral faces is what makes a single slant height enough to describe all of them, and it is why the lateral-area formula below can use one value of $l$.

$$L.A. = \tfrac{1}{2} P l$$

$$S.A. = L.A. + B$$

Here $P$ is the perimeter of the base and $B$ the area of the base. The lateral area is a sum of triangle areas: each lateral face has area $\tfrac{1}{2} \times (\text{its base edge}) \times l$, and adding them over the whole base gives $\tfrac{1}{2} P l$.

## Cones

A **cone** is a solid figure with a circular base that tapers to a single point. In a **right cone**, the altitude, height, and slant height $l$ are the same as for a pyramid.

$$L.A. = \pi r l$$

$$S.A. = L.A. + B$$

## Comparing the two

| Solid | Lateral area | Surface area |
|---|---|---|
| Regular pyramid | $\tfrac{1}{2} P l$ | $L.A. + B$ |
| Right cone | $\pi r l$ | $L.A. + B$ |

The cone formula is the pyramid formula in the limit: replacing the perimeter $P$ of the base with the circumference $2\pi r$ of the circular base turns $\tfrac{1}{2} P l$ into $\tfrac{1}{2}(2\pi r) l = \pi r l$. And unlike a prism or a cylinder, a pyramid and a cone each have only one base, so the surface area adds a single $B$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Pyramid** | A polyhedron in which the base can be any polygon and the other faces are triangles that meet at a common vertex |
| **Altitude of a pyramid** | The perpendicular segment from the vertex to the plane of the base |
| **Height $h$** | The length of the altitude |
| **Slant height $l$** | The length of the altitude of a lateral face of a pyramid |
| **Regular pyramid** | A pyramid whose base is a regular polygon and whose lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles |
| **Cone** | A figure with a circular base that tapers to a single point |
| **Right cone** | A cone in which the altitude, height, and slant height $l$ are the same as for a pyramid |
