# 1.1 Sets and Venn Diagrams

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definitions

A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right. The second half of that phrase is what makes set theory useful: once a collection is treated as a single object, it can be combined with other sets, compared with them, and counted.

An **element**, or **member**, is an object that makes up the set.

The **empty set**, or **null set**, is a set that does not contain any elements.

## Symbols and operations

| Symbol | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $A \cap B$ | **Intersection** | The set containing elements common to both set $A$ and set $B$ |
| $A \cup B$ | **Union** | The set containing all elements of $A$ and $B$ |
| $\lvert A \rvert$ | **Cardinality** | The number of elements in the set $A$ |
| $x \in A$ | **Element** | Set $A$ contains the element $x$; reads "$x$ is an element of $A$" |
| $x \notin A$ | **Not an element** | Set $A$ does not contain $x$; reads "$x$ is not an element of $A$" |
| $A \subset B$, $A \subseteq B$ | **Subset** | Every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| $B \supset A$, $B \supseteq A$ | **Superset** | Every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| $A'$ | **Complement** | The set of elements in the universal set that are not in $A$ |
| $A - B$ | **Difference** | The set of all elements which are in $A$ but not in $B$ |

The two subset symbols are not interchangeable. $A \subset B$ means $A$ is a **proper subset** of $B$, so $B$ has elements not in $A$, while $A \subseteq B$ can also mean $A$ equals $B$.

**Superset** is the opposite of subset, in which the second set is a subset of the first set and not the other way around.

On notation for the complement: textbooks also denote it as a bar on top of the name of the set, but that cannot be entered on a computer, so the prime is used here instead.

The difference can also be defined through operations. For a set $C$,

$$C = A - B \quad \text{when for every } n \in C,\ n \in A,\ n \notin B$$

or, in set-builder form,

$$C = \{n \mid n \in A,\ n \notin B\}$$

## Laws of sets

For sets $A$, $B$ and $C$:

**1. Commutative laws**

$$A \cup B = B \cup A \quad \text{(union of sets)}$$
$$A \cap B = B \cap A \quad \text{(intersection of sets)}$$

**2. Associative laws**

$$(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$$
$$(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)$$

**3. Distributive laws**

$$A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$$
$$A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$$

Note that each operation distributes over the other — unlike arithmetic, where multiplication distributes over addition but not the reverse.

**4. Identity laws**

$$A \cup \emptyset = A \quad \text{(the empty set is the identity element for union)}$$
$$A \cap U = A \quad \text{(the universal set is the identity for intersection)}$$

**5. Complement laws**

$$A \cup A' = U \quad \text{(union of a set and its complement is the universal set)}$$
$$A \cap A' = \emptyset \quad \text{(intersection of a set and its complement is an empty set)}$$

**6. Idempotent laws**

$$A \cup A = A \qquad A \cap A = A$$

**7. Null laws**

$$A \cup U = U \quad \text{(a union with the universal set is the universal set)}$$
$$A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset \quad \text{(an intersection with an empty set is an empty set)}$$

**8. Absorption laws**

$$A \cup (A \cap B) = A \qquad A \cap (A \cup B) = A$$

**9. Difference law**

$$A - B = A \cap B' \quad \text{(the difference of } A \text{ and } B \text{ is the intersection of } A \text{ and the complement of } B)$$

**10. De Morgan's laws** — flagged in the guide as the ones to know:

$$(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$$
$$(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$$

Taking the complement swaps union and intersection. This is the law that lets you push a complement inwards through an expression.

## Venn diagrams

A **Venn diagram** is a diagram that shows all possible logical relations between a finite collection of different sets. Each set is represented by a **circle**, usually inside a rectangular field representing the universal set.

## Counting formulas

$$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$$

$$n(A') = n(U) - n(A) \quad \text{— the number of elements not in set } A$$

The first formula subtracts $n(A \cap B)$ because the elements in both sets were counted twice, once in $n(A)$ and once in $n(B)$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Set** | A collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right |
| **Element / member** | An object that makes up the set |
| **Empty set (null set)** | A set that does not contain any elements |
| **Intersection** | $A \cap B$, the set containing elements common to both $A$ and $B$ |
| **Union** | $A \cup B$, the set containing all elements of $A$ and $B$ |
| **Cardinality** | $\lvert A \rvert$, the number of elements in the set $A$ |
| **Subset** | $A$ is a subset of $B$ if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| **Proper subset** | $A \subset B$, where $B$ has elements not in $A$ |
| **Superset** | $B$ is a superset of $A$ if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| **Complement** | $A'$, the set of elements in the universal set that are not in $A$ |
| **Difference** | $A - B$, the set of all elements which are in $A$ but not in $B$ |
| **De Morgan's laws** | $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$ |
| **Venn diagram** | A diagram that shows all possible logical relations between a finite collection of different sets |

# 1.2 Inductive and Deductive Reasoning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two kinds of logical thinking run in opposite directions, and knowing which one an argument uses tells you how much its conclusion is worth.

## Inductive reasoning

**Inductive reasoning** is a type of logical thinking that involves forming generalisations based on specific incidents you have experienced, observations you have made, or facts you know to be true or false.

It moves from the particular to the general. Because the conclusion covers cases that were never examined, it goes beyond the evidence that produced it.

## Deductive reasoning

**Deductive reasoning** is a type of logical thinking where you start with a general fact, rule, or premise and then deduce or infer certain specific details or conclusions.

It moves in the reverse direction, from the general to the particular. The conclusion is already contained in the premise, which is why deduction is the mode of reasoning used for proof.

## Comparison

| | Starts from | Arrives at |
|---|---|---|
| **Inductive reasoning** | Specific incidents, observations, or facts | A generalisation |
| **Deductive reasoning** | A general fact, rule, or premise | Specific details or conclusions |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inductive reasoning** | A type of logical thinking that involves forming generalisations based on specific incidents experienced, observations made, or facts known to be true or false |
| **Deductive reasoning** | A type of logical thinking where you start with a general fact, rule, or premise and then deduce or infer certain specific details or conclusions |

# 1.3 Logic Statements

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Deductive reasoning needs something precise to reason about. A logic statement supplies it: a sentence stripped down until the only thing that matters about it is whether it is true.

## Propositions

A **proposition**, also known as a **statement**, is a declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both. The two halves of that condition do equal work — a sentence that is neither (a question, a command) is not a proposition, and neither is one that could be both.

A **compound proposition** is a combination of two or more propositions using logical operators. They include conjunctions, disjunctions, implications, and biconditionals.

## The logical operators

| Operator | Symbol | True when |
|---|---|---|
| **Conjunction** | $p \wedge q$ | Both $p$ and $q$ are true |
| **Disjunction** | $p \vee q$ | Either $p$ or $q$ is true |
| **Negation** | $\neg p$ (or ${\sim} p$) | $p$ is false |
| **Conditional (implication)** | $p \to q$ | Always, except when $p$ is true and $q$ is false |
| **Biconditional** | $p \leftrightarrow q$ (or $p \equiv q$) | $p$ and $q$ have the same truth values |

A **conjunction** is a compound proposition that uses the logical operator AND. For the conjunction $p \wedge q$ to be true, both $p$ and $q$ must be true.

A **disjunction** is a compound proposition that uses the logical operator OR. For the disjunction $p \vee q$, it is enough for either $p$ or $q$ to be true for the entire disjunction to be true. Set against the conjunction, this is what makes OR the weaker demand of the two: AND requires everything, OR requires only something.

The **negation** of a proposition $p$ is not $p$, denoted as ${\sim} p$ or $\neg p$. If $p$ is true, then $\neg p$ is false, and vice versa.

A **conditional statement**, or **implication**, is a compound proposition of the form if $p$ then $q$, represented as $p \to q$. It is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false; otherwise it is true. The asymmetry matters: an implication makes no claim at all about what happens when $p$ is false, so it cannot be broken by such a case.

A **biconditional statement** of the form $p$ if and only if $q$ is true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth values, and false when they are different. It is represented as $p \leftrightarrow q$ or $p \equiv q$.

## Classifying a compound proposition

Once a compound proposition is built, it can be sorted by how it behaves across every possible assignment of truth values to the propositions inside it.

A **contradiction** is a compound proposition that is always false regardless of the truth values of the individual propositions that constitute it.

A **contingency** is a compound proposition that could be either true or false depending on the truth values of its constituent propositions.

A proposition is **satisfiable** if there is at least one assignment of truth values to its variables that makes it true. A contradiction is therefore exactly the case that satisfiability rules out, while every contingency is satisfiable by definition — there is an assignment making it true, and another making it false.

## Sufficient and necessary

**Sufficient:** when given $A$, we can know $B$, then $A$ is sufficient for $B$.

**Necessary:** when given $A$, we can know $B$, then $B$ is necessary for $A$.

Both definitions start from the same situation — knowing $A$ lets you conclude $B$ — and differ only in which proposition is being described. That single situation is the conditional $A \to B$, so "$A$ is sufficient for $B$" and "$B$ is necessary for $A$" are two readings of one arrow, taken from opposite ends.

## Converse, inverse and contrapositive

In a conditional statement of the form if $p$ then $q$, also written as $p \to q$, there are different forms created by switching or negating the hypothesis and conclusion.

| Form | Statement | Symbols | Formed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original | If $p$ then $q$ | $p \to q$ | — |
| **Converse** | If $q$ then $p$ | $q \to p$ | Switching the hypothesis and the conclusion |
| **Inverse** | If not $p$ then not $q$ | $\neg p \to \neg q$ | Negating both the hypothesis and conclusion |
| **Contrapositive** | If not $q$ then not $p$ | $\neg q \to \neg p$ | Both switching and negating the hypothesis and conclusion |

In terms of the truth values, there are certain relationships that always hold true.

A statement and its contrapositive are **logically equivalent**. This means that they are both either true or false. If if $p$ then $q$ is true, then if not $q$ then not $p$ is also true, and vice versa.

Similarly, a converse and an inverse are logically equivalent. This means that they are both either true or false. If if $q$ then $p$ is true, then if not $p$ then not $q$ is also true, and vice versa.

The second equivalence is the first one applied a second time. Take the converse $q \to p$ and form its contrapositive by switching and negating: the result is $\neg p \to \neg q$, which is the inverse. So the converse and inverse stand in exactly the relationship that the first rule already declared equivalent.

The practical use is that a conditional you cannot prove directly can be replaced by its contrapositive, which says the same thing; but it cannot be replaced by its converse or its inverse, which are a different pair.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Proposition (statement)** | A declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both |
| **Compound proposition** | A combination of two or more propositions using logical operators |
| **Conjunction** | A compound proposition using AND; $p \wedge q$ is true only when both $p$ and $q$ are true |
| **Disjunction** | A compound proposition using OR; $p \vee q$ is true when either $p$ or $q$ is true |
| **Negation** | Not $p$, denoted ${\sim} p$ or $\neg p$; false when $p$ is true and true when $p$ is false |
| **Conditional statement (implication)** | If $p$ then $q$, written $p \to q$; false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false |
| **Biconditional statement** | $p$ if and only if $q$, written $p \leftrightarrow q$ or $p \equiv q$; true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth values |
| **Contradiction** | A compound proposition that is always false regardless of the truth values of its constituent propositions |
| **Contingency** | A compound proposition that could be either true or false depending on the truth values of its constituent propositions |
| **Satisfiability** | A proposition is satisfiable if at least one assignment of truth values to its variables makes it true |
| **Sufficient** | When given $A$ we can know $B$, then $A$ is sufficient for $B$ |
| **Necessary** | When given $A$ we can know $B$, then $B$ is necessary for $A$ |
| **Converse** | The converse of if $p$ then $q$ is if $q$ then $p$, formed by switching hypothesis and conclusion |
| **Inverse** | The inverse of if $p$ then $q$ is if not $p$ then not $q$, formed by negating both |
| **Contrapositive** | The contrapositive of if $p$ then $q$ is if not $q$ then not $p$, formed by switching and negating |
| **Logically equivalent** | Two statements that are both either true or false together |

# 1.4 Geometric Theorems and Postulates

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

These are the results the rest of the geometry rests on. They are worth learning as statements rather than as pictures, because a proof cites the statement.

## Measuring segments and angles

The **Ruler Postulate** states that the points on a line can be paired with the real numbers in such a way that any given point can always be paired with zero and any other with a positive number. This is what turns a line into something measurable: once its points carry numbers, the distance between two of them is a number too.

The **Segment Addition Postulate** states that if $B$ is between $A$ and $C$, then

$$AB + BC = AC$$

The **Protractor Postulate** states that, considering $OA$ and $OB$ to be opposite rays in a plane, we can measure angles $AOB$ for every rotation about point $O$.

The **Angle Addition Postulate** states that if point $B$ lies in the interior of $\angle AOC$, then

$$\angle AOB + \angle BOC = \angle AOC$$

The four come in two matched pairs. The Ruler and Protractor Postulates say that lengths and angles can be measured at all; the two Addition Postulates then say that those measures behave additively when one figure is split into two. The condition attached to each addition rule is what guarantees the split is genuine — "between" for the segment, "in the interior of" for the angle.

## The Parallel Postulate

The **Parallel Postulate** (Euclidean geometry) states that given a line and a point not on the line, there is exactly one line through the point that is parallel to the given line.

The guide marks this one as belonging to Euclidean geometry specifically, which is a reminder that it is an assumption rather than a consequence of the others.

## Angle relationships

| Result | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Vertical Angles Theorem** | Vertical angles are always congruent |
| **Linear Pair Postulate** | If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary — their sum is $180^\circ$ |
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the pairs of corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the alternate interior angles are congruent |

The last two share a hypothesis: two parallel lines cut by a transversal. That configuration is the standard source of equal angles in a diagram, and either result can be quoted from it.

## Triangle results

The **Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem** states that the sum of the interior angles in any triangle is $180^\circ$. It is the starting point of the triangle work in 2.1.

The **Isosceles Triangle Theorem** states that if two sides of a triangle are congruent — that is, the triangle is isosceles — then the angles opposite those sides are congruent. It reappears with its converse in 2.3.

## The converses

The converses of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem, the Corresponding Angles Postulate and the other parallel lines theorems and postulates all hold up.

This doubles what the parallel-line results are worth. Read forwards, they take parallel lines and hand you congruent angles. Read backwards, they take congruent angles and let you conclude that the lines are parallel — which is how parallelism gets proved rather than assumed.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ruler Postulate** | The points on a line can be paired with the real numbers so that any given point can be paired with zero and any other with a positive number |
| **Segment Addition Postulate** | If $B$ is between $A$ and $C$, then $AB + BC = AC$ |
| **Protractor Postulate** | Taking $OA$ and $OB$ as opposite rays in a plane, angles $AOB$ can be measured for every rotation about $O$ |
| **Angle Addition Postulate** | If $B$ lies in the interior of $\angle AOC$, then $\angle AOB + \angle BOC = \angle AOC$ |
| **Parallel Postulate** | Given a line and a point not on the line, there is exactly one line through the point parallel to the given line (Euclidean geometry) |
| **Vertical Angles Theorem** | Vertical angles are always congruent |
| **Linear Pair Postulate** | If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary, their sum being $180^\circ$ |
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the pairs of corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the alternate interior angles are congruent |
| **Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem** | The sum of the interior angles in any triangle is $180^\circ$ |
| **Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent |

# 2.1 Concept and Properties of Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Every result in this unit rests on a single fact about how the three angles of a triangle fit together. Once that is fixed, the behaviour of the exterior angles follows from it without any new assumptions.

## The angle sum

The **triangle angle-sum theorem** states that in a triangle, the sum of all three angles is $180^\circ$. For $\triangle ABC$,

$$m\angle A + m\angle B + m\angle C = 180^\circ$$

This is the constraint that makes triangles rigid in the angular sense: fix two angles and the third is forced.

## Exterior angles

An exterior angle is formed by extending one side of the triangle. The two interior angles that do not share a vertex with it are its **remote interior angles**.

The **triangle exterior angle theorem** states that the measure of each exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the measures of its two remote interior angles. If the exterior angle at $C$ is $\angle 1$, then

$$m\angle 1 = m\angle A + m\angle B$$

From this the **corollary to the triangle exterior angle theorem** follows at once: the measure of each exterior angle of a triangle is greater than the measure of any remote interior angle. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, and both of those are genuine angles of a triangle, so the sum must exceed either one on its own.

## The exterior angle sum

The **triangle exterior angle-sum theorem** states that the sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a triangle is $360^\circ$ — one exterior angle taken at each vertex. Each exterior angle is the supplement of its interior angle, so the three of them together account for $3 \times 180^\circ = 540^\circ$ minus the interior angle sum of $180^\circ$.

$$m\angle 1 + m\angle 2 + m\angle 3 = 360^\circ$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Triangle angle-sum theorem** | In a triangle, the sum of all three angles is $180^\circ$ |
| **Triangle exterior angle theorem** | The measure of each exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the measures of its two remote interior angles |
| **Corollary to the triangle exterior angle theorem** | The measure of each exterior angle of a triangle is greater than the measure of any remote interior angle |
| **Triangle exterior angle-sum theorem** | The sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a triangle is $360^\circ$ |
| **Remote interior angles** | The two interior angles of a triangle that do not lie at the vertex of a given exterior angle |

# 2.2 Congruent Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Congruence is the strongest relationship two figures can have short of being the same figure: same size, same shape, differing only in position.

## Congruent figures

**Congruent figures** have the same size and shape, and can exactly fit each other when moved. They are produced through **translation**, **rotation** and **reflection** — the motions that reposition a figure without distorting it. Congruence of triangles is denoted

$$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle A'B'C'$$

The order of the letters carries information: it names which vertex corresponds to which.

## CPCTC

Once a congruence is established, everything about the two triangles matches up: **corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent**, abbreviated **CPCTC**. This is what makes congruence useful in proof — it is the step that converts a statement about whole triangles into statements about individual sides and angles.

## Triangle congruence criteria

A triangle has six parts, but three of them, correctly chosen, are enough to force congruence.

| Criterion | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SSS** | Side–side–side |
| **SAS** | Side–angle–side |
| **ASA** | Angle–side–angle |
| **AAS** | Angle–angle–side |
| **HL** | Hypotenuse–leg |

The **HL** criterion applies to right triangles: the hypotenuse and one leg determine the triangle.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Congruent figures** | Figures that have the same size and shape, and can exactly fit each other when moved |
| **CPCTC** | Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent |
| **SSS** | Side–side–side triangle congruence |
| **ASA** | Angle–side–angle triangle congruence |
| **AAS** | Angle–angle–side triangle congruence |
| **SAS** | Side–angle–side triangle congruence |
| **HL** | Hypotenuse–leg triangle congruence |

# 2.3 Special Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Three families of triangle carry extra structure: isosceles, equilateral and right. Each has its own vocabulary and its own theorems, and each set of theorems comes with a converse worth learning separately, because in proof you usually need the direction that turns a measurement back into a classification.

## Isosceles triangles

An isosceles triangle has two congruent sides. The vocabulary is specific:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Leg** | Either of the congruent sides |
| **Base** | The third side |
| **Vertex angle** | The angle formed by the two congruent sides |
| **Base angles** | The angles formed by the base and a leg |

The **isosceles triangle theorem** says that in $\triangle ABC$, if $AB = AC$, then $\angle B = \angle C$. Congruent legs force congruent base angles.

The **converse of the isosceles triangle theorem** runs the other way: in $\triangle ABC$, if $\angle B = \angle C$, then $AB = AC$. This is the version that lets you prove a triangle is isosceles from angle information alone.

There is also a coincidence of lines that does a great deal of work in proofs. **Property of isosceles triangles:** in an isosceles triangle, the angle bisector of its vertex angle and the perpendicular bisector of its base are the same line. One construction therefore delivers two facts at once.

## Perpendicular bisectors

The **perpendicular bisector theorem** states that a point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment.

Its **converse** states that if a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of that segment. Together the two say that "equidistant from the endpoints" and "on the perpendicular bisector" describe exactly the same set of points — which is why the perpendicular bisector reappears in 2.5 as the tool for locating a point equidistant from three vertices.

## Equilateral triangles

An **equilateral triangle** is a triangle with three congruent interior angles. Equivalently, it is an isosceles triangle with an interior angle of $60^\circ$ — because once one angle of an isosceles triangle is $60^\circ$, the angle sum leaves no room for the other two to be anything else.

An equilateral triangle has the same properties as isosceles triangles; it simply has them with respect to all three choices of "base".

## Right triangles

In a right triangle the side opposite the right angle is the **hypotenuse**, and it is the longest side in $\triangle ABC$.

The **Pythagorean theorem**: in $\mathrm{Rt}\triangle ABC$ with $m\angle C = 90^\circ$,

$$AC^2 + BC^2 = AB^2$$

The **converse of the Pythagorean theorem**: if $AC^2 + BC^2 = AB^2$, then $m\angle C = 90^\circ$.

**Property of right triangles:** in $\mathrm{Rt}\triangle ABC$ with $m\angle C = 90^\circ$, if $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$, then

$$CD = \tfrac{1}{2}AB$$

The median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse.

**30–60–90 right triangles:** in $\mathrm{Rt}\triangle ABC$ with $m\angle C = 90^\circ$, if $m\angle A = 30^\circ$, then $BC = \tfrac{1}{2}AB$, and the three sides stand in the ratio

$$BC : AB : AC = 1 : 2 : \sqrt{3}$$

## Angle bisectors

The **angle bisector theorem** states that a point on the angle bisector is equidistant from both sides of the angle.

Its **converse** states that if a point is equidistant from both sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector. This pair mirrors the perpendicular bisector pair exactly — one characterises distance to two points, the other distance to two lines.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Leg** (isosceles) | A congruent side of an isosceles triangle |
| **Base** | The third side of an isosceles triangle |
| **Vertex angle** | The angle formed by two congruent sides |
| **Base angles** | The angles formed by the base and a leg |
| **Isosceles triangle theorem** | In $\triangle ABC$, if $AB = AC$, then $\angle B = \angle C$ |
| **Converse of the isosceles triangle theorem** | In $\triangle ABC$, if $\angle B = \angle C$, then $AB = AC$ |
| **Property of isosceles triangles** | In an isosceles triangle, the angle bisector of the vertex angle and the perpendicular bisector of the base are the same line |
| **Perpendicular bisector theorem** | A point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment |
| **Converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem** | If a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of that segment |
| **Equilateral triangle** | A triangle with three congruent interior angles; an isosceles triangle with an interior angle of $60^\circ$ |
| **Hypotenuse** | The longest side of a right triangle |
| **Pythagorean theorem** | In $\mathrm{Rt}\triangle ABC$ with $m\angle C = 90^\circ$, $AC^2 + BC^2 = AB^2$ |
| **Converse of the Pythagorean theorem** | If $AC^2 + BC^2 = AB^2$, then $m\angle C = 90^\circ$ |
| **Angle bisector theorem** | A point on the angle bisector is equidistant from both sides of the angle |
| **Converse of the angle bisector theorem** | If a point is equidistant from both sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector |

# 2.4 Inequalities in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Congruence answers when two triangles are the same. Inequality answers a prior question: which triples of lengths are triangles at all, and, once they are, which side is longest.

## Segment inequality

Given three distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$,

$$AC + CB \geq AB$$

with equality exactly when $C$ is on segment $AB$. Detouring through a third point is never shorter than going directly, and it is equally short only when the detour is not a detour.

## Triangle inequality

In $\triangle ABC$ with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, any two sides together exceed the third:

$$a + b > c, \qquad b + c > a, \qquad a + c > b$$

Equivalently, each side is trapped between the sum and the difference of the other two:

$$|a - b| < c < a + b$$

**Corollary to the triangle inequality.** If the perimeter of a triangle is $p$ and the longest side is $c$, then

$$\frac{p}{3} \leq c < \frac{p}{2}$$

The lower bound holds because $c$ is the longest of three sides summing to $p$; the upper bound holds because the other two sides sum to $p - c$, and the triangle inequality demands $p - c > c$.

## Determining the shape of a triangle

Given three sides of $\triangle ABC$ equal to $a$, $b$, $c$ where $c$ is the longest side, comparing $c^2$ against $a^2 + b^2$ classifies the triangle:

| Comparison | Shape |
|---|---|
| $c^2 > a^2 + b^2$ | Obtuse |
| $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$ | Right |
| $c^2 < a^2 + b^2$ | Acute |

The middle line is the converse of the Pythagorean theorem; the other two are what happens when the largest angle opens past or falls short of a right angle.

## Sides against angles

In $\triangle ABC$,

$$\angle A > \angle B \iff BC > AC$$

The larger angle lies opposite the longer side, and this holds in both directions — so an ordering of the sides gives you an ordering of the angles for free, and vice versa.

## Hinge theorem

The **hinge theorem** compares two triangles that agree on two sides. In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle A'B'C'$, if $AB = A'B'$, $BC = B'C'$ and $\angle B > \angle B'$, then

$$AC > A'C'$$

Two fixed sides behave like the arms of a hinge: widening the angle between them widens the gap they span.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Segment inequality** | For three distinct points, $AC + CB \geq AB$, with equality exactly when $C$ is on segment $AB$ |
| **Triangle inequality** | In $\triangle ABC$ with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, the sum of any two sides exceeds the third: $|a-b| < c < a+b$ |
| **Corollary to the triangle inequality** | If the perimeter is $p$ and the longest side is $c$, then $\frac{p}{3} \leq c < \frac{p}{2}$ |
| **Hinge theorem** | In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle A'B'C'$, if $AB = A'B'$, $BC = B'C'$ and $\angle B > \angle B'$, then $AC > A'C'$ |

# 2.5 Centres in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A triangle has no single centre. It has several, each produced by a different family of lines, and each with its own distance property.

## Concurrency

If lines intersect at a point $P$, they are **concurrent lines**, and $P$ is the **point of concurrency**. Every centre below exists because a particular set of three lines turns out to be concurrent rather than forming a small triangle of its own.

## Circumcentre

The **circumcentre**, written $O$, is the point where the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle intersect.

Because a point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from that segment's endpoints, a point lying on all three perpendicular bisectors is equidistant from all three vertices. The circumcentre of a triangle is therefore equidistant from the three vertices of the triangle, and it is the centre of the **circumscribed circle** — the circle through all three vertices. Its radius is denoted $R$.

## Incentre

The **incentre**, written $I$, is the point where the angle bisectors of a triangle intersect.

The angle bisector theorem gives the parallel argument: a point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the two sides of that angle, so a point on all three bisectors is equidistant from all three sides. The incentre of a triangle is equidistant from the three sides, and it is the centre of the **inscribed circle** — the circle touching all three sides. Its radius is denoted $r$.

Note the contrast worth keeping straight: the circumcentre measures distance to **vertices**, the incentre distance to **sides**.

## Excentre

The **excentre** is the point where the angle bisectors of two exterior angles of a triangle intersect with the angle bisector of the third interior angle. It is the centre of a circle **escribed** about the triangle.

## Orthocentre

The **orthocentre**, written $H$, is the point where the altitudes of a triangle intersect.

## Centroid

The **centroid**, written $G$, is the point where the medians of a triangle intersect. It divides each median in a fixed ratio: the distance from the centroid to a vertex is two times the distance from the centroid to the midpoint of the corresponding side.

$$AG = 2 \cdot GM$$

where $M$ is the midpoint of the side opposite $A$ — that is, the centroid sits two-thirds of the way along each median from the vertex.

## Summary

| Centre | Symbol | Concurrent lines | Distance property |
|---|---|---|---|
| Circumcentre | $O$ | Perpendicular bisectors | Equidistant from the three vertices; centre of the circumscribed circle, radius $R$ |
| Incentre | $I$ | Angle bisectors | Equidistant from the three sides; centre of the inscribed circle, radius $r$ |
| Excentre | — | Bisectors of two exterior angles and the third interior angle | Centre of an escribed circle |
| Orthocentre | $H$ | Altitudes | — |
| Centroid | $G$ | Medians | Distance to a vertex is twice the distance to the opposite midpoint |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Concurrent lines** | Lines that intersect at a single point $P$ |
| **Point of concurrency** | The point $P$ at which concurrent lines meet |
| **Circumcentre** | The point where the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle intersect; equidistant from the three vertices |
| **Circumscribed circle** | The circle centred at the circumcentre passing through the vertices, with radius $R$ |
| **Incentre** | The point where the angle bisectors of a triangle intersect; equidistant from the three sides |
| **Inscribed circle** | The circle centred at the incentre touching the three sides, with radius $r$ |
| **Excentre** | The point where the angle bisectors of two exterior angles meet the angle bisector of the third interior angle; the centre of an escribed circle |
| **Orthocentre** | The point where the altitudes of a triangle intersect |
| **Centroid** | The point where the medians of a triangle intersect |

# 3.1 Concepts and Properties of Polygons

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What counts as a polygon

A **polygon** is a closed, planar figure with at least three straight sides, such that no three adjacent points are collinear and edges only intersect at common vertices. Each clause of that definition rules something out: "closed" excludes an open chain of segments, "no three adjacent points collinear" stops a straight side being counted as two, and "edges only intersect at common vertices" forbids a figure whose sides cross one another.

A **diagonal** is a segment that connects two non-adjacent points in a polygon.

## Special polygons

| Type | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Equilateral** | All sides are congruent in length |
| **Equiangular** | All angles are congruent |
| **Regular** | Both equilateral and equiangular |

Regularity requires both conditions because neither implies the other in a general polygon.

## Convex and concave

**Convex polygons** are polygons which have all diagonals inside. **Concave polygons** are polygons that are not convex.

To determine whether a polygon is convex, check if any angle is greater than $180^\circ$; if so, it is concave, otherwise it is convex. A reflex angle is precisely what allows a diagonal to escape the figure.

## Angle sums

**Polygon interior angle-sum theorem.** The sum of the interior angles of an $n$-gon is

$$(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ$$

**Polygon exterior angle-sum theorem.** The sum of the exterior angles of an $n$-gon is

$$360^\circ$$

The exterior sum does not depend on $n$ at all — the same result already seen for triangles in 2.1.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polygon** | A closed, planar figure with three or more straight sides such that no three adjacent points are collinear and edges only intersect at common vertices |
| **Diagonal** | A segment that connects two non-adjacent points in a polygon |
| **Equilateral polygon** | A polygon in which all sides are congruent in length |
| **Equiangular polygon** | A polygon in which all angles are congruent |
| **Regular polygon** | A polygon that is both equilateral and equiangular |
| **Convex polygon** | A polygon which has all diagonals inside |
| **Concave polygon** | A polygon that is not convex |
| **Polygon interior angle-sum theorem** | The sum of the interior angles of an $n$-gon is $(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ$ |
| **Polygon exterior angle-sum theorem** | The sum of the exterior angles of an $n$-gon is $360^\circ$ |

# 3.2 Parallelograms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A **parallelogram** is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel — and, as a consequence, equal.

**Property theorem 1 (definition).** If a quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, then

$$AB \parallel CD, \qquad AD \parallel BC$$

This is the theorem that unpacks the name: it is stated as a property because in a proof you will normally be handed "$ABCD$ is a parallelogram" and need the parallelism, rather than the reverse.

The parallelogram is the parent figure for everything in 3.3. Rectangles, rhombi and squares are all defined as parallelograms with one extra condition imposed, which means every parallelogram property is automatically available for each of them.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Parallelogram** | A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel (and equal) |
| **Parallelogram property theorem 1** | If quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, then $AB \parallel CD$ and $AD \parallel BC$ |

# 3.3 Special Parallelograms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Three figures are built from the parallelogram by adding one condition at a time.

| Figure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | A parallelogram with $90^\circ$ angles |
| **Rhombus** | A parallelogram with equal-length sides |
| **Square** | A parallelogram with $90^\circ$ angles and equal-length sides |

A square is therefore both a rectangle and a rhombus, and inherits every property of each.

## Diagonals

The diagonals are where the three figures separate most sharply, and diagonal facts are usually the fastest route through a problem.

- A **rectangle** has congruent diagonals.
- A **rhombus** has perpendicular diagonals. Because the diagonals cross at right angles, the area is
  $$S = \tfrac{1}{2} d_1 d_2$$
  where $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the lengths of its diagonals.
- A **square** has congruent, perpendicular diagonals, whose lengths are equal to
  $$d = \sqrt{2}\, s$$
  where $s$ is the square's side length. The square combines both diagonal properties because it satisfies both defining conditions.

## Rectangles

**Property theorem 1 (definition).** If quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a rectangle, then

$$\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90^\circ$$

## Rhombi

**Property theorem 1 (definition).** If $ABCD$ is a rhombus, then

$$AB = BC = CD = DA$$

**Property theorem 2.** If $ABCD$ is a rhombus, then, with $O$ the intersection of the diagonals,

$$AC \perp BD, \quad \angle BAO = \angle DAO, \quad \angle ABO = \angle CBO, \quad \angle BCO = \angle DCO, \quad \angle CDO = \angle ADO$$

Each diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angles at the two vertices it joins — which is what you would expect, since each diagonal cuts the rhombus into two isosceles triangles.

**Determination theorem 2.** In parallelogram $ABCD$, if $AC \perp BD$, then $ABCD$ is a rhombus. Note the hypothesis: the figure must already be known to be a parallelogram before perpendicular diagonals are enough.

## Squares

**Property theorem 1 (definition).** If $ABCD$ is a square, then

$$\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad AB = BC = CD = DA$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | A parallelogram with $90^\circ$ angles |
| **Rhombus** | A parallelogram with equal-length sides |
| **Square** | A parallelogram with $90^\circ$ angles and equal-length sides |

# 3.4 Trapezoids

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A **trapezoid** is a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides, called the **bases**; the non-parallel sides are its **legs**. The word "exactly" matters: a figure with two pairs of parallel sides is a parallelogram, not a trapezoid.

A **right trapezoid** is a trapezoid with a right angle.

An **isosceles trapezoid** has congruent legs.

## Theorems

**Property theorem 1 (definition).** If $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid where $AD \parallel BC$, then

$$AB = CD$$

**Determination theorem 2.** In trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AD \parallel BC$, if $\angle B = \angle C$, then $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid. Equal base angles are enough to force equal legs.

## Solving trapezoid problems

A trapezoid has no formula machinery of its own, so the standard technique is to convert it into figures that do.

- **Cut it up.** If the trapezoid is isosceles, cut it into a right triangle and a right trapezoid. The right triangle then carries the Pythagorean theorem and the trigonometry of Chapter 4.
- **Extend the legs to intersect at a point.** The two legs, being non-parallel, must meet if extended. This is very useful for isosceles trapezoids: it embeds the trapezoid in a triangle, and the trapezoid's bases become two parallel cross-sections of that triangle.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Trapezoid** | A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides |
| **Bases** | The parallel sides of a trapezoid |
| **Legs** (trapezoid) | The non-parallel sides of a trapezoid |
| **Right trapezoid** | A trapezoid with a right angle |
| **Isosceles trapezoid** | A trapezoid whose legs are congruent |

# 4.1 Ratios and Proportions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ratios

A **ratio** is a comparison of two quantities. It is expressed as

$$a : b \qquad \text{or} \qquad \frac{a}{b}$$

The two notations carry the same information, but the fractional form is the one that lets you use ordinary algebra on a ratio.

## Proportion properties

A proportion sets two ratios equal. The property that does nearly all the work is cross-multiplication:

$$\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d} \implies ad = bc$$

This converts a statement about ratios, which is awkward to manipulate, into a statement about products, which is not — and it is the step behind every proportional argument in 4.2.

## The golden ratio

The one ratio to note is the **golden ratio**, approximately

$$1.618 \qquad \text{and its reciprocal} \qquad 0.618$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ratio** | A comparison of two quantities, expressed as $a : b$ or $\frac{a}{b}$ |
| **Golden ratio** | The ratio approximately equal to $1.618$, with reciprocal approximately $0.618$ |

markdown:
# 4.2 Similar Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Congruence in Unit 2 demanded same size and same shape. Similarity relaxes the first requirement and keeps the second, which is why its conclusions are equations between ratios rather than between lengths.

## What similarity gives you

If $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$, then the angles match exactly,

$$\angle A = \angle D, \qquad \angle B = \angle E, \qquad \angle C = \angle F$$

and the sides match up to a common scale factor,

$$\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{BC}{EF} = \frac{CA}{FD}$$

As with congruence, the order of the letters in the similarity statement records the correspondence, so read it before writing any ratio down.

## The side-splitter theorem

**Side-splitter theorem.** If a line parallel to one side of a triangle intersects the lines containing the other two sides, then the line divides the segments proportionally.

This is the source of most similarity in a diagram: wherever there is a pair of parallel lines cutting a triangle, there is a proportion waiting to be written.

## Determining similarity from a parallel line

**Similar triangle determination.** In $\triangle ABC$, if a line $l \parallel BC$ meets the other two sides at $D$ and $E$ — with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$ — then

$$\triangle ABC \sim \triangle ADE$$

The small triangle sits inside the large one sharing the angle at $A$, and the parallel line copies the other two angles across.

## The Euclidean theorem

**Euclidean theorem.** In $\mathrm{Rt}\triangle ABC$ with $\angle C = 90^\circ$, if $CD \perp AB$ at $D$, then

$$CD^2 = AD \cdot BD, \qquad AC^2 = AD \cdot AB, \qquad BC^2 = BD \cdot AB$$

The altitude to the hypotenuse splits the right triangle into two triangles similar to it and to each other, and these three relations are what that similarity says in terms of lengths. Each of the three is a "mean proportional": the altitude is the mean proportional between the two pieces of the hypotenuse, and each leg is the mean proportional between the whole hypotenuse and the piece adjacent to it.

## Angle bisector theorems

**Triangle interior angle bisector theorem.** In $\triangle ABC$, if $AD$ bisects $\angle A$ and $AD$ meets $BC$ at $D$, then

$$\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC}$$

and the converse also holds — a cevian dividing $BC$ in the ratio of the adjacent sides must be the bisector.

**Triangle exterior angle bisector theorem.** In $\triangle ABC$, if $AD$ bisects the exterior angle at $A$ and $AD$ meets line $BC$ at $D$, then

$$\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC}$$

again with a converse. The ratio is the same as for the interior bisector; what changes is that $D$ now falls outside segment $BC$, on the extension.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Similar triangles** | Triangles whose corresponding angles are equal and whose corresponding sides are in a common ratio; written $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ |
| **Side-splitter theorem** | If a line parallel to one side of a triangle intersects the lines containing the other two sides, then the line divides the segments proportionally |
| **Euclidean theorem** | In $\mathrm{Rt}\triangle ABC$ with $\angle C = 90^\circ$ and $CD \perp AB$ at $D$: $CD^2 = AD \cdot BD$, $AC^2 = AD \cdot AB$, $BC^2 = BD \cdot AB$ |
| **Triangle interior angle bisector theorem** | If $AD$ bisects $\angle A$ and meets $BC$ at $D$, then $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC}$ |
| **Triangle exterior angle bisector theorem** | If $AD$ bisects the exterior angle at $A$ and meets line $BC$ at $D$, then $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC}$ |

# 4.3 Trigonometric Ratios in Acute Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Similarity says that all triangles of the same shape have proportional sides. The trigonometric ratios are what you get when you name those proportions: for an acute angle $A$ in a right triangle, the ratios below depend only on $A$, not on how large the triangle is.

## The four ratios

$$\sin A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \cos A = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$

$$\tan A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}, \qquad \cot A = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{opposite}}$$

## Trigonometric identities

| Identity | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Reciprocal** | $\tan A \cdot \cot A = 1$ |
| **Quotient** | $\tan A = \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}$ |
| **Square** | $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$ |
| **Complement** | If $A$ and $B$ are complementary, then $\sin A = \cos B$ and $\tan A = \cot B$ |

The reciprocal identity is immediate from the definitions, since $\tan A$ and $\cot A$ are the same fraction turned over. The square identity is the Pythagorean theorem divided through by the square of the hypotenuse. The complement identity holds because in a right triangle the two acute angles are complementary, and the side opposite one is the side adjacent to the other.

## Area of a triangle

The area of $\triangle ABC$ is

$$S_{\triangle ABC} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$$

Two sides and the angle between them are enough, because $a \sin C$ is exactly the height dropped onto side $b$.

Note the accompanying fact: if $A$ and $B$ are supplementary, then $\sin A = \sin B$. This is why the formula does not need a separate case for an obtuse included angle — the sine of the obtuse angle equals the sine of its supplement, which is the acute angle that actually appears in the height.

## Law of sines

In $\triangle ABC$,

$$\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$$

Each side is proportional to the sine of the angle opposite it, so knowing one side–angle pair fixes the constant of proportionality for the whole triangle.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sine** | $\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ |
| **Cosine** | $\cos A = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ |
| **Tangent** | $\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ |
| **Cotangent** | $\cot A = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{opposite}}$ |
| **Law of sines** | In $\triangle ABC$, $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$ |

# 4.4 Applications of Trigonometry

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The ratios of 4.3 become useful once a real situation is described in a way that supplies a right triangle. Each term below is a convention for doing exactly that: naming an angle precisely enough that it can be dropped into a triangle.

## Elevation and depression

An **angle of elevation** is an angle above the horizontal. An **angle of depression** is an angle below the horizontal. In both cases the horizontal is the reference line, so the horizontal side of the triangle is one leg and the line of sight is the hypotenuse.

## Course and compass bearing

A **course** is the angle measured clockwise from the north direction to the direction of the ship or plane. Bearings are written in the form $\mathrm{N}20^\circ\mathrm{E}$, which is $20^\circ$ East of North.

## Gradient and inclination

The **gradient**, or **inclination**, written $i$, is the ratio of the vertical altitude $h$ to the horizontal length $l$:

$$i = \frac{h}{l}$$

The **angle of inclination** is the angle between the horizontal face and the surface of the ramp. Since $h$ is the opposite side and $l$ the adjacent side for that angle, the gradient is its tangent.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Angle of elevation** | An angle above the horizontal |
| **Angle of depression** | An angle below the horizontal |
| **Course** | The angle measured clockwise from the north direction to the direction of the ship or plane |
| **Gradient / inclination ($i$)** | The ratio of the vertical altitude $h$ to the horizontal length $l$ |
| **Angle of inclination** | The angle between the horizontal face and the surface of the ramp |

# 6.1 Concepts and Properties of Circles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition and basic vocabulary

A **circle** is a set of points on the same plane equidistant from a fixed point, the **centre**. The **radius** is the distance from a point on the circle to the centre. Because the radius is the only quantity in the definition, **congruent circles have congruent radii** — size is the whole of a circle's identity.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Arc** | Part of a circle |
| **Semicircle** | Half of a circle |
| **Minor arc** | An arc smaller than a semicircle |
| **Major arc** | An arc greater than a semicircle |
| **Chord** | A segment with endpoints on a circle |
| **Diameter** | A chord through the centre |
| **Central angle** | An angle whose vertex is the centre of the circle |
| **Apothem** | The distance from the centre to the chord |

## Where a point sits

Given a point $P$ and circle $C$ with radius $R$, comparing $|PC|$ against $R$ settles the position completely:

| Position | Condition |
|---|---|
| $P$ is interior to $\odot C$ | $\lvert PC \rvert < R$ |
| $P$ is on $\odot C$ | $\lvert PC \rvert = R$ |
| $P$ is exterior to $\odot C$ | $\lvert PC \rvert > R$ |

## Central angle theorem

**Central angle theorem.** In the same or congruent circle, if two central angles are congruent, then their intercepted arcs, intercepted chords, and their apothems are respectively congruent.

The four quantities — central angle, arc, chord and apothem — travel together. Fixing any one of them in a given circle fixes the other three, so a problem that supplies one may be answered in terms of any of the rest.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Circle** | A set of points on the same plane equidistant from a fixed point (the centre) |
| **Radius** | The distance from a point on the circle to the centre |
| **Arc** | Part of a circle |
| **Semicircle** | Half of a circle |
| **Minor arc** | An arc smaller than a semicircle |
| **Major arc** | An arc greater than a semicircle |
| **Chord** | A segment with endpoints on a circle |
| **Diameter** | A chord through the centre |
| **Central angle** | An angle whose vertex is the centre of the circle |
| **Apothem** | The distance from the centre to the chord |
| **Central angle theorem** | In the same or congruent circle, congruent central angles have respectively congruent intercepted arcs, intercepted chords and apothems |

markdown:
# 6.2 Chords and Arcs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A chord and the arc it cuts off are two descriptions of the same slice of a circle, so any result about one is a result about the other.

## Perpendicular diameter theorem

**Perpendicular diameter theorem.** If a diameter is perpendicular to a chord, it bisects the chord and its corresponding arcs.

This is the workhorse for chord calculations: dropping the perpendicular from the centre to a chord halves the chord, and the half-chord, the apothem and the radius form a right triangle to which the Pythagorean theorem applies.

## Parallel chords

**Corollary to the perpendicular diameter theorem.** Arcs included by two parallel chords are congruent.

The two arcs caught between a pair of parallel chords have equal measure, on either side of the figure.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Perpendicular diameter theorem** | If a diameter is perpendicular to a chord, it bisects the chord and its corresponding arcs |
| **Corollary to the perpendicular diameter theorem** | Arcs included by two parallel chords are congruent |

markdown:
# 6.3 Relationship Between Lines and Circles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Counting intersections

A line and a circle can meet in nought, one or two points, and each case has a name.

- If a line and a circle have no intersection point, the line is **exterior** to the circle.
- If a line and a circle have one intersection point, the line is **tangent** to the circle. The line is called the **tangent line** and the point is called the **point of tangency**.
- If a line and a circle have two intersection points, the line **intersects** the circle. The line is called the **secant line**.

## The distance criterion

Counting intersections by eye is unreliable; comparing distances is not. Given a line $l$ and circle $C$ with radius $R$, let $d$ be the distance from $C$ to line $l$:

| Relationship | Condition |
|---|---|
| $l$ is exterior to $\odot C$ | $d > R$ |
| $l$ is tangent to $\odot C$ | $d = R$ |
| $l$ intersects $\odot C$ | $d < R$ |

## Properties of tangent lines

Three lines are involved at a point of tangency — the tangent, the radius, and the perpendicular — and any two of the following determine the third:

- A line through the centre perpendicular to the tangent line must pass through the point of tangency.
- A line through the point of tangency perpendicular to the tangent line must pass through the centre.

**Tangent lines theorem.** Through an exterior point of a circle, there are two tangent lines, and the line segments from this point to the points of tangency are congruent. The line through the centre and this point bisects the angle formed by the two tangent lines.

The whole configuration is symmetric about the line joining the exterior point to the centre, which is why the two tangent segments are equal and the angle is bisected.

## Relationship between two circles

Two circles are classified the same way, by counting intersection points:

- **No intersection point:** one circle is exterior to the other, or one is interior to the other.
- **Same centre:** the circles are **concentric**.
- **One intersection point:** the circles are **externally tangent** or **internally tangent**; the intersection point is the point of tangency.
- **Two intersection points:** the circles **intersect**.

As with lines, the distance between centres decides the case. Writing $O_1O_2$ for the distance between the centres and $R_1$, $R_2$ for the radii:

| Relationship | Condition |
|---|---|
| $\odot O_1$ is external to $\odot O_2$ | $O_1O_2 > R_1 + R_2$ |
| $\odot O_1$ is externally tangent to $\odot O_2$ | $O_1O_2 = R_1 + R_2$ |
| $\odot O_1$ intersects $\odot O_2$ | $\lvert R_1 - R_2 \rvert < O_1O_2 < R_1 + R_2$ |
| $\odot O_1$ is internally tangent to $\odot O_2$ | $O_1O_2 = \lvert R_1 - R_2 \rvert$ |
| $\odot O_1$ interior to $\odot O_2$ (with $R_1 < R_2$), or $\odot O_2$ interior to $\odot O_1$ (with $R_2 < R_1$) | $O_1O_2 < \lvert R_1 - R_2 \rvert$ |

Two further facts follow from the symmetry of the figure about the line of centres:

- The line connecting the two centres of intersecting circles is the perpendicular bisector of their common chord.
- The line connecting the two centres of tangent circles passes through the point of tangency.

## Common tangents

A **common tangent** is a common tangent segment formed by two points of tangency.

- An **external common tangent** has the two circles on the same side of it.
- An **internal common tangent** has the two circles on different sides of it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Tangent line** | A line meeting a circle at exactly one point |
| **Point of tangency** | The single point where a tangent line meets the circle |
| **Secant line** | A line meeting a circle at two points |
| **Tangent lines theorem** | Through an exterior point there are two tangent lines whose tangent segments are congruent; the line through the centre and that point bisects the angle between them |
| **Concentric circles** | Circles with the same centre |
| **Externally tangent circles** | Circles meeting at one point with $O_1O_2 = R_1 + R_2$ |
| **Internally tangent circles** | Circles meeting at one point with $O_1O_2 = \lvert R_1 - R_2 \rvert$ |
| **Common tangent** | A common tangent segment formed by two points of tangency |
| **External common tangent** | A common tangent with both circles on the same side of it |
| **Internal common tangent** | A common tangent with the circles on different sides of it |

markdown:
# 6.4 Angles and Segments in Circles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Section 6.1 measured angles from the centre. This section measures them from the circle itself, and the recurring theme is the factor of one half.

## Inscribed angles

An **inscribed angle** is an angle in which the vertex is on the circle and both sides intersect the circle.

**Inscribed angle theorem.** The measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc.

$$m\angle = \tfrac{1}{2}\,m\overset{\frown}{AB}$$

Two corollaries follow directly:

- The measures of inscribed angles with the same or congruent intercepted arcs are congruent. The arc alone determines the angle, so where the vertex sits on the remaining arc makes no difference.
- The measure of an inscribed angle of a semicircle is a right angle. A semicircle is an arc of $180^\circ$, and half of that is $90^\circ$.

## Tangent-chord angles

A **tangent-chord angle** is an angle with its vertex on the circle in which one side is tangent to the circle.

**Tangent chord theorem.** The measure of the tangent-chord angle is congruent to the measure of half of its intercepted arc.

This is the same halving rule as for inscribed angles, extended to the limiting case where one side of the angle has slid until it touches the circle at a single point.

## The power of a point

Through a fixed point $P$ not on $\odot O$, a line intersects $\odot O$ at $A$ and $B$. Then

$$PA \cdot PB = \lvert r^2 - OP^2 \rvert$$

The quantity $r^2 - OP^2$ is the **power of $P$ about $\odot O$**.

The product $PA \cdot PB$ does not depend on which line through $P$ was drawn — it depends only on $P$ and the circle, which is exactly what the right-hand side records. The sign of $r^2 - OP^2$ tells you where $P$ lies, by the criterion of 6.1: positive when $P$ is interior, negative when $P$ is exterior, which is why the absolute value is taken to give a length product.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inscribed angle** | An angle whose vertex is on the circle and whose sides both intersect the circle |
| **Inscribed angle theorem** | The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc |
| **Tangent-chord angle** | An angle with its vertex on the circle in which one side is tangent to the circle |
| **Tangent chord theorem** | The measure of a tangent-chord angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc |
| **Power of a point** | For $P$ not on $\odot O$, the quantity $r^2 - OP^2$; for any line through $P$ cutting the circle at $A$ and $B$, $PA \cdot PB = \lvert r^2 - OP^2 \rvert$ |

# 7 Basic Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Functions and relations

A **function** is a correspondence or rule that assigns to every element in a **domain** exactly one element in a **range**. The word "exactly" is the whole content of the definition: a rule that assigns two outputs to one input is not a function.

A **relation** is any correspondence or rule that pairs the members of two sets. Every function is a relation; the converse fails precisely when some input receives more than one output.

The **vertical-line test** turns that distinction into something you can see: if no vertical line intersects a given graph in more than one point, then the graph is the graph of a function. A vertical line collects all the outputs assigned to a single input, so two crossings means two outputs.

## Representation of functions

| Representation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Function rule** | $y = f(x)$, or $f : x \mapsto y$ |
| **Graph** | Plotted with $x$ the independent variable and $y$ the dependent variable |
| **Zeros** | The $x$-intercepts of the graph |

Note carefully: **zeros are values, not coordinates**. A zero is reported as $x = 3$, not as $(3, 0)$.

## Two step functions

The **greatest integer function** assigns to each number the greatest integer less than or equal to the number, written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ — the floor of $x$. Its partner is $\lceil x \rceil$, the ceiling of $x$: the least integer greater than or equal to $x$.

## Linear functions

For any first-degree equation of the form

$$Ax + By + C = 0$$

the graph is a line, where $A$ and $B$ are not both equal to zero. If both vanished, no $x$ or $y$ would remain and the equation would not describe a line at all.

### Inclination and slope

The **inclination** is the angle $\alpha$, where $0^\circ \leq \alpha < 180^\circ$, measured from the positive $x$-axis to the line. The **slope** is its tangent:

$$k = \tan\alpha$$

The restriction $0^\circ \leq \alpha < 180^\circ$ gives every direction exactly one representative. A vertical line has $\alpha = 90^\circ$ and therefore no slope, since $\tan 90^\circ$ is undefined.

### Different forms

| Form | Equation |
|---|---|
| **General** | $Ax + By + C = 0$ |
| **Slope-intercept** | $y = kx + b$ |
| **Point-slope** | $y - y_1 = k(x - x_1)$ |
| **Two-point** | $\dfrac{y - y_1}{y_2 - y_1} = \dfrac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ |
| **Intercept** | $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$ |

### Perpendicular and parallel lines

Given $l_1 : y = k_1x + b_1$ and $l_2 : y = k_2x + b_2$,

$$l_1 \parallel l_2 \iff k_1 = k_2, \qquad l_1 \perp l_2 \iff k_1k_2 = -1$$

### Distance from a point to a line

Given a point $P(x_0, y_0)$ and line $l : Ax + By + C = 0$, the distance from $P$ to $l$ is

$$d = \frac{\lvert Ax_0 + By_0 + C \rvert}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}$$

### Distance between parallel lines

Given $l_1 : Ax + By + C_1 = 0$ and $l_2 : Ax + By + C_2 = 0$, the distance between $l_1$ and $l_2$ is

$$d = \frac{\lvert C_1 - C_2 \rvert}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}$$

This is the previous formula applied to any point of one line, with the $Ax_0 + By_0$ terms cancelling because the coefficients match.

## Quadratic functions

| Form | Equation | What it displays |
|---|---|---|
| **General form** | $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ | The coefficients |
| **Vertex form** | $y = a(x - h)^2 + k$ | The vertex $(h, k)$ |
| **$x$-intercept form** | $y = a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)$ | The zeros $x_1$, $x_2$ |

The graph of a quadratic function is symmetrical about the **axis of symmetry**,

$$x = -\frac{b}{2a}$$

The sign of $a$ fixes the direction of opening, and with it whether the vertex is the lowest or the highest point:

- When $a > 0$, the quadratic function opens upwards, and it has a minimum value of $\dfrac{4ac - b^2}{4a}$ at $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}$.
- When $a < 0$, the quadratic function opens downwards, and it has a maximum value of $\dfrac{4ac - b^2}{4a}$ at $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}$.

The number of $x$-intercepts is decided by the discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$:

| Discriminant | $x$-intercepts |
|---|---|
| $\Delta > 0$ | Two |
| $\Delta = 0$ | One |
| $\Delta < 0$ | None |

## Complex numbers

A **complex number** is any number in the form

$$z = a + bi, \qquad a, b \in \mathbb{R}, \quad i^2 = -1$$

Here $a$ is the **real part** and $b$ is the **imaginary part** of $z$.

### Complex conjugates

Suppose $z = a + bi$ where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The **complex conjugate** of $z$ is

$$\bar{z} = a - bi$$

**Equality of complex numbers.** Two complex numbers are equal exactly when both parts match:

$$a + bi = c + di \iff a = c \text{ and } b = d$$

A single complex equation is therefore two real equations, which is what makes complex algebra useful for solving pairs of real conditions at once.

### Properties of complex conjugates

$$\overline{\bar{z}} = z$$
$$\overline{z_1 + z_2} = \bar{z}_1 + \bar{z}_2$$
$$\overline{z_1 - z_2} = \bar{z}_1 - \bar{z}_2$$
$$\overline{z_1 z_2} = \bar{z}_1 \bar{z}_2$$
$$\overline{\left(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\right)} = \frac{\bar{z}_1}{\bar{z}_2} \quad \text{for } z_2 \neq 0$$
$$z + \bar{z} = 2a, \qquad z - \bar{z} = 2bi$$
$$z\bar{z} = \lvert z \rvert^2, \quad \text{where } \lvert z \rvert = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \text{ is the modulus of } z$$
$$z = \bar{z} \iff z \in \mathbb{R}$$

## Polynomial functions

For $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, a **polynomial function** is given by

$$f(x) = a_nx^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1x + a_0, \qquad a_n \neq 0$$

**Power functions** are polynomial functions of the form $f(x) = ax^n$.

### End behaviour

The **leading coefficient test** determines the rise or fall of the graph at the extremes from the polynomial function's degree and from its leading coefficient. For large $\lvert x \rvert$ the leading term dominates every other term, so those two pieces of information settle the behaviour at both ends.

### Real zeros

A function of degree $n$ has at most $n$ real zeros and at most $n - 1$ turns.

### Rational root test

When the polynomial $f$ has integer coefficients, every rational zero of $f$ has the form $\dfrac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ have no common factors other than $1$, $p$ is a factor of the constant term, and $q$ is a factor of the leading coefficient.

This converts the search for rational zeros from an infinite hunt into a finite list of candidates to test.

### The division algorithm

When $f(x)$ and $d(x)$ are polynomials such that $d(x) \neq 0$, and the degree of $d(x)$ is less than or equal to the degree of $f(x)$, there exist unique polynomials $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ such that

$$f(x) = d(x)\,q(x) + r(x)$$

**Synthetic division** is the shortcut for carrying this out when the divisor is linear.

### Remainder theorem and factor theorem

**Remainder theorem.** When the polynomial $f(x)$ is divided by $x - k$, the remainder is $f(k)$.

**Factor theorem.** If $x - k$ is a factor of the polynomial $f(x)$, then $f(k) = 0$.

The factor theorem is the remainder theorem with remainder zero: dividing exactly means no remainder, and the remainder is $f(k)$.

### Fundamental theorem of algebra

If $f$ is a polynomial of degree $n$, then $f$ has exactly $n$ zeros, each of which may be written in the form $a + bi$ where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The consequences worth memorising:

- Every real polynomial of degree $n$ can be factorised into $n$ complex linear factors, some of which may be repeated.
- Every real polynomial can be expressed as a product of real linear and real irreducible quadratic factors.
- Every real polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ zeros, some of which may be repeated.
- If $z$ is a zero of a real polynomial, then its complex conjugate $\bar{z}$ is also a zero. Non-real zeros therefore arrive in pairs.
- Every real polynomial of odd degree has at least one real zero. Since non-real zeros pair up, an odd count cannot be made of pairs alone.

### Vieta's theorem

For the polynomial function $f(x) = a_nx^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1x + a_0$, the sum of the zeros is

$$-\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}$$

and the product of the zeros is

$$(-1)^n \frac{a_0}{a_n}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Function** | A correspondence or rule that assigns to every element in a domain exactly one element in a range |
| **Relation** | Any correspondence or rule that pairs the members of two sets |
| **Vertical-line test** | If no vertical line intersects a given graph in more than one point, then the graph is the graph of a function |
| **Zeros** | The $x$-intercepts of a graph, given as values rather than coordinates |
| **Greatest integer function** | The function assigning to each number the greatest integer less than or equal to it, $\lfloor x \rfloor$ |
| **Ceiling** | $\lceil x \rceil$, the least integer greater than or equal to $x$ |
| **Inclination** | The angle $\alpha$, $0^\circ \leq \alpha < 180^\circ$, measured from the positive $x$-axis to the line |
| **Axis of symmetry** | The vertical line $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$ about which a quadratic graph is symmetrical |
| **Complex number** | Any number of the form $z = a + bi$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $i^2 = -1$ |
| **Real part / imaginary part** | In $z = a + bi$, the numbers $a$ and $b$ respectively |
| **Complex conjugate** | For $z = a + bi$, the number $\bar{z} = a - bi$ |
| **Modulus** | $\lvert z \rvert = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ |
| **Power function** | A polynomial function of the form $f(x) = ax^n$ |
| **Leading coefficient test** | Determining the rise or fall of a polynomial graph from its degree and its leading coefficient |
| **Rational root test** | For integer coefficients, every rational zero has the form $\frac{p}{q}$ in lowest terms with $p$ a factor of the constant term and $q$ a factor of the leading coefficient |
| **Division algorithm** | For polynomials with $d(x) \neq 0$, there exist unique $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ with $f(x) = d(x)q(x) + r(x)$ |
| **Remainder theorem** | When $f(x)$ is divided by $x - k$, the remainder is $f(k)$ |
| **Factor theorem** | If $x - k$ is a factor of $f(x)$, then $f(k) = 0$ |
| **Fundamental theorem of algebra** | A polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ zeros of the form $a + bi$ |
| **Vieta's theorem** | The zeros of $f(x) = a_nx^n + \cdots + a_0$ sum to $-\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}$ and multiply to $(-1)^n\frac{a_0}{a_n}$ |

# 8.1 Solve Equations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Quadratic equations

For the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with $a \neq 0$, the real roots of the equation are

$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$

The roots are also tied to the coefficients directly. If $x_1$ and $x_2$ satisfy

$$x_1 + x_2 = -\frac{b}{a}, \qquad x_1x_2 = \frac{c}{a}$$

then $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the roots of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$. This is Vieta's theorem for degree $2$, read in the useful direction: it lets you build the equation from its roots, or extract symmetric information about the roots without solving at all.

## Relationship between functions and equations

For the equation $f(x) = g(x)$, the $x$-coordinates of the intersections of $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x)$ are exactly the solutions to $f(x) = g(x)$.

This correspondence is the reason graphs are worth sketching before solving. An equation you cannot factor may still yield the number of its solutions immediately, because that number is the number of crossings. In the special case $g(x) = 0$, the solutions are the zeros of $f$ — the $x$-intercepts of its graph.

## Further equation types

The section also covers the following types of equation:

| Type | Form |
|---|---|
| **Polynomial equations** | Degree higher than $2$ |
| **Equations with absolute values** | The unknown appears inside $\lvert \cdot \rvert$ |
| **Irrational equations** | The unknown appears under a radical |
| **Fractional equations** | The unknown appears in a denominator |
| **Partial fractions** | Decomposing a rational expression into a sum of simpler fractions |
| **Systems of equations** | Several equations solved simultaneously |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Quadratic formula** | The real roots of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ |
| **Partial fractions** | The decomposition of a rational expression into a sum of simpler fractions |
