# 8.2 Solve Inequalities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Comparing real numbers

Two standard comparisons reduce an inequality to a question about sign or size.

For $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, subtract:

$$a - b > 0 \iff a > b, \qquad a - b = 0 \iff a = b, \qquad a - b < 0 \iff a < b$$

For $a, b > 0$, divide:

$$\frac{a}{b} > 1 \iff a > b, \qquad \frac{a}{b} = 1 \iff a = b, \qquad \frac{a}{b} < 1 \iff a < b$$

The division method requires positivity, which is why it is stated separately.

## Properties of inequalities

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| Transitivity | If $a > b$ and $b > c$, then $a > c$ |
| Addition | If $a > b$, then $a + c > b + c$ |
| Multiplication by a positive | If $a > b$ and $c > 0$, then $ac > bc$ |
| Multiplication by a negative | If $a > b$ and $c < 0$, then $ac < bc$ |

The last line is the one that generates most errors: multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality.

## Quadratic inequalities

The connection between functions, equations and inequalities is important in algebra, and quadratic inequalities are where it first pays off. Solving $ax^2 + bx + c > 0$ means finding where the parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ sits above the $x$-axis. So: find the zeros by solving the corresponding equation, then read the sign off the graph, using the direction of opening determined by the sign of $a$.

The equation supplies the boundary points; the function supplies the sign between them; the inequality is the answer you read off.

## Inequalities with absolute values

Basic forms:

$$\lvert x \rvert < a \iff -a < x < a$$
$$\lvert x \rvert > a \iff x < -a \text{ or } x > a$$

The general method for an inequality with absolute values is to reduce it to these basic forms, then solve the resulting inequality or pair of inequalities.

## Polynomial inequalities

For a polynomial inequality, use the zeros to cut the number line into intervals.

1. Sketch the number line and mark all zeros.
2. From the right-hand side, the graph of the polynomial is above the number line — the leading behaviour on the far right is positive when the polynomial is written with positive leading coefficient.
3. Complete the rest of the graph with a wave shape, moving leftwards through the marked zeros.
4. At each zero, the multiplicity decides what the wave does. **When the multiplicity is even, it bounces back at that zero; when the multiplicity is odd, it crosses at that zero.**

Reading the finished sketch gives the solution set directly: the intervals where the wave lies above the line satisfy $> 0$, those below satisfy $< 0$.

## Irrational inequalities

For inequalities of the form $\sqrt{f(x)} > g(x)$ or $\sqrt{f(x)} < g(x)$:

1. First restrict to the possible values of $x$, those where $f(x) \geq 0$ — outside that set the radical does not exist.
2. Then discuss the cases $g(x) < 0$ and $g(x) \geq 0$ separately.
3. When $g(x) \geq 0$, both sides are non-negative and we can square both sides.

The case split is not optional: squaring is only safe when both sides are known to be non-negative, since squaring reverses the order of negative numbers.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Irrational inequality** | An inequality in which the unknown appears under a radical, handled by restricting to $f(x) \geq 0$ and splitting on the sign of $g(x)$ |

# 9.1 Powers and Exponents

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Properties of exponents

Given $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$:

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Multiplication** | $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$ |
| **Division with the same base** | $\dfrac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}$ |
| **Division with the same power** | $\dfrac{a^m}{b^m} = \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^m$ |
| **Power of a power with the same base** | $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ |
| **Power of a power with the same power** | $a^m \times b^m = (ab)^m$ |

**Negative one to a power:**

$$(-1)^n = \begin{cases} -1 & n = 2k - 1 \\ 1 & n = 2k \end{cases} \qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}$$

Odd powers keep the sign, even powers destroy it — the pattern that will reappear in the parity of functions and in the multiplicity rule for polynomial inequalities.

## Extending the index

The definition of $a^n$ as repeated multiplication only makes sense for positive integers. The remaining cases are defined so that the property $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$ continues to hold.

**Zero power:**

$$a^0 = 1 \qquad (a \neq 0)$$

**Negative index:**

$$a^{-m} = \frac{1}{a^m} \qquad (a \neq 0)$$

**Rational index:**

$$a^{\frac{m}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a^m}$$

If $n$ is even, then $a^m \geq 0$; if $n$ is odd, then $a^m \in \mathbb{R}$. An even root demands a non-negative radicand, whereas an odd root is defined for every real number.

## Real exponents

The properties survive the final extension. For $a, b > 0$ and $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$, we still have

$$a^s \times a^t = a^{s+t}, \qquad (a^s)^t = a^{st}, \qquad (ab)^t = a^tb^t$$

The restriction to $a, b > 0$ is what makes this extension safe, and it is the reason the exponential function in 9.3 is defined only for a positive base.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Zero power** | $a^0 = 1$ for $a \neq 0$ |
| **Negative index** | $a^{-m} = \frac{1}{a^m}$ for $a \neq 0$ |
| **Rational index** | $a^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{a^m}$ |

# 9.2 Logarithms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A logarithm answers the question the exponential poses in reverse: given the base and the result, what was the exponent?

$$y = b^N \iff N = \log_b y, \qquad y > 0,\ b > 0,\ b \neq 1$$

$N$ is the **logarithm of $y$ to base $b$**. The restrictions come straight from 9.1: a positive base raised to a real power is always positive, which is why $y > 0$; and base $1$ is excluded because $1^N$ never varies, so no exponent could be recovered.

## Special notations

$$\log_{10} x = \log x \ (\lg x), \qquad \log_e x = \ln x, \qquad e = \lim_{x \to \infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right)^x$$

## Laws of logarithms

For $x, y > 0$, $a > 0$, $a \neq 1$:

$$\textbf{Addition:} \quad \log_a x + \log_a y = \log_a xy$$

$$\textbf{Difference:} \quad \log_a x - \log_a y = \log_a\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$$

These are the exponent laws of 9.1 read backwards: multiplying powers adds exponents, so multiplying arguments adds logarithms.

## Taking logarithms of both sides

$$x = y \iff \log_a x = \log_a y$$

Because the logarithm is one-to-one, applying it to both sides of an equation loses nothing and gains nothing — which makes it a legitimate move in either direction when solving.

## Change of base

$$\log_a b = \frac{\log_k b}{\log_k a}, \qquad a, k \in \mathbb{R}^+ / \{1\}$$

$$\log_a b = \frac{1}{\log_b a}$$

The second is the first with $k = b$, since $\log_b b = 1$.

## Other properties

For $a > 0$, $a \neq 1$, $x > 0$:

$$\log_a a = 1, \qquad \log_a 1 = 0$$
$$\log_a x^{-1} = -\log_a x, \qquad \log_{\frac{1}{a}} x = -\log_a x$$
$$a^{\log_a x} = x$$
$$\log_{a^M} b^N = \frac{N}{M}\log_a b$$

The identity $a^{\log_a x} = x$ is the definition restated: $\log_a x$ is by construction the exponent that turns $a$ into $x$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Logarithm** | In $y = b^N \iff N = \log_b y$, $N$ is the logarithm of $y$ to base $b$, with $y > 0$, $b > 0$, $b \neq 1$ |
| **Common logarithm** | $\log_{10}x$, written $\log x$ or $\lg x$ |
| **Natural logarithm** | $\log_e x$, written $\ln x$, where $e = \lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)^x$ |
| **Change of base** | $\log_a b = \frac{\log_k b}{\log_k a}$ |

# 9.3 Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Supplementary notice

Any function

$$y = \frac{ax + b}{cx + d} \qquad (ad \neq bc)$$

can be translated into the function

$$y = \frac{k}{x} \qquad (k \neq 0)$$

The condition $ad \neq bc$ is what stops the fraction collapsing to a constant. A function of this shape is therefore a shifted hyperbola, and the translation techniques of 10.2 apply to it directly.

## Exponential functions

$$f(x) = b^x \qquad (b > 0,\ b \neq 1)$$

| Property | $b \in (0, 1)$ | $b \in (1, \infty)$ |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | $\mathbb{R}$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |
| Range | $(0, \infty)$ | $(0, \infty)$ |
| Even/odd | Neither | Neither |
| Monotonicity | Strictly decreasing | Strictly increasing |
| Asymptote | $y = 0$ | $y = 0$ |

The range is $(0, \infty)$ for both, never including $0$ — a positive base raised to any real power is positive, and the asymptote $y = 0$ is the line the graph approaches without reaching.

## Logarithmic functions

$$f(x) = \log_b x \qquad (b > 0,\ b \neq 1)$$

| Property | $b \in (0, 1)$ | $b \in (1, \infty)$ |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | $(0, \infty)$ | $(0, \infty)$ |
| Range | $\mathbb{R}$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |
| Even/odd | Neither | Neither |
| Monotonicity | Strictly decreasing | Strictly increasing |
| Asymptote | $x = 0$ | $x = 0$ |

Set the two tables side by side and every row is swapped: domain against range, and the horizontal asymptote $y = 0$ against the vertical asymptote $x = 0$. That is what it means for the two functions to be inverses of one another, as the definition in 9.2 states.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Exponential function** | $f(x) = b^x$ with $b > 0$, $b \neq 1$ |
| **Logarithmic function** | $f(x) = \log_b x$ with $b > 0$, $b \neq 1$ |

# 9.4 Exponential and Logarithmic Equations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Every equation below is solved by removing the exponential or the logarithm, either by taking the inverse operation or by matching the two sides so the base cancels.

## Types of exponential equations

**Type 1.**

$$a^x = b \quad (a > 0,\ a \neq 1,\ b > 0) \iff x = \log_a b$$

This is the definition of the logarithm applied directly.

**Type 2.**

$$a^{f(x)} = a^{\phi(x)} \quad (a > 0,\ a \neq 1) \iff f(x) = \phi(x)$$

Equal powers of the same base force equal exponents, because the exponential function is one-to-one.

**Type 3.**

$$A \cdot a^{2x} + B \cdot a^{x} + C = 0 \qquad (a > 0,\ a \neq 1)$$

**Type 4.**

$$A \cdot a^{2x} + B \cdot a^{x} \cdot b^{x} + C \cdot b^{2x} = 0 \qquad (a > 0,\ a, b \neq 1,\ a \neq b)$$

Types 3 and 4 are quadratic in disguise: $a^{2x} = (a^x)^2$, so a substitution turns each into a quadratic equation of the kind solved in 8.1.

## Types of logarithmic equations

**Type 1.**

$$A \cdot \log_a^2 x + B \cdot \log_a x + C = 0 \qquad (a > 0,\ a \neq 1)$$

Again quadratic in disguise, this time in $\log_a x$.

**Type 2.**

$$\log_a f(x) = \log_a \phi(x) \quad (a > 0,\ a \neq 1) \iff \begin{cases} f(x) > 0 \\ \phi(x) > 0 \\ f(x) = \phi(x) \end{cases}$$

The two positivity conditions are not optional extras. Cancelling the logarithms is only valid where both arguments lie in the domain of the logarithm, so a solution of $f(x) = \phi(x)$ that makes either side non-positive must be discarded.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Exponential equation** | An equation with the unknown in an exponent, reduced by taking logarithms or by matching bases |
| **Logarithmic equation** | An equation with the unknown inside a logarithm, reduced by matching logarithms subject to the domain conditions $f(x) > 0$ and $\phi(x) > 0$ |

# 10.1 Properties of Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Operations on functions

Two functions can be combined pointwise, one input at a time:

$$\textbf{Sum:} \quad (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$$
$$\textbf{Difference:} \quad (f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x)$$
$$\textbf{Product:} \quad (fg)(x) = f(x)\,g(x)$$
$$\textbf{Quotient:} \quad \left(\frac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}, \qquad g(x) \neq 0$$

## Composite functions

A **composite function** combines two functions by successive application:

$$(f \circ g)(x) = f\big(g(x)\big)$$

and is read "$f$ of $g$ of $x$". Note the order: $g$ acts first, even though $f$ is written first.

The domain of $f \circ g$ is the set of elements $x$ in the domain of $g$ such that $g(x)$ is in the domain of $f$. Two conditions, not one — $x$ must be a legal input for $g$, and the value $g$ returns must be a legal input for $f$.

## Monotonicity

Let $f$ be a function defined on an interval $I$, and let $x_1, x_2 \in I$ with $x_1 < x_2$.

| Description | Condition |
|---|---|
| $f$ is **strictly increasing** on $I$ | $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ |
| $f$ is **strictly decreasing** on $I$ | $f(x_1) > f(x_2)$ |
| $f$ is **increasing** on $I$ | $f(x_1) \leq f(x_2)$ |
| $f$ is **decreasing** on $I$ | $f(x_1) \geq f(x_2)$ |

The difference between the strict and non-strict versions is whether the function is allowed to stay level over part of the interval.

## Even and odd functions

For any $x$ in the domain:

$$f \text{ is an } \textbf{even function} \iff f(-x) = f(x)$$
$$f \text{ is an } \textbf{odd function} \iff f(-x) = -f(x)$$

An even function is unchanged by reflecting its graph in the $y$-axis; an odd function is unchanged by rotating its graph a half-turn about the origin. A function need be neither — the exponential and logarithmic functions of 9.3 are examples.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Composite function** | $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$, read "$f$ of $g$ of $x$" |
| **Domain of a composite** | The set of elements $x$ in the domain of $g$ such that $g(x)$ is in the domain of $f$ |
| **Strictly increasing** | For $x_1 < x_2$ in $I$, $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ |
| **Strictly decreasing** | For $x_1 < x_2$ in $I$, $f(x_1) > f(x_2)$ |
| **Even function** | $f(-x) = f(x)$ for any $x$ |
| **Odd function** | $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for any $x$ |

# 10.2 Transformations in Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Locus

A **locus** is a set of points, all of which meet a stated condition. The general steps for finding the equation of a locus:

1. Let the points be $(x, y)$.
2. Set an equation according to the condition.
3. Simplify.

The method converts a geometric description into an algebraic one, so that a curve defined by a property can be handled with the tools of Chapter 7.

## Translation of functions

Given a function $y = f(x)$ and $k > 0$, if the graph of $y = f(x)$ is

| Translated | The resulting function is |
|---|---|
| Horizontally to the left by $k$ units | $y = f(x + k)$ |
| Horizontally to the right by $k$ units | $y = f(x - k)$ |
| Vertically upwards by $k$ units | $y = f(x) + k$ |
| Vertically downwards by $k$ units | $y = f(x) - k$ |

The horizontal cases run against intuition: shifting **left** requires $+k$ inside the bracket. The reason is that the transformed graph must reach at $x$ the value the original reached at $x + k$.

## Reflection of functions

Given a function $y = f(x)$, with $a$ and $b$ constants, if the graph of $y = f(x)$ is

| Reflected about | The new curve is |
|---|---|
| The line $x = a$ | $y = f(2a - x)$ |
| The line $y = b$ | $y = 2b - f(x)$ |
| The point $(a, b)$ | $y = 2b - f(2a - x)$ |

Each formula is the same idea applied to a different coordinate: reflecting a value $v$ in the level $c$ sends it to $2c - v$. Reflection in a point is reflection in both coordinates at once, which is why the third row is the first two combined.

## Symmetry in a function

A curve is symmetric when reflecting it returns the same curve, so the symmetry conditions are exactly the reflection formulas applied to the function itself:

$$y = f(x) \text{ is symmetric about the line } x = a \iff f(a + x) = f(a - x)$$

$$y = f(x) \text{ is symmetric about the point } (a, b) \iff f(a + x) + f(a - x) = 2b$$

Setting $a = 0$ in the first recovers the condition for an even function; setting $a = 0$, $b = 0$ in the second recovers the condition for an odd function.

## Special functions

Two graphs are built from the graph of $y = f(x)$ by folding rather than sliding.

**The graph of $y = f(\lvert x \rvert)$.** Keep the graph of $y = f(x)$ on the right side of the $y$-axis and reflect it about the $y$-axis. Since $\lvert x \rvert$ discards the sign of the input, only the positive half of the original graph is ever used, and the result is necessarily even.

**The graph of $y = \lvert f(x) \rvert$.** Keep the graph of $y = f(x)$ above the $x$-axis and reflect the part of the graph of $y = f(x)$ below the $x$-axis about the $x$-axis. Here it is the sign of the output that is discarded, so nothing can end up below the axis.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Locus** | A set of points, all of which meet a stated condition |

# 11.1 Measure of Angles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Radian measure

The **radian measure** of a central angle is the number of radius units in the length of the corresponding arc. Measuring an angle by the arc it subtends, in units of the radius, makes the measure independent of the size of the circle.

**Conversion formulas.** Writing $\alpha$ for the measure in degrees and $\theta$ for the measure in radians,

$$\frac{\alpha}{180} = \frac{\theta}{\pi}$$

$$l = \theta r$$

$$S = \frac{1}{2}lr = \frac{1}{2}\theta r^2$$

The arc-length formula $l = \theta r$ is the definition of radian measure rearranged, and the sector-area formula follows by substituting it into $S = \frac{1}{2}lr$.

## Angles as rotations

An angle is formed by rotating a ray about the vertex to another ray. The rotation carries a sign:

- If the rotation is counterclockwise, the angle is positive.
- If the rotation is clockwise, the angle is negative.

Defining an angle by rotation rather than by a static figure is what allows measures beyond $360^\circ$ and below $0^\circ$, and it is the reason the trigonometric ratios of 11.2 extend to arbitrary angles.

## Coterminal angles

**Coterminal angles** are angles of different measure in standard position but having the same terminal side. For a given $\theta$ they form the set

$$\{x \mid x = \theta + 2k\pi,\ k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$$

Since coterminal angles share a terminal side, they share every trigonometric value — which is the origin of the periodicity results in 11.2.

## Quadrantal angles

**Quadrantal angles** are those whose terminal side lies along an axis:

$$\theta = \frac{k\pi}{2}, \qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Radian measure** | The number of radius units in the length of the arc corresponding to a central angle |
| **Coterminal angles** | Angles of different measure in standard position but having the same terminal side |
| **Quadrantal angles** | Angles with $\theta = \frac{k\pi}{2}$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |

# 11.2 Trigonometric Ratios of Arbitrary Angles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The right-triangle definitions of 4.3 only reach acute angles. Placing the angle in the coordinate plane removes that limit, because a terminal ray exists whatever the measure.

## Definition by a point on the terminal ray

Let $\theta$ be an angle in standard position, and let $(x, y)$ be a point distinct from the origin on the terminal ray of $\theta$. Then

$$\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}, \qquad \sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}, \qquad \text{where } r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$

Since $r > 0$ always, the signs of the ratios are inherited from the signs of $x$ and $y$ — that is, from the quadrant.

## The unit circle

The terminal ray of an angle $\theta$ in standard position intersects the unit circle at a unique point $P(x, y)$ where

$$x = \cos\theta \qquad \text{and} \qquad y = \sin\theta$$

Taking $r = 1$ removes the denominators, so the coordinates of the point *are* the cosine and sine.

## Basic properties

**1. Ranges.**

$$\sin\theta \in [-1, 1], \qquad \cos\theta \in [-1, 1], \qquad \tan\theta \in \mathbb{R}$$

Sine and cosine are coordinates of a point on the unit circle, so neither can exceed $1$ in size; the tangent is a quotient and is unbounded.

**2. Signs by quadrant.**

| Ratio | Positive in | Negative in |
|---|---|---|
| $\sin\theta$ | I, II | III, IV |
| $\cos\theta$ | I, IV | II, III |
| $\tan\theta$ | I, III | II, IV |

**3. Periodicity.**

$$\sin(\theta + 2k\pi) = \sin\theta, \qquad \cos(\theta + 2k\pi) = \cos\theta, \qquad \tan(\theta + 2k\pi) = \tan\theta$$

Coterminal angles have the same terminal ray, hence the same values.

## Relations

**1. Reciprocals.**

$$\tan\alpha \cdot \cot\alpha = 1, \qquad \sin\alpha \cdot \csc\alpha = 1, \qquad \cos\alpha \cdot \sec\alpha = 1$$

**2. Quotients.**

$$\frac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha} = \tan\alpha = \frac{\sec\alpha}{\csc\alpha}, \qquad \frac{\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha} = \cot\alpha = \frac{\csc\alpha}{\sec\alpha}$$

**3. Pythagorean identities.**

$$\sin^2\alpha + \cos^2\alpha = 1, \qquad 1 + \tan^2\alpha = \sec^2\alpha, \qquad 1 + \cot^2\alpha = \csc^2\alpha$$

The second and third are the first divided through by $\cos^2\alpha$ and by $\sin^2\alpha$ respectively.

## Induction formulas

(奇变偶不变，符号看象限)

**1.**
$$\sin(\alpha + 2k\pi) = \sin\alpha, \quad \cos(\alpha + 2k\pi) = \cos\alpha, \quad \tan(\alpha + 2k\pi) = \tan\alpha$$

**2.**
$$\sin(-\alpha) = -\sin\alpha, \quad \cos(-\alpha) = \cos\alpha, \quad \tan(-\alpha) = -\tan\alpha$$

**3.**
$$\sin(\pi - \alpha) = \sin\alpha, \quad \cos(\pi - \alpha) = -\cos\alpha, \quad \tan(\pi - \alpha) = -\tan\alpha$$

**4.**
$$\sin(\pi + \alpha) = -\sin\alpha, \quad \cos(\pi + \alpha) = -\cos\alpha, \quad \tan(\pi + \alpha) = \tan\alpha$$

**5.**
$$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \cos\alpha, \quad \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \sin\alpha, \quad \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \cot\alpha$$

**6.**
$$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = \cos\alpha, \quad \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = -\sin\alpha, \quad \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = -\cot\alpha$$

**7.**
$$\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = -\cos\alpha, \quad \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = -\sin\alpha, \quad \tan\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \cot\alpha$$

**8.**
$$\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = -\cos\alpha, \quad \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = \sin\alpha, \quad \tan\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = -\cot\alpha$$

The mnemonic sorts these into two decisions rather than sixteen facts: whether the function name changes depends on whether the added angle is an odd or even multiple of $\frac{\pi}{2}$, and the sign is read off the quadrant.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Standard position** | An angle with vertex at the origin and initial side along the positive $x$-axis |
| **Unit circle** | The circle of radius $1$; the terminal ray of $\theta$ meets it at $P(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ |
| **Induction formulas** | The identities relating $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ of $-\alpha$, $\pi \pm \alpha$, $\frac{\pi}{2} \pm \alpha$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2} \pm \alpha$ back to those of $\alpha$ |

markdown:
# 11.3 Formulas in Trigonometry

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

For the equation $\cos\theta = a$ or $\sin\theta = b$, the terminal ray of $\theta$ can be determined by $P(a, b)$, the intersection of the terminal ray of $\theta$ with the unit circle. Every formula below is ultimately a statement about that point.

## Addition and difference formulas

$$\cos(\alpha \pm \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta \mp \sin\alpha\sin\beta$$

$$\sin(\alpha \pm \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta \pm \cos\alpha\sin\beta$$

$$\tan(\alpha \pm \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha \pm \tan\beta}{1 \mp \tan\alpha\tan\beta}$$

Mind the signs in the cosine and tangent formulas: they run opposite to the sign on the left.

## Reference angle formula

For $a, b, x \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$a\sin x + b\cos x = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\sin x + \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\cos x\right) = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\sin(x + \phi)$$

where

$$\sin\phi = \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cos\phi = \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$$

It can also be expressed as

$$a\sin x + b\cos x = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\sin\!\left(x + \arctan\frac{b}{a}\right)$$

The point of the manoeuvre is that the two coefficients are rescaled into a sine and a cosine of a single angle $\phi$, so the sum collapses into one sine by the addition formula. A combination of two trigonometric terms becomes one, and its maximum and minimum are then immediate: $\pm\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

## Double angle formulas

$$\sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha$$

$$\cos 2\alpha = \cos^2\alpha - \sin^2\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^2\alpha = 2\cos^2\alpha - 1$$

$$\tan 2\alpha = \frac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^2\alpha}$$

The three versions of $\cos 2\alpha$ differ by applications of $\sin^2\alpha + \cos^2\alpha = 1$; pick whichever leaves you with the function you already have.

## Triple angle formulas

$$\sin 3\alpha = 3\sin\alpha - 4\sin^3\alpha = 4\sin\alpha\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3} + \alpha\right)\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3} - \alpha\right)$$

$$\cos 3\alpha = 4\cos^3\alpha - 3\cos\alpha = 4\cos\alpha\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3} + \alpha\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3} - \alpha\right)$$

$$\tan 3\alpha = \frac{3\tan\alpha - \tan^3\alpha}{1 - 3\tan^2\alpha} = \tan\alpha\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3} + \alpha\right)\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3} - \alpha\right)$$

## Omnipotent formula

Everything can be written in terms of $\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}$ alone:

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{2\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}}{1 - \tan^2\frac{\alpha}{2}}, \qquad \sin\alpha = \frac{2\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}}{1 + \tan^2\frac{\alpha}{2}}, \qquad \cos\alpha = \frac{1 - \tan^2\frac{\alpha}{2}}{1 + \tan^2\frac{\alpha}{2}}$$

This is what earns the name: a single substitution converts any rational expression in $\sin\alpha$ and $\cos\alpha$ into a rational expression in one variable.

## Half angle formulas

$$\sin\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{2}}, \qquad \cos\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos\alpha}{2}}$$

$$\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{1 + \cos\alpha}} = \frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{\sin\alpha}{1 + \cos\alpha}$$

The $\pm$ is settled by the quadrant of $\frac{\alpha}{2}$, not of $\alpha$. The last two expressions for $\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}$ carry no ambiguity at all, which is usually reason enough to prefer them.

## Sum-to-product formulas

$$\sin\alpha + \sin\beta = 2\sin\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)$$

$$\cos\alpha + \cos\beta = 2\cos\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)$$

$$\sin\alpha - \sin\beta = 2\cos\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)$$

$$\cos\alpha - \cos\beta = -2\sin\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)$$

## Product-to-sum formulas

$$\sin\alpha\cos\beta = \frac{1}{2}\big[\sin(\alpha+\beta) + \sin(\alpha-\beta)\big]$$

$$\cos\alpha\sin\beta = \frac{1}{2}\big[\sin(\alpha+\beta) - \sin(\alpha-\beta)\big]$$

$$\cos\alpha\cos\beta = \frac{1}{2}\big[\cos(\alpha+\beta) + \cos(\alpha-\beta)\big]$$

$$\sin\alpha\sin\beta = -\frac{1}{2}\big[\cos(\alpha+\beta) - \cos(\alpha-\beta)\big]$$

The two families are inverse to each other, and both are obtained by adding or subtracting the addition and difference formulas at the top of this lesson.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Reference angle formula** | $a\sin x + b\cos x = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin(x+\phi)$, with $\sin\phi = \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ and $\cos\phi = \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ |
| **Omnipotent formula** | The expressions for $\sin\alpha$, $\cos\alpha$ and $\tan\alpha$ in terms of $\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}$ alone |

markdown:
# 11.4 Sine and Cosine Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Periodicity

A **periodic function** is one for which there is a positive number $p$, the **period** of $f$, such that

$$f(x + p) = f(x)$$

for all $x$ in the domain of $f$. The **fundamental period** is the smallest period of a periodic function.

Sine and cosine are periodic because coterminal angles share a terminal ray, as 11.2 established — adding a full revolution returns the same point of the unit circle.

The **amplitude** $A$ is

$$A = \frac{1}{2}(M - m)$$

where $M$ and $m$ are the maximum and minimum values: half the total vertical spread.

## The sine curve

$$y = \sin x$$

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Domain | $\mathbb{R}$ |
| Range | $[-1, 1]$ |
| Parity | Odd |
| Periodicity | Periodic function with fundamental period $2\pi$ |
| Monotonicity | Increasing on $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi,\ \frac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi\right]$, decreasing on $\left[\frac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi,\ \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2k\pi\right]$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Axis of symmetry | $x = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Point of symmetry | $(k\pi, 0)$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Zeros | $x = k\pi$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |

## The cosine curve

$$y = \cos x$$

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Domain | $\mathbb{R}$ |
| Range | $[-1, 1]$ |
| Parity | Even |
| Periodicity | Periodic function with fundamental period $2\pi$ |
| Monotonicity | Increasing on $[\pi + 2k\pi,\ 2\pi + 2k\pi]$, decreasing on $[2k\pi,\ \pi + 2k\pi]$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Axis of symmetry | $x = k\pi$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Point of symmetry | $\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi,\ 0\right)$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Zeros | $x = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |

The two tables are the same table shifted. The parity differs — sine is odd, cosine even — and each curve's axes of symmetry are the other's points of symmetry, which is what the induction formula $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \sin\alpha$ from 11.2 predicts.

## Dilation

Given the graph of $y = f(x)$:

- **Vertical dilation:** $y = cf(x)$
- **Horizontal dilation:** $y = f(cx)$

For $y = cf(x)$:

- Vertical stretch with scale factor $\lvert c \rvert$ when $\lvert c \rvert > 1$
- Vertical shrink with scale factor $\lvert c \rvert$ when $\lvert c \rvert < 1$

For $y = f(cx)$:

- Horizontal stretch with scale factor $\left\lvert \frac{1}{c} \right\rvert$ when $\left\lvert \frac{1}{c} \right\rvert > 1$
- Horizontal shrink with scale factor $\left\lvert \frac{1}{c} \right\rvert$ when $\left\lvert \frac{1}{c} \right\rvert < 1$

The horizontal case inverts $c$ for the same reason translation inverts the sign in 10.2: the factor acts on the input before the function does, so its effect on the picture is the reciprocal.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Periodic function** | A function for which there is a positive number $p$ with $f(x+p) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain |
| **Period** | Such a number $p$ |
| **Fundamental period** | The smallest period of a periodic function |
| **Amplitude** | $A = \frac{1}{2}(M - m)$ |

# 11.5 Tangent Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The tangent curve

$$y = \tan x$$

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Domain | $\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} \ \middle\vert\ x \neq \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi,\ k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$ |
| Range | $\mathbb{R}$ |
| Parity | Odd |
| Periodicity | Periodic function with fundamental period $\pi$ |
| Monotonicity | Increasing on $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi,\ \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi\right)$ |
| Axis of symmetry | $x = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Point of symmetry | $\left(\frac{k\pi}{2},\ 0\right)$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| Zeros | $x = k\pi$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |

Two features separate the tangent from the sine and cosine curves of 11.4.

Its domain is not all of $\mathbb{R}$. Since $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$ by the definition in 11.2, the tangent is undefined wherever the terminal ray meets the unit circle at $x = 0$ — that is, at the quadrantal angles $\frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$. Its range is the whole of $\mathbb{R}$ rather than $[-1, 1]$, because it is a quotient rather than a coordinate.

Its fundamental period is $\pi$, not $2\pi$. Induction formula 4 of 11.2 states $\tan(\pi + \alpha) = \tan\alpha$, so the tangent repeats after a half revolution: the terminal rays of $\alpha$ and $\pi + \alpha$ point in opposite directions, which negates both $x$ and $y$ and leaves their quotient unchanged.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Tangent curve** | $y = \tan x$, with domain $x \neq \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, range $\mathbb{R}$, odd parity and fundamental period $\pi$ |

# 11.6 Inverse Trigonometric Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Inverse functions

A function $f$ has an **inverse function** $g$, written $f^{-1}$, if and only if

1. $f\big(g(x)\big) = x$ for all $x$ in the domain of $g(x)$
2. $g\big(f(x)\big) = x$ for all $x$ in the domain of $f(x)$

Both conditions are needed: each says that one function undoes the other, and the inverse must undo in both directions.

A function only has an inverse function if no horizontal line intersects its graph at more than one point. This is the **horizontal-line test**, and it is the mirror image of the vertical-line test of Chapter 7 — that test asked whether each input has one output, this one asks whether each output came from one input.

## Properties

1. The domain and range of $f$ are the range and domain of $f^{-1}$ respectively.
2. All functions must be one-to-one functions to have an inverse function.
3. The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ about $y = x$.
4. $f\big(f^{-1}(x)\big) = x \implies x \in D^{-1}$, and $f^{-1}\big(f(x)\big) = x \implies x \in D$.

Property 3 explains property 1 pictorially: reflecting in $y = x$ swaps the two axes, and with them the roles of domain and range.

## The inverse trigonometric functions

The trigonometric functions of 11.4 and 11.5 are periodic and so fail the horizontal-line test outright. Each is therefore restricted to an interval on which it is monotonic before the inverse is taken, and that restriction becomes the range of the inverse.

| Property | $y = \arcsin x$ | $y = \arccos x$ | $y = \arctan x$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Domain | $[-1, 1]$ | $[-1, 1]$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |
| Range | $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ | $[0, \pi]$ | $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ |
| Parity | Odd | Neither | Odd |
| Monotonicity | Increasing | Decreasing | Increasing |

The domains are the ranges of the originals — $[-1,1]$ for sine and cosine, $\mathbb{R}$ for tangent — exactly as property 1 requires.

## Identities

$$\sin(\arcsin x) = x,\ x \in [-1, 1]; \qquad \cos(\arccos x) = x,\ x \in [-1, 1]; \qquad \tan(\arctan x) = x,\ x \in \mathbb{R}$$

$$\arcsin(\sin x) = x,\ x \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]; \qquad \arccos(\cos x) = x,\ x \in [0, \pi]; \qquad \arctan(\tan x) = x,\ x \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$

The second line carries a restriction the first does not. Composing in that order only returns $x$ when $x$ already lies in the restricted interval; outside it, the inverse returns the representative angle from that interval instead.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inverse function** | $g = f^{-1}$ where $f(g(x)) = x$ for all $x$ in the domain of $g$, and $g(f(x)) = x$ for all $x$ in the domain of $f$ |
| **Horizontal-line test** | A function has an inverse function only if no horizontal line intersects its graph at more than one point |
| **One-to-one function** | A function that must be so for an inverse function to exist |

# 11.7 Trigonometric Equations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A trigonometric equation has infinitely many solutions whenever it has one, because the functions are periodic. The answer is therefore a general solution: a formula indexed by an integer $k$.

## General solutions

| Equation | General solution |
|---|---|
| $\sin x = a$, $\lvert a \rvert < 1$ | $x = k\pi + (-1)^k \cdot \arcsin a$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| $\cos x = a$, $\lvert a \rvert < 1$ | $x = 2k\pi \pm \arccos a$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |
| $\tan x = a$ | $x = k\pi + \arctan a$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ |

The three forms differ because the symmetries differ. Cosine is even, so solutions come in $\pm$ pairs about the axis; sine is odd and symmetric about $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, which the alternating factor $(-1)^k$ encodes; tangent has period $\pi$ rather than $2\pi$, so a single family with step $\pi$ suffices.

## Type 1

$$a\sin^2 x + b\sin x + c = 0 \qquad (a \neq 0)$$

Quadratic in $\sin x$: solve for $\sin x$, then apply the general solution above.

## Type 2

$$a\sin x + b\cos x + c = 0 \qquad (a^2 + b^2 \neq 0,\ c \neq 0)$$

The reference angle formula of 11.3 collapses $a\sin x + b\cos x$ into a single sine, after which this is again an equation of the basic kind.

## Type 3

$$a\sin x + b\cos x = 0 \iff a\tan x + b = 0$$

$$a\sin^2 x + b\sin x\cos x + c\cos^2 x = 0 \iff a\tan^2 x + b\tan x + c = 0 \iff A\sin 2x + B\cos 2x = C$$

Both are homogeneous — every term has the same total degree in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ — so dividing through by the highest power of $\cos x$ converts the equation into one in $\tan x$ alone.

## Type 4

$$\sin f(x) = \sin \phi(x) \implies f(x) = 2k\pi + \phi(x) \ \text{ or } \ 2k\pi + \pi - \phi(x), \qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}$$

$$\cos f(x) = \cos \phi(x) \implies f(x) = 2k\pi \pm \phi(x), \qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}$$

$$\tan f(x) = \tan \phi(x) \implies f(x) = k\pi + \phi(x), \qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}$$

Equal values do not mean equal angles: they mean angles related by the symmetry of the function, which is what each right-hand side lists.

## Type 5

The substitution method can be used for equations with $\sin x \pm \cos x$ and $\sin x\cos x$. Let

$$\sin x \pm \cos x = t \qquad (\lvert t \rvert \leq \sqrt{2})$$

Then

$$\sin x\cos x = \pm\,\frac{t^2 - 1}{2}$$

Squaring $t$ produces $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x \pm 2\sin x\cos x = 1 \pm 2\sin x\cos x$, so the product is recoverable from $t$ and the whole equation becomes an equation in $t$. The bound $\lvert t \rvert \leq \sqrt{2}$ is the reference angle formula of 11.3 applied to $\sin x \pm \cos x$, and any root of the $t$-equation outside it must be discarded.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **General solution** | A formula indexed by $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ giving all solutions of a trigonometric equation |

title: Sets and Venn Diagrams
summary: A set is a collection of distinct numbers or objects. Each object in the set is called an element, or a member, of the set. Sets are written inside braces, so the set of primes below twenty is written
markdown:
# 0.1 Sets and Venn Diagrams

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a set is

A **set** is a collection of distinct numbers or objects. Each object in the set is called an **element**, or a member, of the set. Sets are written inside braces, so the set of primes below twenty is written

$$\{2,\,3,\,5,\,7,\,11,\,13,\,17,\,19\}$$

Three rules follow from that description, and every question about sets depends on them. An element is either in the set or not in the set — there is no halfway. The elements of a set are distinct, so each element can only appear once. And there is no fixed order when we describe the elements of a set, so listing the same elements in a different order does not make a different set.

Because a set is fixed entirely by which elements it holds, two sets are **equal** if they contain exactly the same elements.

## Membership and size notation

The symbol $\in$ is read "is an element of" or "is in", and $\notin$ is read "is not an element of" or "is not in". So if $A=\{1,2,3\}$, then $2 \in A$.

The number of elements in a set $A$ is written $n(A)$ or $\lvert A \rvert$.

That count is what separates the two types of set. A set is a **finite set** if $n(A)$ has a definite value — $\{1,2,3\}$ is finite because it has a limited number of elements. If instead a set has an endless number of elements, it is an **infinite set**.

## The empty set

The **empty set** is written $\{\ \}$ or $\emptyset$. It is the set that contains no elements at all.

## Subsets and proper subsets

Given two sets $A$ and $B$: if for any $x \in A$ it is also true that $x \in B$, then $A$ is a **subset** of $B$, written $A \subseteq B$.

Three consequences of that definition are worth memorising:

- Any set is a subset of itself, because every element of $A$ is certainly an element of $A$.
- $\emptyset$ is a subset of any set.
- $A = B$ if and only if $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$ — each set containing the other is exactly the condition that they hold the same elements.

A **proper subset** of a set $A$ is a subset of $A$ that is not equal to $A$, written $A \subset B$.

## Intersection and union

The **intersection** of two sets $A$ and $B$, written $A \cap B$, is the set of elements that are in both $A$ and $B$:

$$\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\} \cap \{2,3,5,7,9,11\} = \{2,3,5,7\}$$

Only $2$, $3$, $5$ and $7$ appear in both lists, so only they survive.

The **union** of two sets $A$ and $B$, written $A \cup B$, is the set of elements that are in either $A$ or $B$ — in effect, counting up all the elements in both sets:

$$\{1,2,3\} \cup \{4,5,6\} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$$

## The universal set and complements

A **universal set**, written $U$, is the set of all elements under discussion. The **complement** of $A$, written $A'$, is the set of all elements of $U$ that are *not* elements of $A$.

For example, if $U=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $A=\{2,3,5\}$, then

$$A' = \{1,4\}$$

Everything in $U$ that $A$ did not take is what is left.

## Number sets and interval notation

Alongside the brace notation above, the course also describes sets of numbers using **interval notation**, which is another way to describe a set on a number line, written with bracket notation.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Set** | Collection of distinct numbers or objects |
| **Element** (member) | Each individual object in a set; $\in$ means "is an element of", $\notin$ means "is not an element of" |
| **$n(A)$, $\lvert A\rvert$** | The number of elements in set $A$ |
| **Equal sets** | Two sets that contain exactly the same elements |
| **Empty set** | $\{\ \}$ or $\emptyset$; a set that contains no elements |
| **Finite set** | A set for which $n(A)$ has a definite value — a limited number of elements |
| **Infinite set** | A set with an endless number of elements |
| **Subset** | $A \subseteq B$: for any $x \in A$, $x \in B$ |
| **Proper subset** | $A \subset B$: a subset of $A$ that is not equal to $A$ |
| **Intersection** | $A \cap B$: the elements that are in both $A$ and $B$ |
| **Union** | $A \cup B$: the elements that are in either $A$ or $B$ |
| **Universal set** | $U$, the set of all elements |
| **Complement** | $A'$: the set of all elements of $U$ that are not elements of $A$ |
| **Interval notation** | Another way to describe a set on a number line, using bracket notation |

# 1.1 Patterns and Inductive Reasoning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Reasoning from a pattern

**Inductive reasoning** is reasoning that is based on patterns you observe. If you observe a pattern in a sequence, you can use inductive reasoning to tell what the next terms in the sequence will be.

The conclusion you reach that way is called a **conjecture**.

## Worked example

Consider the sequence

$$1,\ 2,\ 6,\ 24,\ 120$$

The terms are the factorials: $1 = 1!$, $2 = 2!$, $6 = 3!$, $24 = 4!$ and $120 = 5!$. Once the pattern is identified, the conjecture writes itself — the next term would be

$$6! = 720$$

## Testing a conjecture

A conjecture reached by inductive reasoning is only as good as the pattern behind it, so it can be wrong. A **counterexample** is an example for which the conjecture is incorrect. One counterexample is enough: if a single case does not fit, the conjecture as stated cannot stand.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inductive reasoning** | Reasoning that is based on patterns you observe |
| **Conjecture** | Conclusion you reach using inductive reasoning |
| **Counterexample** | Example for which a conjecture is incorrect |

## Nets

A **net** is a two-dimensional pattern that you can fold to form a three-dimensional figure.

What makes a net useful as a model is that it shows all of the surfaces of a figure in one view. A drawing of a solid always hides the faces at the back; a net lays every surface out flat at once, so nothing is concealed and every face can be counted and measured.

| **Net** | Two-dimensional pattern that you can fold to form a three-dimensional figure; it shows all of the surfaces of a figure in one view |

# 1.3 Points, Lines, and Planes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three undefined terms

A **point** is a location. It has no size, and it is represented by a small dot and named by a capital letter.

A **line** is a series of points that extends in two opposite directions without end. Because a line goes on for ever, there is no "whole" of it to name, so you name it using any two points on the line.

A **plane** is a flat surface that has no thickness. It extends for eternity, containing many lines and points.

Two words describe how these objects sit together. **Collinear points** are points that lie on the same line, and **coplanar** points and lines are those in the same plane.

## Postulates

A **postulate**, or axiom, is any statement or fact accepted as a starting point. Three of them fix how points, lines and planes may meet.

| Postulate | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Postulate 1-1** | Through any two points there is exactly one line |
| **Postulate 1-2** | If two lines intersect, then they intersect in exactly one point |
| **Postulate 1-3** | If two planes intersect, then they intersect in exactly one line |

Notice the pattern in the last two: the intersection is always one dimension lower than the objects meeting. Two lines meet at a point; two planes meet in a line.

## Always, sometimes, or never

Fill in each statement with *always*, *sometimes* or *never*.

| Statement | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Intersecting lines are __ coplanar | Always | Two lines that cross lie together in one flat surface |
| Two planes __ intersect in exactly one point | Never | By Postulate 1-3, planes that intersect do so in exactly one line, never a single point |
| Three points are __ coplanar | Always | A plane can always be found containing three points |
| A plane containing two points of a line __ contains the entire line | Always | Through those two points there is exactly one line (Postulate 1-1), and it lies in that plane |
| Four points are __ coplanar | Sometimes | They may all lie in one plane, but the fourth can lift off the plane of the other three |
| Two lines __ meet in more than one point | Never | By Postulate 1-2, intersecting lines meet in exactly one point |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Point** | Location with no size, represented by a small dot and named by a capital letter |
| **Line** | Series of points that extends in two opposite directions without end |
| **Plane** | Flat surface that has no thickness |
| **Collinear points** | Points that lie on the same line |
| **Coplanar** | Points and lines in the same plane |
| **Postulate** (axiom) | Any statement or fact taken as given |

# 1.4 Segments, Rays, Parallel Lines and Planes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Parts of a line

A **segment** is the part of a line consisting of two endpoints and all points between them. A segment therefore has a definite length, which a line does not.

A **ray** is the part of a line consisting of one endpoint and all the points of the line on one side of the endpoint. A ray is endless in one direction only.

**Opposite rays** are two collinear rays with the same endpoint. Opposite rays always form a line — between them they cover both directions from the shared endpoint, which is exactly what a line is.

## Lines that do not meet

There are two quite different ways for two lines to fail to intersect, and the distinction is whether they share a plane.

**Parallel lines** are coplanar lines that do not intersect. **Skew lines** are noncoplanar lines that do not intersect; they are neither intersecting nor parallel. Skew lines miss each other because they lie in different planes altogether.

**Parallel planes** are planes that never intersect.

## Always, sometimes, or never

| Statement | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Two parallel lines are __ coplanar | Always | Being coplanar is part of the definition of parallel lines |
| Two skew lines are __ coplanar | Never | Skew lines are noncoplanar by definition |
| Two opposite rays __ form a line | Always | Opposite rays always form a line |
| Two planes that do not intersect are __ parallel | Always | Parallel planes are exactly the planes that never intersect |
| Two lines that lie in parallel planes are __ parallel | Sometimes | They never meet, but if they are noncoplanar they are skew rather than parallel |
| Two lines in intersecting planes are __ skew | Sometimes | They may be skew, but they may also meet on the line where the planes intersect |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Segment** | Part of a line consisting of two endpoints and all points between them |
| **Ray** | Part of a line consisting of one endpoint and all the points of the line on one side of the endpoint |
| **Opposite rays** | Two collinear rays with the same endpoint; they always form a line |
| **Parallel lines** | Coplanar lines that do not intersect |
| **Skew lines** | Noncoplanar lines that do not intersect and are not parallel |
| **Parallel planes** | Planes that never intersect |

# 1.5 Measuring Segments

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The ruler postulate

**Postulate 1-5:** The points of a line can be put into one-to-one correspondence with the real numbers so that the distance between any two points is the absolute value of the difference of the corresponding numbers.

This is what allows a line to be measured at all. If point $A$ corresponds to the number $a$ and point $B$ corresponds to the number $b$, then

$$AB = \lvert a - b \rvert$$

The absolute value is there because distance does not depend on which endpoint you start from.

## Congruence and midpoints

**Congruent segments** are two segments with the same length.

A **midpoint** is a point that divides a segment into two congruent segments. A midpoint, or any line, ray, or other segment through a midpoint, is said to **bisect** the segment.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Postulate 1-5** | The points of a line can be put into one-to-one correspondence with the real numbers so that the distance between any two points is the absolute value of the difference of the corresponding numbers |
| **Congruent segments** | Two segments with the same length |
| **Midpoint** | Point that divides a segment into two congruent segments |
| **Bisect** | To divide into two congruent parts, as a midpoint does to a segment |

# 1.6 Measuring Angles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Angles

An **angle** is formed by two rays with the same endpoint.

**Congruent angles** are angles with the same measure. Note that this is a statement about measure only, not about how long the rays are drawn — rays have no length to compare.

## Classifying angles by measure

| Angle | Measure |
|---|---|
| **Acute angle** | Measure smaller than $90^\circ$ |
| **Right angle** | Measure equal to $90^\circ$ |
| **Obtuse angle** | Measure larger than $90^\circ$ |

## Adding and halving angles

The **Angle Addition Postulate** lets you add the measurements of two angles: where one angle sits alongside another, the two measures together give the measure of the whole angle. In symbols, for a point $C$ in the interior of $\angle ABD$,

$$m\angle ABC + m\angle CBD = m\angle ABD$$

Working the other way, an **angle bisector** splits an angle in half, using a line drawn from the vertex so that the two parts have equal measure.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Angle** | Formed by two rays with the same endpoint |
| **Congruent angles** | Angles with the same measure |
| **Acute angle** | Angle whose measure is smaller than $90^\circ$ |
| **Right angle** | Angle whose measure is $90^\circ$ |
| **Obtuse angle** | Angle whose measure is larger than $90^\circ$ |
| **Angle Addition Postulate** | Adding the measurements of two adjacent angles gives the measure of the whole angle |
| **Angle bisector** | A line that splits an angle in half |

# 1.7 Basic Constructions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The two tools

A **compass** is a geometric tool used to draw circles and parts of circles called arcs. A **straightedge** is a ruler with no markings on it.

The straightedge has no markings because a construction may not measure anything. Every length and every angle in the work below is transferred with the compass, never read off a scale, and that is why the phrase "with the same compass setting" appears in every construction.

## Constructing congruent segment CD given a segment AB

1. Draw a ray with point $C$.
2. Open the compass to the length of $AB$.
3. With the same compass setting, put the compass point on point $C$, draw an arc that intersects the ray, and label the point of intersection $D$.

## Constructing congruent angle S given an angle A

1. Draw a ray with endpoint $S$.
2. With the compass point on point $A$, draw an arc intersecting the sides of angle $A$; label the points of intersection $B$ and $C$.
3. With the same compass setting, put the compass point on point $S$, draw an arc, and label the point of intersection with the ray as $R$.
4. Open the compass to the length of $B$ to $C$; keeping the same compass setting, put the compass point on $R$ and draw an arc to locate point $T$.
5. Draw ray $ST$.

## Perpendicular lines and the perpendicular bisector

**Perpendicular lines** are two lines that intersect to form right angles.

A **perpendicular bisector** is a line, segment, or ray that is perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint, thereby bisecting the segment into two congruent segments. It therefore does two jobs at once — it cuts the segment in half and meets it squarely.

### Constructing the perpendicular bisector XY given AB

1. Put the compass point on point $A$ and draw a long arc, being sure the opening is greater than $\tfrac{1}{2}AB$.
2. With the same compass setting, put the compass point on point $B$ and draw another long arc. Label the points where the two arcs intersect as $X$ and $Y$.
3. Draw $XY$. The point of intersection of $AB$ and $XY$ is the midpoint, and the sides form right angles.

The opening must be greater than $\tfrac{1}{2}AB$ in step 1, because otherwise the two arcs are too small to reach each other and there are no intersection points to label.

## The angle bisector

An **angle bisector** is a ray that divides an angle into two congruent coplanar angles.

### Constructing the angle bisector AX given an angle A

1. Put the compass point on vertex $A$. Draw an arc that intersects the sides of angle $A$. Label the points of intersection $B$ and $C$.
2. Put the compass point on point $C$ and draw an arc. With the same compass setting, draw an arc using point $B$, being sure the arcs intersect. Label the point where the two arcs intersect as $X$.
3. Draw $AX$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Compass** | Geometric tool used to draw circles and parts of circles called arcs |
| **Straightedge** | Ruler with no markings on it |
| **Perpendicular lines** | Two lines that intersect to form right angles |
| **Perpendicular bisector** | Line, segment, or ray that is perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint, bisecting it into two congruent segments |
| **Angle bisector** | Ray that divides an angle into two congruent coplanar angles |

# 1.8 The Coordinate Plane

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distance formula

For two points $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ in the coordinate plane, the distance between them is

$$d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$$

The differences are squared, so it makes no difference which point you call the first — a sign error in $x_2 - x_1$ disappears in the squaring.

## The midpoint formula

The midpoint of the segment joining $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is

$$M = \left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$$

Each coordinate of the midpoint is simply the average of the corresponding coordinates of the two endpoints, which is what "halfway between" means in each direction separately.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Distance formula** | $d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$ |
| **Midpoint formula** | $M=\left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$ |

title: Conditional Statements
summary: A conditional is an if-then statement. The part following the *if* is the hypothesis, and the part following the *then* is the conclusion. Written with letters, a conditional is p \to q: "if p then q"
markdown:
# 2.1 Conditional Statements

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Hypothesis and conclusion

A **conditional** is an if-then statement. The part following the *if* is the **hypothesis**, and the part following the *then* is the **conclusion**.

Written with letters, a conditional is $p \to q$: "if $p$ then $q$", or "$p$ implies $q$", where $p$ is the hypothesis and $q$ is the conclusion.

For example: *if today is raining, I need to bring an umbrella.* Here "today is raining" is the hypothesis and "I need to bring an umbrella" is the conclusion.

## Truth value

The **truth value** of a conditional is whether the conditional is true or false. Judging it means asking whether the hypothesis really does force the conclusion.

If a conditional is false you have to provide a **counterexample** — a case in which the hypothesis holds but the conclusion does not. Asserting that a conditional is false without producing such a case proves nothing.

## The converse

The **converse** of a conditional switches the hypothesis and the conclusion: from $p \to q$ you get $q \to p$.

The converse of the umbrella statement is *if I brought an umbrella, today is raining.* This shows why converses have to be tested separately rather than assumed: the original conditional may well be true while its converse is not, since an umbrella might have been packed for any number of reasons.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conditional** | An if-then statement, $p \to q$ |
| **Hypothesis** | The part of a conditional following the *if* |
| **Conclusion** | The part of a conditional following the *then* |
| **Truth value** | Whether the conditional is true or false |
| **Counterexample** | The case you must give to show a conditional is false |
| **Converse** | The conditional with hypothesis and conclusion switched, $q \to p$ |

# 2.2 Biconditionals and Definitions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Biconditionals

When a conditional and its converse are both true, you can combine them as a true **biconditional**, connecting the hypothesis and the conclusion with the words *if and only if*:

$$p \leftrightarrow q$$

Both halves must be true first. A biconditional claims $p \to q$ and $q \to p$ at once, so it is only available when each of those directions has been checked on its own.

## What makes a good definition

A **good definition** is a statement that can help you identify or classify an object. Three requirements follow from that purpose:

- It **uses clearly understood terms**. The terms should be commonly understood or already defined, otherwise the definition explains one unknown by another.
- It is **precise**, avoiding words such as *large*, *sort of* and *almost*, which cannot be used to decide whether a particular object qualifies.
- It is **reversible** — you can rewrite it as a true biconditional. This is the test that the definition captures exactly the right objects: everything defined has the property, and everything with the property is one of the objects defined.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biconditional** | The combination of a conditional and its converse when both are true, joined by *if and only if* |
| **Good definition** | Statement that can help you identify or classify an object; it uses clearly understood terms, is precise, and is reversible |

# 2.3 Deductive Reasoning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Reasoning from given statements

**Deductive reasoning**, also called logical reasoning, is the process of reasoning logically from given statements to a conclusion. If the given statements are true, then deductive reasoning will always produce a true conclusion.

That guarantee is what separates it from the inductive reasoning of 1.1. Inductive reasoning generalises from a pattern and can be overturned by a counterexample; deductive reasoning takes statements already accepted as true and extracts what must follow from them.

## The two laws

| Law | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Law of Detachment** | If a conditional is true and its hypothesis is true, then its conclusion is true |
| **Law of Syllogism** | If $p \to q$ and $q \to r$ are true statements, then $p \to r$ is true |

The Law of Syllogism allows you to state a conclusion from two true conditional statements when the conclusion of one statement is the hypothesis of the other. The shared middle statement $q$ is what links them: the first conditional carries you as far as $q$, and the second carries you on from $q$ to $r$, so the two chain into a single conditional from $p$ to $r$.

A conditional of the kind these laws are applied to: *if a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 10.* Given also that a particular number ends in 0, the Law of Detachment lets you conclude that it is divisible by 10.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Deductive reasoning** (logical reasoning) | Process of reasoning logically from given statements to a conclusion |
| **Law of Detachment** | If a conditional is true and its hypothesis is true, then its conclusion is true |
| **Law of Syllogism** | If $p \to q$ and $q \to r$ are true statements, then $p \to r$ is true |

# 2.4 Reasoning in Algebra

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Properties of equality

Every step of algebra used inside a geometry proof has to be named, and these are the properties that name them.

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Addition Property** | If $a=b$, then $a+c=b+c$ |
| **Subtraction Property** | If $a=b$, then $a-c=b-c$ |
| **Multiplication Property** | If $a=b$, then $a \cdot c = b \cdot c$ |
| **Division Property** | If $a=b$ and $c \neq 0$, then $\dfrac{a}{c}=\dfrac{b}{c}$ |
| **Reflexive Property** | $a=a$ |
| **Symmetric Property** | If $a=b$, then $b=a$ |
| **Transitive Property** | If $a=b$ and $b=c$, then $a=c$ |
| **Substitution Property** | If $a=b$, then $b$ can replace $a$ in any expression |
| **Distributive Property** | $a(b+c)=ab+ac$ |

The condition $c \neq 0$ on the Division Property is the only restriction in the list, and it is there because division by zero is not defined.

## Properties of congruence

The same three structural properties hold for congruence of segments, so that congruence statements can be rearranged and chained in a proof exactly as equalities are.

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Reflexive Property of Congruence** | $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AB}$ |
| **Symmetric Property of Congruence** | If $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CD}$, then $\overline{CD} \cong \overline{AB}$ |
| **Transitive Property of Congruence** | If $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CD}$ and $\overline{CD} \cong \overline{EF}$, then $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{EF}$ |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Addition Property** | If $a=b$, then $a+c=b+c$ |
| **Subtraction Property** | If $a=b$, then $a-c=b-c$ |
| **Multiplication Property** | If $a=b$, then $ac=bc$ |
| **Division Property** | If $a=b$ and $c\neq 0$, then $a/c=b/c$ |
| **Reflexive Property** | $a=a$ |
| **Symmetric Property** | If $a=b$, then $b=a$ |
| **Transitive Property** | If $a=b$ and $b=c$, then $a=c$ |
| **Substitution Property** | If $a=b$, then $b$ can replace $a$ in any expression |
| **Distributive Property** | $a(b+c)=ab+ac$ |

# 2.5 Proving Angles Congruent

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Supplementary and complementary angles

**Supplementary angles** are two angles that add up to $180^\circ$. **Complementary angles** are two angles that add up to $90^\circ$.

These two relationships are the source of most of the congruence results below, because two angles that make up the same total have no freedom left once one of them is known.

## The theorems

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 2-1** | Vertical angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-2: Congruent Supplements Theorem** | If two angles are supplements of the same angle (or of congruent angles), then the two angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-3: Congruent Complements Theorem** | If two angles are complements of the same angle (or of congruent angles), then the two angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-4** | All right angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-5** | If two angles are congruent and supplementary, then each is a right angle |

Theorem 2-4 is immediate once you know that congruent angles are angles with the same measure: every right angle measures $90^\circ$, so any two right angles have the same measure.

## Why Theorem 2-5 holds

Suppose two angles are both congruent and supplementary, and let the measure of each be $x$. Congruent angles have equal measure, so both are $x$; supplementary angles add to $180$, so

$$x + x = 180$$
$$2x = 180$$
$$x = 90$$

Each angle measures $90^\circ$, so each is a right angle. The two steps use the properties of 2.4 — combining like terms and then the Division Property.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Supplementary angles** | Two angles that add up to $180^\circ$ |
| **Complementary angles** | Two angles that add up to $90^\circ$ |
| **Theorem 2-1** | Vertical angles are congruent |
| **Congruent Supplements Theorem** | If two angles are supplements of the same angle (or of congruent angles), then the two angles are congruent |
| **Congruent Complements Theorem** | If two angles are complements of the same angle (or of congruent angles), then the two angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-4** | All right angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-5** | If two angles are congruent and supplementary, then each is a right angle |

# 3.1 Properties of Parallel Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Transversals and angle pairs

A **transversal** is a line that intersects two coplanar lines at two distinct points. It creates eight angles, four at each crossing point, and the names of the pairs record where the two angles sit.

Angles between the two lines are *interior*; angles outside them are *exterior*. A pair is *alternate* when its two angles are on opposite sides of the transversal, and *same-side* when they are on the same side of it. **Corresponding angles** occupy matching positions at the two crossings.

In the guide's numbered diagram, angles 4 and 6 are **alternate interior angles**, angles 4 and 5 are **same-side interior angles**, and angles 4 and 8 are **corresponding angles**.

## What happens when the lines are parallel

| Result | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate** (Postulate 3-1) | If a transversal intersects two parallel lines, then corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If a transversal intersects two parallel lines, then alternate interior angles are congruent |
| **Same-Side Interior Angles Theorem** | If a transversal intersects two parallel lines, then same-side interior angles are supplementary |
| **Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem** | If a transversal intersects two parallel lines, then alternate exterior angles are congruent |
| **Same-Side Exterior Angles Theorem** | If a transversal intersects two parallel lines, then same-side exterior angles are supplementary |

The guide numbers these results 3-1 to 3-4 after the Corresponding Angles Postulate.

There is a pattern here worth carrying into every problem: the *alternate* pairs and the *corresponding* pairs are congruent, while the *same-side* pairs are supplementary. So a same-side pair gives you

$$m\angle 1 + m\angle 2 = 180$$

rather than an equality, and confusing the two is the usual way marks are lost.

Note also that all of these hold only when the two lines are parallel. Without that condition none of the relationships is available.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Transversal** | Line that intersects two coplanar lines at two distinct points |
| **Alternate interior angles** | Interior angles on opposite sides of the transversal; congruent when the lines are parallel |
| **Same-side interior angles** | Interior angles on the same side of the transversal; supplementary when the lines are parallel |
| **Corresponding angles** | Angles in matching positions at the two crossings; congruent when the lines are parallel |
| **Alternate exterior angles** | Exterior angles on opposite sides of the transversal; congruent when the lines are parallel |
| **Same-side exterior angles** | Exterior angles on the same side of the transversal; supplementary when the lines are parallel |

# 3.2 Proving Lines Parallel

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Running the angle results backwards

Every result in 3.1 starts from parallel lines and concludes something about angles. The results of this section are their converses: they start from the angles and conclude that the lines are parallel. That reversal is the whole content of the section — each postulate and theorem of 3.1 has an opposite that works in the other direction.

| Result | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Converse of the Corresponding Angles Postulate** (Postulate 3-2) | If two lines and a transversal form corresponding angles that are congruent, then the two lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-5: Converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If two lines and a transversal form alternate interior angles that are congruent, then the two lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-6: Converse of the Same-Side Interior Angles Theorem** | If two lines and a transversal form same-side interior angles that are supplementary, then the two lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-7: Converse of the Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem** | If two lines and a transversal form alternate exterior angles that are congruent, then the two lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-8: Converse of the Same-Side Exterior Angles Theorem** | If two lines and a transversal form same-side exterior angles that are supplementary, then the two lines are parallel |

Keep the hypothesis of each converse exactly right: the alternate and corresponding versions require *congruent* angles, while both same-side versions require *supplementary* angles. Using the wrong condition proves nothing.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Converse of the Corresponding Angles Postulate** | If two lines and a transversal form congruent corresponding angles, then the lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-5** | If two lines and a transversal form congruent alternate interior angles, then the lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-6** | If two lines and a transversal form supplementary same-side interior angles, then the lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-7** | If two lines and a transversal form congruent alternate exterior angles, then the lines are parallel |
| **Theorem 3-8** | If two lines and a transversal form supplementary same-side exterior angles, then the lines are parallel |

# 3.3 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Three theorems about a shared line

These theorems let you conclude that two lines are parallel without looking at any angle pair, simply from how each of them relates to a third line.

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 3-9** | If two lines are parallel to the same line, then they are parallel to each other |
| **Theorem 3-10** | In a plane, if two lines are perpendicular to the same line, then they are parallel to each other |
| **Theorem 3-11** | In a plane, if a line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, then it is also perpendicular to the other |

Theorems 3-10 and 3-11 both carry the condition *in a plane*, and it cannot be dropped. Outside a plane, two lines perpendicular to the same line need not be parallel, since noncoplanar lines that do not meet are skew rather than parallel.

Theorem 3-11 is the useful one in problems that mix the two relationships: it says a perpendicular to one of a pair of parallel lines cuts the other at a right angle too, so a single right angle in the figure gives you a second one for free.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 3-9** | If two lines are parallel to the same line, then they are parallel to each other |
| **Theorem 3-10** | In a plane, if two lines are perpendicular to the same line, then they are parallel to each other |
| **Theorem 3-11** | In a plane, if a line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, then it is also perpendicular to the other |

# 3.4 Parallel Lines and the Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The angle sum of a triangle

**Theorem 3-12: Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem.** The sum of the measures of the angles of a triangle is $180$.

For a triangle $ABC$,

$$m\angle A + m\angle B + m\angle C = 180$$

This is why two angles of a triangle always determine the third: subtract their sum from $180$.

## Exterior angles

The **remote interior angles** of an exterior angle are the two nonadjacent interior angles of the triangle.

**Theorem 3-13: Triangle Exterior Angle Theorem.** The measure of each exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the measures of its two remote interior angles.

If $\angle 1$ is an exterior angle and $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$ are its remote interior angles, then

$$m\angle 1 = m\angle 2 + m\angle 3$$

The word *remote* is doing real work: the interior angle next to the exterior angle is not included, only the two further away.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem** | The sum of the measures of the angles of a triangle is $180$ |
| **Remote interior angles** | The two nonadjacent interior angles for a given exterior angle |
| **Triangle Exterior Angle Theorem** | The measure of each exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the measures of its two remote interior angles |

# 3.5 The Polygon Angle-Sum Theorems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What counts as a polygon

A **polygon** is a closed plane figure with at least three sides that are segments. The sides intersect only at their endpoints, and no adjacent sides are collinear.

Each clause rules something out. Sides that crossed anywhere but at endpoints would not enclose a single region, and two adjacent collinear sides would really be one longer side with a mark on it.

## Convex and concave

A **convex polygon** has no diagonal with points outside the polygon. A **concave polygon** has at least one diagonal with points outside the polygon.

## The two angle-sum theorems

**Theorem 3-14: Polygon Angle-Sum Theorem.** The sum of the measures of the angles of an $n$-gon is

$$(n-2)\,180$$

**Theorem 3-15: Polygon Exterior Angle-Sum Theorem.** The sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a polygon, one at each vertex, is $360$.

The contrast is worth noticing. The interior sum grows with the number of sides, since $(n-2)180$ depends on $n$; the exterior sum is $360$ for every polygon, however many sides it has.

Setting $n=3$ in Theorem 3-14 gives $(3-2)180 = 180$, which is the Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem of 3.4 — the triangle case is included in the general rule.

## Equilateral, equiangular, and regular

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Equilateral polygon** | All sides congruent |
| **Equiangular polygon** | All angles congruent |
| **Regular polygon** | Both equilateral and equiangular |

A polygon needs both conditions to be regular; having only one of them is not enough.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polygon** | Closed plane figure with at least three sides that are segments; the sides intersect only at their endpoints, and no adjacent sides are collinear |
| **Convex polygon** | Polygon with no diagonal with points outside the polygon |
| **Concave polygon** | Polygon with at least one diagonal with points outside the polygon |
| **Polygon Angle-Sum Theorem** | The sum of the measures of the angles of an $n$-gon is $(n-2)180$ |
| **Polygon Exterior Angle-Sum Theorem** | The sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a polygon, one at each vertex, is $360$ |
| **Equilateral polygon** | All sides congruent |
| **Equiangular polygon** | All angles congruent |
| **Regular polygon** | Both equilateral and equiangular |
