# 3.7 Slopes of Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Not tested

The guide marks both 3.6 Lines in the Coordinate Plane and 3.7 Slopes of Parallel and Perpendicular Lines as not tested. The one piece of content it records is the slope formula.

## Slope

The **slope** of a line, written $m$, is its rise divided by its run:

$$m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$$

The rise is the change in $y$ between two points of the line and the run is the change in $x$ between the same two points, so both differences must be taken in the same order.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Slope** | $m = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$ |

# 3.8 Constructing Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Constructing line NM parallel to line L

1. Label two points $H$ and $J$ on $L$, and draw $HN$.
2. Construct angle 1 with vertex at $N$ so that angle $1 = \angle NHJ$ and the two angles are corresponding angles. Label the line constructed $M$.

The construction works because of the Converse of the Corresponding Angles Postulate from 3.2: once you have copied the angle into the corresponding position, congruent corresponding angles force the two lines to be parallel. Copying the angle is the congruent-angle construction of 1.7.

## Constructing line RG from point R perpendicular to line L

1. Open the compass to a size greater than the distance from $R$ to $L$. With the compass point on point $R$, draw an arc that intersects $L$ at two points, and label the points $E$ and $F$.
2. Place the compass point on $E$ and make an arc.
3. Keeping the same compass setting, with the compass tip on $F$, draw an arc that intersects the arc from step 2. Label the point of intersection $G$.
4. Draw line $RG$.

The opening in step 1 has to be greater than the distance from $R$ to $L$, or the arc will not reach the line and there will be no points $E$ and $F$ to work from.

markdown:
# 4.1 Congruent Figures

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Congruent polygons

**Congruent polygons** are polygons with congruent corresponding parts — their matching sides and matching angles. The matching vertices are called **corresponding vertices**.

When you name congruent polygons, always list corresponding vertices in the same order. The naming is not a label but a statement of which part matches which, so a statement such as $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$ tells the reader that $A$ matches $D$, $B$ matches $E$ and $C$ matches $F$, and hence that $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{DE}$ and $\angle A \cong \angle D$. List the vertices in the wrong order and you have asserted the wrong correspondence.

## The third angles

**Theorem 4-1.** If two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another triangle, then the third angles are congruent.

This follows from the Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem of 3.4. The three angles of each triangle total $180$, so once two of them are matched, what is left over in each triangle is the same amount:

$$m\angle 3 = 180 - (m\angle 1 + m\angle 2)$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Congruent polygons** | Polygons with congruent corresponding parts — matching sides and angles |
| **Corresponding vertices** | The matching vertices of congruent polygons; always listed in the same order when naming the polygons |
| **Theorem 4-1** | If two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another triangle, then the third angles are congruent |

title: Triangle Congruence by SSS and SAS
summary: Congruent triangles have six pairs of congruent corresponding parts — three sides and three angles. The postulates of this section and the next say that certain sets of three are enough to force all s
markdown:
# 4.2 Triangle Congruence by SSS and SAS

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why shortcuts exist

Congruent triangles have six pairs of congruent corresponding parts — three sides and three angles. The postulates of this section and the next say that certain sets of three are enough to force all six, so a proof never has to check every part.

## The two postulates

**Postulate 4-1: Side-Side-Side (SSS) Postulate.** If three sides of one triangle are congruent to the three sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.

**Postulate 4-2: Side-Angle-Side (SAS) Postulate.** If two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.

| Test | What must be congruent |
|---|---|
| **SSS** | Three sides |
| **SAS** | Two sides and the angle included between them |

The word **included** in SAS is the whole of the condition: the angle has to be the one lying between the two sides you have matched. An angle elsewhere in the triangle does not satisfy the postulate.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **SSS Postulate** | If three sides of one triangle are congruent to the three sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent |
| **SAS Postulate** | If two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent |
| **Included angle** | The angle lying between the two named sides |

title: Triangle Congruence by ASA and AAS
summary: Postulate 4-3: Angle-Side-Angle (ASA) Postulate. If two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of another triangle, then the two triangles are c
markdown:
# 4.3 Triangle Congruence by ASA and AAS

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The two results

**Postulate 4-3: Angle-Side-Angle (ASA) Postulate.** If two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.

**Theorem 4-2: Angle-Angle-Side (AAS) Theorem.** If two angles and a nonincluded side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the corresponding nonincluded side of another triangle, then the triangles are congruent.

| Test | What must be congruent |
|---|---|
| **ASA** | Two angles and the side included between them |
| **AAS** | Two angles and a nonincluded side |

Both begin with two angles, and they are told apart by where the side sits: ASA needs the side *between* the two angles, AAS a side *outside* them. AAS is available at all because of Theorem 4-1 — matching two angles matches the third as well, so the nonincluded side becomes an included side for a different pair of angles.

## There is no ASS

Note that the proving way of ASS does not exist. Two sides and an angle that is *not* included between them do not force the triangles to be congruent, so an argument that matches parts in that order proves nothing. The four valid tests for triangles in general are SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **ASA Postulate** | If two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent |
| **AAS Theorem** | If two angles and a nonincluded side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the corresponding nonincluded side of another triangle, then the triangles are congruent |

title: Using Congruent Triangles: CPCTC
summary: Once you have proved two triangles congruent, you can make conclusions about their other parts, because by definition corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent — abbreviated CPCTC. This
markdown:
# 4.4 Using Congruent Triangles: CPCTC

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What CPCTC gives you

Once you have proved two triangles congruent, you can make conclusions about their other parts, because by definition **corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent** — abbreviated **CPCTC**.

This is what makes triangle congruence worth proving. The tests of 4.2 and 4.3 each need only three pairs of congruent parts, but congruence then hands back all six. So the standard shape of a proof is: use SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS or HL to establish that the triangles are congruent, then quote CPCTC to claim the particular side or angle you actually wanted.

The order matters. CPCTC is a conclusion drawn *after* congruence has been established, never a reason for establishing it.

The guide returns to this idea at 4.7, Using Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles, where the same abbreviation is applied in longer proofs.

## Keywords

# 4.5 Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Naming the parts

In an isosceles triangle, the two congruent sides are the **legs** and the third side is the **base**. The **vertex angle** is the angle formed by the two congruent sides, and the other two angles are the **base angles**.

## The isosceles triangle theorems

**Theorem 4-3: Isosceles Triangle Theorem.** If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent.

**Theorem 4-4: Converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem.** If two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite the angles are congruent.

Taken together, these say that congruent sides and congruent angles come as a pair in a triangle: you may argue from equal sides to equal angles, or from equal angles to equal sides. Both link a side to the angle *opposite* it, not to the angles beside it.

**Theorem 4-5.** The bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is the perpendicular bisector of the base.

One line therefore does three jobs at once in an isosceles triangle — it halves the vertex angle, halves the base, and meets the base at right angles.

## Corollaries

A **corollary** is a statement that follows immediately from a theorem.

| Corollary | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Corollary to Theorem 4-3** | If a triangle is equilateral, then the triangle is equiangular |
| **Corollary to Theorem 4-4** | If a triangle is equiangular, then the triangle is equilateral |

Each corollary is its theorem applied to all three pairs of parts at once rather than to one pair.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Legs** | The congruent sides of an isosceles triangle |
| **Base** | The third side of an isosceles triangle |
| **Vertex angle** | The angle formed by the two congruent sides |
| **Base angles** | The other two angles of an isosceles triangle |
| **Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent |
| **Converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite the angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 4-5** | The bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is the perpendicular bisector of the base |
| **Corollary** | Statement that follows immediately from a theorem |

# 4.6 Congruence in Right Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Naming the sides

In a right triangle, the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite the right angle, and it is the longest side. The other two sides are the **legs**.

## The Hypotenuse-Leg Theorem

**Theorem 4-6: Hypotenuse-Leg (HL) Theorem.** If the hypotenuse and a leg of one right triangle are congruent to the hypotenuse and a leg of another right triangle, then the triangles are congruent.

HL is a test available only for right triangles. Matching a hypotenuse, a leg and the right angle is a matching of two sides and a nonincluded angle, which in a general triangle proves nothing — knowing the triangles are right-angled is exactly what rescues it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hypotenuse** | In a right triangle, the side opposite the right angle and the longest side |
| **Legs** | The other two sides of a right triangle |
| **Hypotenuse-Leg (HL) Theorem** | If the hypotenuse and a leg of one right triangle are congruent to the hypotenuse and a leg of another right triangle, then the triangles are congruent |

# 5.1 Midsegments of Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The midsegment

A **midsegment** of a triangle is a segment connecting the midpoints of two sides.

**Theorem 5-1: Triangle Midsegment Theorem.** If a segment joins the midpoints of two sides of a triangle, then the segment is parallel to the third side, and half its length.

So a single midsegment gives you two facts at once. If $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of two sides of a triangle and $\overline{BC}$ is the third side, then

$$\overline{MN} \parallel \overline{BC} \qquad \text{and} \qquad MN = \tfrac{1}{2}BC$$

Read the length relation carefully in both directions: the midsegment is half the third side, so the third side is twice the midsegment.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Midsegment** | Segment connecting the midpoints of two sides of a triangle |
| **Triangle Midsegment Theorem** | If a segment joins the midpoints of two sides of a triangle, then the segment is parallel to the third side, and half its length |

# 5.2 Bisectors in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Perpendicular bisectors and distance from endpoints

**Theorem 5-2: Perpendicular Bisector Theorem.** If a point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment, then it is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment.

**Theorem 5-3: Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem.** If a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

## Angle bisectors and distance from the sides

**Theorem 5-4: Angle Bisector Theorem.** If a point is on the bisector of an angle, then the point is equidistant from the sides of the angle.

**Theorem 5-5: Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem.** If a point in the interior of an angle is equidistant from the sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector.

## How the four fit together

| Bisector | Being on it means | And the converse |
|---|---|---|
| **Perpendicular bisector of a segment** | Equidistant from the two endpoints | Equidistant from the endpoints puts a point on it |
| **Bisector of an angle** | Equidistant from the two sides of the angle | Equidistant from the sides puts a point on it |

Each pair works in both directions, so a bisector can be used either to produce equal distances or to prove that a point lies on it. Note the extra condition in Theorem 5-5: the point must be *in the interior* of the angle.

These theorems are what make the concurrency results of 5.3 possible, since each point of concurrency is defined by being equidistant from something.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Perpendicular Bisector Theorem** | If a point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment, then it is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment |
| **Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem** | If a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment |
| **Angle Bisector Theorem** | If a point is on the bisector of an angle, then the point is equidistant from the sides of the angle |
| **Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem** | If a point in the interior of an angle is equidistant from the sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector |

# 5.3 Concurrent Lines, Medians, and Altitudes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Concurrency

Lines are **concurrent** when three or more of them intersect in one point, and that point is the **point of concurrency**.

A triangle has four such points, one for each of four families of lines drawn from its sides or vertices.

## The perpendicular bisectors and the angle bisectors

**Theorem 5-6.** The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the vertices.

**Theorem 5-7.** The bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the sides.

The distances in these two theorems are exactly what Theorems 5-2 and 5-4 of the previous section promise, applied to all three sides or angles at once.

The **circumcenter** is the point of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors. Because it is equidistant from the vertices, a circle drawn about it passes through all three of them: when a circle is circumscribed about a triangle, it surrounds the triangle.

The **incenter** is the point of concurrency of the angle bisectors. Because it is equidistant from the sides, a circle drawn about it touches all three sides: when a circle is inscribed in a triangle, it is inside the triangle.

## Medians and altitudes

A **median** is a segment whose endpoints are a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.

**Theorem 5-8.** The medians of a triangle are concurrent at a point that is $\tfrac{2}{3}$ the distance from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

The point of concurrency of the medians is the **centroid**. The fraction is measured from the vertex, so the centroid sits twice as far from the vertex as it does from the midpoint.

An **altitude** is a perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side.

**Theorem 5-9.** The lines that contain the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

The point of concurrency of the altitudes is the **orthocenter**. Note that Theorem 5-9 is stated for the *lines containing* the altitudes, because for some triangles the altitudes themselves meet outside the triangle.

## The four points of concurrency

| Point | Concurrency of | Property |
|---|---|---|
| **Circumcenter** | Perpendicular bisectors of the sides | Equidistant from the vertices; centre of the circumscribed circle |
| **Incenter** | Angle bisectors | Equidistant from the sides; centre of the inscribed circle |
| **Centroid** | Medians | $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the way from each vertex to the opposite midpoint |
| **Orthocenter** | Altitudes | The lines containing the altitudes are concurrent there |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Concurrent** | When three or more lines intersect in one point |
| **Point of concurrency** | The point at which concurrent lines intersect |
| **Circumcenter** | Point of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors |
| **Circumscribed circle** | Circle about a triangle that surrounds it |
| **Incenter** | Point of concurrency of the angle bisectors |
| **Inscribed circle** | Circle in a triangle that is inside it |
| **Median** | Segment whose endpoints are a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side |
| **Centroid** | Point of concurrency of the medians |
| **Altitude** | Perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side |
| **Orthocenter** | Point of concurrency of the altitudes |

markdown:
# 5.4 Inverses, Contrapositives, and Indirect Reasoning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Negation

The **negation** of a statement has the opposite truth value. If a statement is true its negation is false, and if it is false its negation is true. Negation is written with a tilde: the negation of $p$ is $\sim p$.

## Inverse and contrapositive

The **inverse** of a conditional negates both the hypothesis and the conclusion:

- Conditional: if it is finals, then students are sad
- Inverse: if it is not finals, then students are not sad

The **contrapositive** switches the hypothesis and conclusion *and* negates both:

- Conditional: if it is finals, then students are sad
- Contrapositive: if students are not sad, then it is not finals

## The four related statements

| Statement | Symbols |
|---|---|
| **Conditional** | $p \to q$ |
| **Negation** (not $p$) | $\sim p$ |
| **Inverse** | $\sim p \to \sim q$ |
| **Contrapositive** | $\sim q \to \sim p$ |

**Equivalent statements** have the same truth value. A conditional and its contrapositive are related this way, which is why proving the contrapositive is as good as proving the original.

## Indirect reasoning

In **indirect reasoning**, all possibilities are considered and then all but one are proved false; the remaining possibility must be true.

A proof written this way is an **indirect proof**. It works because a statement and its negation often are the only possibilities: if there are just two, ruling one out establishes the other.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Negation** | A statement with the opposite truth value; the negation of $p$ is $\sim p$ |
| **Inverse** | Negates both the hypothesis and the conclusion: $\sim p \to \sim q$ |
| **Contrapositive** | Switches hypothesis and conclusion and negates both: $\sim q \to \sim p$ |
| **Equivalent statements** | Statements that have the same truth value |
| **Indirect reasoning** | All possibilities are considered and then all but one are proved false; the remaining possibility must be true |
| **Indirect proof** | A proof by indirect reasoning, using that a statement and its negation are often the only possibilities |

# 5.5 Inequalities in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Comparing by what is left over

**Comparison Property of Inequality.** If $a = b + c$ and $c > 0$, then $a > b$.

This is the engine behind the next result. **Corollary to the Triangle Exterior Angle Theorem:** the measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than the measure of each of its remote interior angles.

The exterior angle equals the *sum* of the two remote interior angles (Theorem 3-13), and each of those angles is positive, so the sum must exceed either one on its own — which is precisely the Comparison Property with $a$ the exterior angle and $b$, $c$ the two remote interior angles.

## Longer sides and larger angles

**Theorem 5-10.** If two sides of a triangle are not congruent, then the larger angle lies opposite the longer side.

**Theorem 5-11.** If two angles of a triangle are not congruent, then the longer side lies opposite the larger angle.

These are converses of each other, and between them they say that in any triangle the order of the sides by length matches the order of the angles opposite them. Both are about parts that lie *opposite* one another, exactly as in the isosceles triangle theorems of 4.5 — those handled the congruent case, these handle the unequal case.

## The Triangle Inequality Theorem

**Theorem 5-12: Triangle Inequality Theorem.** The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side.

For a triangle $XYZ$ this gives three separate inequalities:

$$XY + YZ > XZ \qquad YZ + ZX > YX \qquad ZX + XY > ZY$$

All three must hold. In practice the shortest test is to add the two smallest lengths and compare them with the largest, since that is the inequality most likely to fail.

## Worked examples: can a triangle have sides with the given lengths?

| Lengths | Test | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| $2$ in, $3$ in, $6$ in | $2+3=5$, and $5 < 6$ | No |
| $11$ cm, $12$ cm, $15$ cm | $11+12=23>15$; $11+15=26>12$; $12+15=27>11$ | Yes |
| $8$ m, $10$ m, $19$ m | $8+10=18$, and $18 < 19$ | No |
| $1$ cm, $15$ cm, $15$ cm | $1+15=16>15$; $15+15=30>1$ | Yes |
| $2$ yd, $9$ yd, $10$ yd | $2+9=11>10$; $2+10=12>9$; $9+10=19>2$ | Yes |
| $4$ m, $5$ m, $9$ m | $4+5=9$, which is not greater than $9$ | No |

The last case is the one that catches people out. The theorem demands that the sum be *greater than* the third side; equality is not enough, because the two shorter sides laid end to end would exactly cover the longest one and enclose no triangle at all.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Comparison Property of Inequality** | If $a=b+c$ and $c>0$, then $a>b$ |
| **Corollary to the Triangle Exterior Angle Theorem** | The measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than the measure of each of its remote interior angles |
| **Theorem 5-10** | If two sides of a triangle are not congruent, then the larger angle lies opposite the longer side |
| **Theorem 5-11** | If two angles of a triangle are not congruent, then the longer side lies opposite the larger angle |
| **Triangle Inequality Theorem** | The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side |

# 6.1 Classifying Quadrilaterals

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The definitions

Each of these figures is defined by a condition on its sides or its angles, and the wording of the condition is what decides which name a given quadrilateral earns.

| Figure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Parallelogram** | Quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel |
| **Rhombus** | Parallelogram with four congruent sides |
| **Rectangle** | Parallelogram with four right angles |
| **Square** | Parallelogram with four congruent sides and four right angles |
| **Kite** | Quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent sides congruent and no opposite sides congruent |
| **Trapezoid** | Quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides |
| **Isosceles trapezoid** | Trapezoid whose nonparallel opposite sides are congruent |

## How the definitions nest

The rhombus, the rectangle and the square are all defined as *parallelograms* with something extra, so every property of parallelograms in 6.2 applies to all three of them. The square carries both extras at once — four congruent sides and four right angles — which is why it is at the same time a rhombus and a rectangle.

The kite and the trapezoid stand outside that family, since neither is defined as a parallelogram. Two details in their definitions do the separating. A kite has congruent sides that are *adjacent*, and no opposite sides congruent, which is what stops a rhombus from counting as a kite. A trapezoid has *exactly* one pair of parallel sides, which is what stops a parallelogram from counting as a trapezoid.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Parallelogram** | Quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel |
| **Rhombus** | Parallelogram with four congruent sides |
| **Rectangle** | Parallelogram with four right angles |
| **Square** | Parallelogram with four congruent sides and four right angles |
| **Kite** | Quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent sides congruent and no opposite sides congruent |
| **Trapezoid** | Quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides |
| **Isosceles trapezoid** | Trapezoid whose nonparallel opposite sides are congruent |

# 6.2 Properties of Parallelograms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What follows from being a parallelogram

Each of these theorems starts from a quadrilateral already known to be a parallelogram and tells you something further about it.

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 6-1** | Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent |
| **Theorem 6-2** | Opposite angles of a parallelogram are congruent |
| **Theorem 6-3** | The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other |

Note what Theorem 6-3 does and does not say. The diagonals bisect *each other* — each one cuts the other in half — but it does not claim the two diagonals are equal in length.

## Parallel lines and transversals

**Theorem 6-4.** If three (or more) parallel lines cut off congruent segments on one transversal, then they cut off congruent segments on every transversal.

This one is not about a single parallelogram but about a family of parallel lines: equal spacing measured along one crossing line is equal spacing measured along any other.

# 6.3 Proving That a Quadrilateral Is a Parallelogram

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Arguing in the other direction

Section 6.2 began with a parallelogram and derived properties. This section runs the argument the other way: each theorem takes a property of a quadrilateral as given and concludes that the quadrilateral must be a parallelogram.

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 6-5** | If both pairs of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are congruent, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram |
| **Theorem 6-6** | If both pairs of opposite angles of a quadrilateral are congruent, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram |
| **Theorem 6-7** | If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram |
| **Theorem 6-8** | If one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is both congruent and parallel, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram |

Theorems 6-5, 6-6 and 6-7 are the converses of Theorems 6-1, 6-2 and 6-3 in that order, so the pair of sections is best learnt together as one list read in two directions.

Theorem 6-8 is the exception, with no partner in 6.2, and it is the most economical of the four: it needs only *one* pair of opposite sides, but that pair must be both congruent and parallel. One of those two conditions on its own is not enough.

## Keywords

|---|---|

| **Theorem 6-6** | If both pairs of opposite angles of a quadrilateral are congruent, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram |
| **Theorem 6-7** | If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram |
| **Theorem 6-8** | If one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is both congruent and parallel, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram |

# 6.4 Special Parallelograms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Properties of rhombuses and rectangles

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 6-9** | Each diagonal of a rhombus bisects two angles of the rhombus |
| **Theorem 6-10** | The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular |
| **Theorem 6-11** | The diagonals of a rectangle are congruent |

The diagonals are what distinguish the two figures. In a rhombus they cross at right angles and cut the angles of the figure in half; in a rectangle they are equal in length. In both, being parallelograms, they also bisect each other by Theorem 6-3.

## Proving a parallelogram is special

These three theorems reverse the ones above, letting you name a parallelogram from a fact about its diagonals.

| Theorem | Statement |

| **Theorem 6-12** | If one diagonal of a parallelogram bisects two angles of the parallelogram, then the parallelogram is a rhombus |
| **Theorem 6-13** | If the diagonals of a parallelogram are perpendicular, then the parallelogram is a rhombus |
| **Theorem 6-14** | If the diagonals of a parallelogram are congruent, then the parallelogram is a rectangle |

Each of these begins "if the diagonals of a **parallelogram**". The figure must already be known to be a parallelogram before the diagonal condition can upgrade it, so in a problem that starts from a general quadrilateral you need the tests of 6.3 first.

Theorem 6-16 puts the isosceles trapezoid alongside the rectangle, which is the other figure in this chapter with congruent diagonals (Theorem 6-11).

**Theorem 6-17.** The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular.

Perpendicular diagonals therefore do not by themselves identify a figure: a rhombus has them too (Theorem 6-10). What separates the two is the definition in 6.1 — a kite has two pairs of congruent *adjacent* sides and no opposite sides congruent, whereas a rhombus has all four sides congruent.

# 0 Sets and Venn Diagrams

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Sets and elements

A **set** is a collection of distinct numbers or objects. The individual numbers or objects that make up a set are its **elements**.

Two symbols record membership. $\in$ means "is an element of", or simply "is in"; $\notin$ means "is not an element of". So if $A$ is the set of even numbers, $4 \in A$ and $5 \notin A$.

The number of elements in a set $A$ is written $n(A)$ or $|A|$. A set with no elements at all is the **empty set**, written $\varnothing$.

## Properties of sets

Three properties follow directly from what a set is, and everything later in the chapter depends on them.

An element is either in a set or it is not — there is no partial membership, which is why membership questions always have a yes-or-no answer. The same element appears only once: a set records *which* objects belong, not how many times they were listed. And two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements, so the order in which elements are written never matters.

## Subsets

Assume throughout that $A$ and $B$ are sets.

$A \subseteq B$ is read "$A$ is a **subset** of $B$". If all elements of $A$ are in $B$, then $A \subseteq B$.

This definition has three consequences worth holding on to:

- Any set is a subset of itself. Every element of $A$ is trivially in $A$.
- $A = B$ if $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$. Each set contains all of the other's elements, so they have the same elements, which is the definition of equality.
- $\varnothing$ is a subset of any set. There is no element of $\varnothing$ that could fail to be in the other set.

$A \subset B$ is read "$A$ is a **proper subset** of $B$". If all elements of $A$ are in $B$ *and* $n(A) < n(B)$, then $A \subset B$. The size condition is what rules out the case $A = B$, which an ordinary subset allows.

## Intersections

$A \cap B$ is the **intersection** of $A$ and $B$: the elements that are in both $A$ and $B$.

If the two sets share nothing, so that $A \cap B = \varnothing$, they are **mutually exclusive**.

| Property | Why it holds |
|---|---|
| $A \cap B = B \cap A$ | "In both" does not depend on the order named |
| $A \cap A = A$ | Every element of $A$ is in $A$ twice over |
| $A \cap \varnothing = \varnothing$ | Nothing is in the empty set, so nothing is in both |
| $A \cap B = A$ if $A \subseteq B$ | Every element of $A$ is already in $B$ |
| $(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)$ | Both sides are the elements in all three sets |

## Unions

$A \cup B$ is the **union** of $A$ and $B$: the elements that are in either set $A$ or set $B$.

| Property | Why it holds |
|---|---|
| $A \cup B = B \cup A$ | "In either" does not depend on the order named |
| $A \cup A = A$ | Combining a set with itself adds nothing new |
| $A \cup \varnothing = A$ | The empty set contributes no elements |
| $A \subseteq A \cup B$ and $B \subseteq A \cup B$ | Every element of each set survives into the union |
| $A \cup B = B$ if $A \subseteq B$ | $A$ contributes only elements $B$ already has |
| $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ | Both sides are the elements in at least one of the three |

Compare the two lists side by side and the pattern is clear: intersection shrinks a set towards $\varnothing$ while union grows it, which is why $\varnothing$ absorbs an intersection but leaves a union unchanged.

## Complement

$A'$ is the **complement** of $A$, read "not $A$" — everything that is not in $A$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Set** | Collection of distinct numbers or objects |
| **Element** | A member of a set |
| **$\in$** | "Is an element of", "is in" |
| **$\notin$** | "Is not an element of" |
| **$n(A)$, $\lvert A\rvert$** | Number of elements in set $A$ |
| **Empty set ($\varnothing$)** | The set with no elements |
| **Subset ($A \subseteq B$)** | If all elements of $A$ are in $B$, then $A$ is a subset of $B$ |
| **Proper subset ($A \subset B$)** | If all elements of $A$ are in $B$ and $n(A) < n(B)$, then $A$ is a proper subset of $B$ |
| **Intersection ($A \cap B$)** | The elements in both $A$ and $B$ |
| **Mutually exclusive** | $A \cap B = \varnothing$ |
| **Union ($A \cup B$)** | The elements in either set $A$ or set $B$ |
| **Complement ($A'$)** | Not $A$ |

markdown:
# 1 Reasoning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Patterns and inductive reasoning

**Inductive reasoning** is reasoning based on patterns you observe. Having noticed a pattern, the rule you propose from it is a **conjecture**.

A conjecture is only ever as good as the cases it has survived, so a single case that breaks it is fatal. A **counterexample** is used to prove that a conjecture is incorrect.

## Conditional statements

**Conditional statements** are if-then statements: *if $p$, then $q$*. The part after "if" is the **hypothesis** $p$; the part after "then" is the **conclusion** $q$.

The **converse** swaps them: *if $q$, then $p$*.

The **truth value** of a conditional is whether it is true or false. A conditional and its converse are separate statements and need not share a truth value.

## Biconditionals and definitions

When a conditional and its converse are both true, they can be combined and joined as a **biconditional**: *$p$, if and only if $q$*.

This matters for definitions. A good definition has three basic elements: it uses clearly understood terms, it is precise, and it is **reversible**. Reversibility is exactly the biconditional condition — a definition and its converse must both hold, otherwise the definition would let in cases it was meant to exclude.

## Inverses, contrapositives, and indirect reasoning

The **negation** of a statement $p$ is written $\sim p$, read "not $p$". Given "The Earth is round", the negation is "The Earth is not round".

Two further statements are built from a conditional by negating its parts.

| Statement | Form | Example from "if the fruit is red, then it's an apple" |
|---|---|---|
| Conditional | if $p$ then $q$ | If the fruit is red, then it's an apple |
| Converse | if $q$ then $p$ | If the fruit is an apple, then it's red |
| **Inverse** | if $\sim p$ then $\sim q$ | If the fruit isn't red, then it's not an apple |
| **Contrapositive** | if $\sim q$ then $\sim p$ | If the fruit isn't an apple, then it isn't red |

Two rules govern truth values here. A conditional and its contrapositive are equal statements — they always have the same truth value. And the negation of a statement always has the opposite truth value to the statement itself.

The contrapositive rule is what makes **indirect proof** work. Start by assuming the negation of what you want to prove; then show that this negation contradicts the given information; that contradiction rules the negation out, and since the negation has the opposite truth value to the original statement, the statement you needed to prove is correct.

## Deductive reasoning

**Deductive reasoning** is the process of reasoning logically from given statements to a conclusion. Unlike inductive reasoning, which only proposes a rule from observed cases, deduction guarantees its conclusion when the given statements are true.

Two laws do most of the work.

**Law of Detachment:** if $p \rightarrow q$ is a true statement and $p$ is true, then $q$ is true.

> If you get 95 or above on an exam, you get an A+.
> Bob gets 96 on his maths quiz.
> Bob gets an A+ on his maths quiz.

**Law of Syllogism:** if $p \rightarrow q$ and $q \rightarrow r$ are true statements, then $p \rightarrow r$ is true.

> If you study well, then you'll get a good score.
> If you get a good score, then your parents will be happy.
> If you study well, then your parents will be happy.

Detachment fires a single conditional once you have its hypothesis; syllogism chains two conditionals together where the conclusion of the first is the hypothesis of the second.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inductive reasoning** | Reasoning based on patterns you observe |
| **Conjecture** | A rule proposed from an observed pattern |
| **Counterexample** | A case used to prove that a conjecture is incorrect |
| **Conditional statement** | An if-then statement: if $p$, then $q$ |
| **Hypothesis** | The $p$ part of a conditional |
| **Conclusion** | The $q$ part of a conditional |
| **Converse** | If $q$, then $p$ |
| **Truth value** | Whether the conditional is true or false |
| **Biconditional** | A conditional and its converse joined when both are true: $p$, if and only if $q$ |
| **Definition** | A statement using clearly understood terms, precise and reversible |
| **Negation ($\sim p$)** | Not $p$ |
| **Inverse** | If $\sim p$ then $\sim q$ |
| **Contrapositive** | If $\sim q$ then $\sim p$ |
| **Indirect proof** | Assume the negation, prove that the negation contradicts the given information, and use that to prove the original statement is correct |
| **Deductive reasoning** | The process of reasoning logically from given statements to a conclusion |
| **Law of Detachment** | If $p \rightarrow q$ is true and $p$ is true, then $q$ is true |
| **Law of Syllogism** | If $p \rightarrow q$ and $q \rightarrow r$ are true, then $p \rightarrow r$ is true |

markdown:
# 1.2 Drawings, Nets, and Other Models

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A three-dimensional solid has to be got onto a flat page somehow. Four conventions do it, each keeping some information and sacrificing the rest, and the choice between them depends on what the drawing has to show.

## Isometric drawing

An **isometric drawing** is a 2D representation of a 3D object where all three dimensions — length, width, and height — are drawn at the same scale and at 30-degree angles from the horizontal.

Its key features:

- **30° angles.** Horizontal edges are drawn at 30° from the baseline; vertical lines remain straight.
- **Equal scaling.** All three axes use the same scale, with no foreshortening.
- **No perspective.** Parallel lines do not converge, unlike in perspective drawings.
- **3D representation.** Width, height and depth appear in a single view.
- **No hidden lines.** Normally only visible edges are shown, unless they are necessary for clarity.

Equal scaling and the absence of perspective are what make measurements from an isometric drawing meaningful — a length on the page corresponds to a length on the solid, whichever of the three directions it runs in.

## Orthographic drawing

An **orthographic drawing** is a 2D technical representation of a 3D object, showing multiple flat views — front, top, side — at right angles to each other.

Its key features:

- **Multiple 2D views.** Front, top and right views, sometimes more.
- **90° alignment.** Views are perfectly aligned, with the top view directly above the front view and the side view to the side.
- **True dimensions.** Each view is drawn to scale without distortion.
- **Hidden lines.** Dashed lines show obscured edges.
- **No depth illusion.** A pure 2D representation, unlike isometric or perspective drawings.

The trade against an isometric drawing is clear: no single orthographic view shows the solid as a whole, but each view is undistorted, and hidden edges are recorded rather than dropped.

## Foundation drawing

A **foundation drawing** is a 2D technical representation of a 3D object, usually showing the top view of it. Each small figure has a number on it representing its height.

Its key features:

- **Top 2D view.** Only the top view is shown, along with the direction it is seen from.
- **90° alignment.** Views are perfectly aligned, directly above the front view.
- **Entire arrangement.** The figure is divided into regular cubes with edge 1 unit.
- **Counting necessity.** Each small square carries a number representing its height — how many cubes are stacked there.

Because heights are written as numbers rather than drawn, a foundation drawing records a stack of cubes completely in a single flat picture.

## Nets

A **net** is a 2D pattern that can be folded along its edges to form a 3D geometric solid, such as a cube, pyramid or prism.

Its key features:

- **Complete face representation.** Every face of the 3D shape is included, with no missing or overlapping parts.
- **Edge alignment.** Edges that will join in 3D must match in length and position in the 2D net.
- **No gaps or overlaps.** Faces must connect edge-to-edge without extra space or unintended overlaps.
- **Foldable design.** The pattern must be physically possible to fold into the intended solid — a valid cube net has 11 distinct configurations.
- **Scale accuracy.** All faces must be proportionally sized to match the 3D solid.

The foldability requirement is the one that most often fails. An arrangement of six squares can satisfy every other condition and still not close up into a cube, which is why only 11 of the possible arrangements count.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Isometric drawing** | A 2D representation of a 3D object where all three dimensions are drawn at the same scale and at 30-degree angles from the horizontal |
| **Orthographic drawing** | A 2D technical representation of a 3D object, showing multiple flat views (front, top, side) at right angles to each other |
| **Foundation drawing** | A 2D technical representation of a 3D object, usually showing the top view, with a number on each small figure representing its height |
| **Net** | A 2D pattern that can be folded along its edges to form a 3D geometric solid |

markdown:
# 2.1 Points, Lines and Planes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three undefined terms

Geometry is built out of three basic objects. None of them is defined in terms of anything simpler; they are described, named, and then used.

A **point** is a location. It is represented by a capital letter — point $A$.

A **line** is a series of points that extends in two directions without end. Because a line has no ends, it cannot be named by them, so a line is named either by any two points on the line or by a single letter. A **line segment** is the finite piece of a line that falls between two of its points.

A **plane** is a flat surface that has no depth. It contains many lines and extends without end in the directions of all of its lines. A plane is named by a capital letter, or by at least three of the points it contains.

## Collinear and coplanar

Two words describe objects sharing one of these figures.

**Collinear** points are points that lie on the same line. **Coplanar** points and lines are those in the same plane.

The distinction is one of dimension: collinearity is a condition on a line, coplanarity a condition on a plane. Any two points are collinear, since a line can be named by any two points; the question only becomes interesting for three or more.

## Postulates

A **postulate**, also called an **axiom**, is an accepted statement of fact. Postulates are the statements a proof is allowed to use without first proving them, and every theorem in the course eventually traces back to them.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Point** | A location, represented by a capital letter |
| **Line** | A series of points that extends in two directions without end, named by any two points on the line, or by a single letter |
| **Line segment** | The part of a line between two of its points |
| **Collinear points** | Points that lie on the same line |
| **Plane** | A flat surface that has no depth, contains many lines, and extends without end in the directions of all of its lines; named by a capital letter or by at least three of its points |
| **Coplanar** | Points and lines in the same plane |
| **Postulate (axiom)** | An accepted statement of fact |

markdown:
# 2.2 Segments, Rays, Parallel Lines, and Planes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Pieces of a line

A line has no endpoints, but two useful figures are carved out of it by adding them.

A **segment** is a part of the line consisting of 2 endpoints and all points between. A **ray** is a part of a line consisting of 1 endpoint and all the points of the line on one side of the endpoint.

Counting endpoints is the whole distinction: a line has none, a ray has one, a segment has two.

**Opposite rays** are two collinear rays with common endpoints. Because they share an endpoint and run in opposite directions along the same line, together they always form a line — between them they account for every point of it.

## Lines that never meet

Two lines that do not intersect fall into two quite different cases, and which one applies depends on whether the lines share a plane.

**Parallel lines** are coplanar lines that don't intersect. **Skew lines** are noncoplanar lines.

So failing to intersect is not by itself enough to be parallel. Parallel lines lie in one plane and miss each other within it; skew lines miss each other because they never occupy a common plane at all, which is only possible in three dimensions.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Segment** | A part of the line consisting of 2 endpoints and all points between |
| **Ray** | A part of a line consisting of 1 endpoint and all the points of the line on one side of the endpoint |
| **Opposite rays** | Two collinear rays with common endpoints; they always form a line |
| **Parallel lines** | Coplanar lines that don't intersect |
| **Skew lines** | Noncoplanar lines |

# 2.5 Proving Angles Congruent

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Five theorems in this section let you declare two angles congruent without measuring either of them. Each one turns a statement about how angles *combine* into a statement about how they *compare*.

## Vertical angles

**Theorem 2-1 (Vertical Angles Theorem):** Vertical angles are congruent.

$$\angle 1 \cong \angle 3, \qquad \angle 2 \cong \angle 4$$

This is the workhorse of the section: any pair of intersecting lines hands you two pairs of congruent angles for free.

## Supplements and complements of the same angle

Recall that supplementary angles sum to $180^\circ$ and complementary angles sum to $90^\circ$. Because those sums are fixed, knowing one angle of a pair pins the other down exactly — which is why the next two theorems work.

**Theorem 2-2 (Congruent Supplements Theorem):** If 2 angles are supplements ($180^\circ$) of the same angle, or of congruent angles, then the 2 angles are congruent.

**Theorem 2-3 (Congruent Complements Theorem):** If 2 angles are complements ($90^\circ$) of the same angle, or of congruent angles, then the 2 angles are congruent.

If $m\angle 1 + m\angle 3 = 180^\circ$ and $m\angle 2 + m\angle 3 = 180^\circ$, then both $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ must measure $180^\circ - m\angle 3$, so $\angle 1 \cong \angle 2$. The complements version is the same argument with $90^\circ$ in place of $180^\circ$.

Note that the theorems extend beyond "the same angle" to "congruent angles" — the supplements need not be taken of one identical angle, only of angles equal in measure.

## Right angles

**Theorem 2-4:** All right angles are congruent.

Every right angle measures $90^\circ$, so any two of them have equal measure.

**Theorem 2-5:** If 2 angles are congruent and supplementary, then each is a right angle.

This is Theorem 2-4 run backwards. Congruent angles have the same measure $x$, and supplementary angles sum to $180^\circ$, so $2x = 180^\circ$ and $x = 90^\circ$. Both conditions are needed: congruent alone or supplementary alone says nothing about right angles.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Vertical Angles Theorem (Th 2-1)** | Vertical angles are congruent |
| **Congruent Supplements Theorem (Th 2-2)** | If 2 angles are supplements ($180^\circ$) of the same angle, or of congruent angles, then the 2 angles are congruent |
| **Congruent Complements Theorem (Th 2-3)** | If 2 angles are complements ($90^\circ$) of the same angle, or of congruent angles, then the 2 angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-4** | All right angles are congruent |
| **Theorem 2-5** | If 2 angles are congruent and supplementary, then each is a right angle |

# 3.1 Properties of Parallel Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

When a **transversal** cuts across two lines, it creates eight angles. If the two lines are parallel, every one of those angles is either congruent or supplementary to every other, and the five results below say which is which.

Everything in this section starts from one accepted statement.

## The corresponding angles postulate

**Postulate 3-1 (Corresponding Angles Postulate):** If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then corresponding angles are congruent.

This is a postulate, not a theorem — it is assumed rather than proved, and the four theorems that follow are derived from it together with the angle results of 2.5.

## The four theorems

| Theorem | Angle pair | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Th 3-1 | Alternate interior angles | Congruent |
| Th 3-2 | Same-side interior angles | Supplementary |
| Th 3-3 | Alternate exterior angles | Congruent |
| Th 3-4 | Same-side exterior angles | Supplementary |

**Theorem 3-1 (Alternate Interior Angles Theorem):** If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then alternate interior angles are congruent.

**Theorem 3-2 (Same-Side Interior Angles Theorem):** If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then same-side interior angles are supplementary.

**Theorem 3-3 (Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem):** If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then alternate exterior angles are congruent.

**Theorem 3-4 (Same-Side Exterior Angles Theorem):** If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then same-side exterior angles are supplementary.

## Reading the pattern

The four theorems are easier to recall as a rule than as a list. Angle pairs on *alternate* sides of the transversal are congruent; angle pairs on the *same side* are supplementary. Whether the pair is interior (between the two parallel lines) or exterior (outside them) does not change which of the two conclusions applies — it only tells you where to look.

So for any two of the eight angles, $m\angle 1 = m\angle 2$ or $m\angle 1 + m\angle 2 = 180^\circ$, and the side of the transversal decides between them.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate (Post. 3-1)** | If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem (Th 3-1)** | If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then alternate interior angles are congruent |
| **Same-Side Interior Angles Theorem (Th 3-2)** | If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then same-side interior angles are supplementary |
| **Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem (Th 3-3)** | If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then alternate exterior angles are congruent |
| **Same-Side Exterior Angles Theorem (Th 3-4)** | If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then same-side exterior angles are supplementary |

# 3.2 Proving Lines Parallel

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Section 3.1 started from parallel lines and deduced facts about angles. This section runs every one of those results backwards: start from the angles, conclude that the lines are parallel. Each statement here is the converse of its counterpart in 3.1.

## The converse postulate

**Postulate 3-2 (Converse of Corresponding Angles Postulate):** If 2 lines and a transversal form corresponding angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel.

As in 3.1, the corresponding-angles statement is the one assumed, and the rest follow from it.

## The four converse theorems

**Theorem 3-5 (Converse of Alternate Interior Angles Theorem):** If 2 lines and a transversal form alternate interior angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel.

**Theorem 3-6 (Converse of Same-Side Interior Angles Theorem):** If 2 lines and a transversal form same-side interior angles that are supplementary, then the 2 lines are parallel.

**Theorem 3-7 (Converse of Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem):** If 2 lines and a transversal form alternate exterior angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel.

**Theorem 3-8 (Converse of Same-Side Exterior Angles Theorem):** If 2 lines and a transversal form same-side exterior angles that are supplementary, then the 2 lines are parallel.

## Matching each result to its converse

| Angle pair | If the lines are parallel (3.1) | If the angles satisfy this, the lines are parallel (3.2) |
|---|---|---|
| Corresponding | Post. 3-1: congruent | Post. 3-2: congruent |
| Alternate interior | Th 3-1: congruent | Th 3-5: congruent |
| Same-side interior | Th 3-2: supplementary | Th 3-6: supplementary |
| Alternate exterior | Th 3-3: congruent | Th 3-7: congruent |
| Same-side exterior | Th 3-4: supplementary | Th 3-8: supplementary |

Because each pair of statements is a conditional and its converse, and both are true, each row is effectively a biconditional: two lines cut by a transversal are parallel *if and only if* the angle condition holds. That is what makes these results usable in both directions — as a source of angle measures once you know the lines are parallel, and as a test for parallelism once you know the angles.

The direction matters when writing a proof. Quoting Theorem 3-1 when what you actually need is Theorem 3-5 assumes the very thing you are trying to establish.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Converse of Corresponding Angles Postulate (Post. 3-2)** | If 2 lines and a transversal form corresponding angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel |
| **Converse of Alternate Interior Angles Theorem (Th 3-5)** | If 2 lines and a transversal form alternate interior angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel |
| **Converse of Same-Side Interior Angles Theorem (Th 3-6)** | If 2 lines and a transversal form same-side interior angles that are supplementary, then the 2 lines are parallel |
| **Converse of Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem (Th 3-7)** | If 2 lines and a transversal form alternate exterior angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel |
| **Converse of Same-Side Exterior Angles Theorem (Th 3-8)** | If 2 lines and a transversal form same-side exterior angles that are supplementary, then the 2 lines are parallel |

title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
summary: The results in 3.1 and 3.2 all involve a transversal. The three theorems here need no transversal at all: they say how parallelism and perpendicularity pass from one pair of lines to another. Theorem
markdown:
# 3.3 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The results in 3.1 and 3.2 all involve a transversal. The three theorems here need no transversal at all: they say how parallelism and perpendicularity pass from one pair of lines to another.

## Parallel to the same line

**Theorem 3-9:** If 2 lines are parallel to the same line, then they are parallel to each other.

This is what lets a chain of parallels be collapsed. If $a \parallel b$ and $b \parallel c$, then $a \parallel c$ — no intermediate line needs to be mentioned again.

Note that this theorem is stated without restriction to a plane, unlike the two that follow.

## Perpendicular to the same line

**Theorem 3-10:** In a plane, if 2 lines are perpendicular to the same line, then they are parallel to each other.

**Theorem 3-11:** In a plane, if a line is perpendicular to 1 of 2 parallel lines, then it is also perpendicular to the other.

Both of these open with "in a plane", and the restriction is doing real work. In three dimensions two lines perpendicular to the same line need not be parallel — they may be skew, since as 2.2 established, lines that fail to intersect are only parallel when they are coplanar.

## How the three fit together

Theorem 3-10 turns a pair of perpendicularity facts into a parallelism fact; Theorem 3-11 turns a parallelism fact plus one perpendicularity fact into a second perpendicularity fact. Together they mean that within a plane, "perpendicular to $\ell$" behaves exactly like a single direction: every line with that property is parallel to every other, and any line parallel to one of them shares the property.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 3-9** | If 2 lines are parallel to the same line, then they are parallel to each other |
| **Theorem 3-10** | In a plane, if 2 lines are perpendicular to the same line, then they are parallel to each other |
| **Theorem 3-11** | In a plane, if a line is perpendicular to 1 of 2 parallel lines, then it is also perpendicular to the other |

# 3.4 Parallel Lines and the Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The angle sum of a triangle

**Theorem 3-12 (Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem):** The sum of the measures of the angles of a triangle is $180$.

$$m\angle A + m\angle B + m\angle C = 180^\circ$$

The theorem belongs to this chapter because it is proved with parallel lines: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side, and the parallel-line results of 3.1 identify the two outer angles at that vertex with the triangle's other two angles. Together the three angles form a straight angle.

One immediate consequence: knowing any two angles of a triangle determines the third.

## Exterior angles

An **exterior angle** is an angle formed by a side and an extension of an adjacent side. For each exterior angle of a triangle, the 2 nonadjacent interior angles are its **remote interior angles**.

**Theorem 3-13 (Triangle Exterior Angle Theorem):** The measure of each exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the measures of its 2 remote interior angles.

$$m\angle 1 = m\angle 2 + m\angle 3$$

This follows from Theorem 3-12. An exterior angle and the interior angle beside it are supplementary, so the exterior angle measures $180^\circ$ minus that interior angle — and by the angle-sum theorem, $180^\circ$ minus one angle is exactly the sum of the other two.

## Classifying triangles

A triangle is classified twice over, once by its angles and once by its sides.

| By angles | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Equiangular** | All angles congruent |
| **Acute** | All angles acute |
| **Right** | One right angle |
| **Obtuse** | One obtuse angle |

| By sides | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Equilateral** | All sides congruent |
| **Isosceles** | At least 2 sides congruent |
| **Scalene** | No sides congruent |

Note the wording of *isosceles*: **at least** two sides congruent, so every equilateral triangle is also isosceles.

Only one angle classification can involve a non-acute angle, because the angle sum is fixed at $180^\circ$ — two right or obtuse angles would already exhaust it.

## Steps to classify a triangle from three side lengths

Given three lengths with $c$ the longest:

1. **Check it is a valid triangle.** The sum of the 2 shortest sides should be greater than the remaining side (the longest side). If it is not, no triangle exists and there is nothing to classify.
2. **Compare $a^2 + b^2$ with $c^2$.**

$$\begin{aligned} a^2 + b^2 &> c^2 && \text{acute triangle} \\ a^2 + b^2 &= c^2 && \text{right triangle} \\ a^2 + b^2 &< c^2 && \text{obtuse triangle} \end{aligned}$$

The comparison must use the longest side as $c$. Substituting a shorter side there gives the wrong classification.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem (Th 3-12)** | The sum of the measures of the angles of a triangle is $180$ |
| **Exterior angle** | An angle formed by a side and an extension of an adjacent side |
| **Remote interior angles** | For each exterior angle of a triangle, the 2 nonadjacent interior angles |
| **Triangle Exterior Angle Theorem (Th 3-13)** | The measure of each exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the measures of its 2 remote interior angles |
| **Equiangular triangle** | All angles congruent |
| **Acute triangle** | All angles acute |
| **Right triangle** | One right angle |
| **Obtuse triangle** | One obtuse angle |
| **Equilateral triangle** | All sides congruent |
| **Isosceles triangle** | At least 2 sides congruent |
| **Scalene triangle** | No sides congruent |

# 4 Congruent Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two triangles have six parts each — three sides and three angles. Proving all six pairs congruent would be laborious, and this chapter shows it is never necessary: three well-chosen congruences always force the other three.

## 4.1 Congruent figures

**Theorem 4-1:** If 2 angles of one triangle are congruent to 2 angles of another triangle, then the 3rd angles are congruent.

This is the angle-sum theorem of 3.4 applied to both triangles. Each set of three angles totals $180^\circ$, so if two of the angles match, whatever is left over must match too. It is the first sign that the six parts are not independent of one another.

## 4.2 Triangle congruence by SSS and SAS

**Postulate 4-1 (SSS):** If the 3 sides of a triangle are congruent to the sides of another triangle, then the 2 triangles are congruent.

**Postulate 4-2 (SAS):** If 2 pairs of sides are congruent and the included angles are also congruent, then the 2 triangles are congruent.

The included angle is the angle *between* the two sides named. It has to be the included angle of the 2 sides — there is no "SSA". Two sides and an angle that is not between them do not fix the triangle, so a congruence claim built that way is invalid no matter how the parts are labelled.

## 4.3 Triangle congruence by ASA and AAS

**Postulate 4-3 (ASA):** If the 2 pairs of angles are congruent and the included sides are congruent, then the 2 triangles are congruent.

**Theorem 4-2 (AAS):** If 2 pairs of angles are congruent and a nonincluded side is congruent to the corresponding nonincluded side of the other triangle, then the 2 triangles are congruent.

AAS is a theorem rather than a postulate because it can be proved from what is already available. Two pairs of congruent angles make the third pair congruent by Theorem 4-1, and once all three angles are known to correspond, the nonincluded side becomes an included side of some other pair — which is ASA.

The contrast with SAS is worth noticing. Moving the angle out from between the two sides destroys the argument, but moving the side out from between the two angles does not.

## Summary of the four criteria

| Criterion | Given | Status |
|---|---|---|
| SSS | 3 pairs of sides | Postulate 4-1 |
| SAS | 2 pairs of sides and the **included** angles | Postulate 4-2 |
| ASA | 2 pairs of angles and the **included** sides | Postulate 4-3 |
| AAS | 2 pairs of angles and a **nonincluded** side | Theorem 4-2 |
| SSA | 2 pairs of sides and a nonincluded angle | Not valid |

## 4.4 Using congruent triangles: CPCTC

**CPCTC** stands for *corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent*. If 2 triangles are proven congruent by 3 congruences, then the other 3 congruences hold true too.

This is what the chapter has been building towards. The four criteria are the way in; CPCTC is the way out. Prove congruence using three parts, then quote CPCTC to obtain any of the remaining three — which is how a fact about a single segment or angle is established by first finding a pair of triangles containing it.

The order is fixed: CPCTC can only be cited *after* a congruence has been established, never as a step towards establishing it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 4-1** | If 2 angles of one triangle are congruent to 2 angles of another triangle, then the 3rd angles are congruent |
| **SSS (Post. 4-1)** | If the 3 sides of a triangle are congruent to the sides of another triangle, then the 2 triangles are congruent |
| **SAS (Post. 4-2)** | If 2 pairs of sides are congruent and the included angles are also congruent, then the 2 triangles are congruent |
| **ASA (Post. 4-3)** | If the 2 pairs of angles are congruent and the included sides are congruent, then the 2 triangles are congruent |
| **AAS (Th 4-2)** | If 2 pairs of angles are congruent and a nonincluded side is congruent to the corresponding nonincluded side of the other triangle, then the 2 triangles are congruent |
| **CPCTC** | Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent: if 2 triangles are proven congruent by 3 congruences, then the other 3 congruences hold true too |

# 6.1 Circles and Arcs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Central angles and arcs

A **central angle** is an angle whose vertex is the center of the circle. Because its vertex sits at the centre, a central angle sweeps out a definite portion of the circle, and that portion is an arc.

An **arc** is a part of a circle. Three kinds are named by size:

- A **semicircle** is half of a circle.
- A **minor arc** is smaller than a semicircle.
- A **major arc** is greater than a semicircle.

## Measure of an arc

The **measure of an arc** is equal to the degree of its central angle in measurement. This one sentence is what ties the two ideas together — an arc is measured not by its length but by the angle that produces it, so an arc measure is always a number of degrees.

Three rules follow:

- The measure of a semicircle is $180$, since the straight angle at the centre that cuts it off measures $180^\circ$.
- The measure of a minor arc is the measure of its corresponding central angle.
- The measure of a major arc is $360$ minus the measure of its related minor arc, because the two together make up the whole circle.

## Adding arcs

**Postulate 10-1 (Arc Addition Postulate):** The measure of the arc formed by two adjacent arcs is the sum of the measures of the two arcs.

$$m\overset{\frown}{AC} = m\overset{\frown}{AB} + m\overset{\frown}{BC}$$

## Circumference and arc length

**Theorem 10-9 (Circumference of a Circle):** The circumference of a circle is

$$C = \pi d = 2\pi r$$

The two forms are the same statement, since the diameter is twice the radius.

**Theorem 10-10 (Arc Length):** The length of an arc of a circle is the product of the ratio of the arc's measure to $360$ and the circumference of the circle.

$$\text{length of } \overset{\frown}{AB} = \frac{m\overset{\frown}{AB}}{360} \cdot 2\pi r$$

Arc measure and arc length are different quantities and must not be confused. The measure is in degrees and depends only on the central angle; the length is in units of distance and grows with the radius. The ratio $\dfrac{m\overset{\frown}{AB}}{360}$ is the fraction of the whole circle the arc occupies, and multiplying the whole circumference by that fraction gives the corresponding fraction of the distance around.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Central angle** | An angle whose vertex is the center of the circle |
| **Arc** | A part of a circle |
| **Semicircle** | Half of a circle |
| **Minor arc** | An arc smaller than a semicircle |
| **Major arc** | An arc greater than a semicircle |
| **Measure of an arc** | Equal to the degree of its central angle in measurement |
| **Arc Addition Postulate (Post. 10-1)** | The measure of the arc formed by two adjacent arcs is the sum of the measures of the two arcs |
| **Circumference (Th 10-9)** | $C = \pi d = 2\pi r$ |
| **Arc Length (Th 10-10)** | The product of the ratio of the arc's measure to $360$ and the circumference |

# 6.2 Chords and Arcs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Chords

A **chord** is a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circle.

Each chord cuts off an arc, and the central angle joining the chord's endpoints to the centre sits between the two. The theorems of this section all exploit the fact that these three objects — central angle, chord, and arc — rise and fall together.

## Central angles, chords, and arcs

**Theorem 12-4:** Within a circle or in congruent circles, congruent central angles also have congruent chords and congruent arcs.

The three quantities are therefore interchangeable as evidence. Establishing any one of them congruent establishes the other two, which is why a problem about arcs can often be attacked by measuring chords instead.

Note the condition "within a circle or in congruent circles". The theorem compares parts of circles of the same size; two circles of different radii can have equal central angles and equal arc *measures* with quite different chords.

## Distance from the centre

**Theorem 12-5:** Within a circle or in congruent circles, chords equidistant from the center are congruent, and congruent chords are equidistant from the center.

$$\text{If } OE = OF, \text{ then } AB = CD$$

The statement runs in both directions, so equal distance from the centre and equal chord length are two ways of saying the same thing. This makes sense of the pattern: the further a chord slides from the centre, the shorter it becomes, until at distance $r$ it shrinks to a single point.

## Diameters perpendicular to chords

**Theorem 12-6:** In a circle, a diameter that is perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord and its arcs.

**Theorem 12-7:** In a circle, a diameter that bisects a chord that is not a diameter is perpendicular to the chord.

These are converses of one another, so within a circle a diameter is perpendicular to a chord exactly when it bisects it.

The exception in Theorem 12-7 is the one to watch. The chord must not itself be a diameter: any two diameters bisect each other, but they certainly need not meet at right angles, so the theorem would be false without the restriction.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chord** | A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circle |
| **Theorem 12-4** | Within a circle or in congruent circles, congruent central angles also have congruent chords and congruent arcs |
| **Theorem 12-5** | Within a circle or in congruent circles, chords equidistant from the center are congruent; congruent chords are equidistant from the center |
| **Theorem 12-6** | In a circle, a diameter that is perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord and its arcs |
| **Theorem 12-7** | In a circle, a diameter that bisects a chord that is not a diameter is perpendicular to the chord |

# 6.3 Inscribed Angles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The inscribed angle

An **inscribed angle** is an angle whose vertex lies on the circle and whose sides are chords of the circle.

Contrast this with the central angle of 6.1, whose vertex is at the centre. Moving the vertex from the centre out to the circle halves the angle, and that is the content of the main theorem.

## The Inscribed Angle Theorem

**Theorem 12-9 (Inscribed Angle Theorem):** The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc.

$$m\angle 1 = \tfrac{1}{2}\, m\overset{\frown}{AB}$$

where $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ is the arc intercepted by $\angle 1$ — the arc lying inside the angle, cut off by the two chords that form its sides.

**Corollary 1:** Two inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are equal.

This falls straight out of the theorem: both angles are half of the same arc measure, so both have the same measure. It is the reason an inscribed angle can be moved anywhere along its arc without changing size — a useful move when the vertex you are given is awkwardly placed.

## Angles formed by a tangent and a chord

**Theorem 12-10 (Tangent-Chord Angle Theorem):** The measure of an angle formed by a tangent and a chord through the point of tangency is half the measure of the intercepted arc.

$$m\angle 1 = \tfrac{1}{2}\, m\overset{\frown}{AB}$$

The formula is identical to the Inscribed Angle Theorem's, and so is the vertex position — on the circle. The only change is that one side of the angle is now a tangent line rather than a chord, and the halving rule survives that substitution unchanged.

So both theorems in this section reduce to one habit: with the vertex on the circle, halve the arc.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inscribed angle** | An angle whose vertex lies on the circle, and whose sides are chords of the circle |
| **Inscribed Angle Theorem (Th 12-9)** | The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc |
| **Corollary 1** | Two inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are equal |
| **Tangent-Chord Angle Theorem (Th 12-10)** | The measure of an angle formed by a tangent and a chord through the point of tangency is half the measure of the intercepted arc |
