# 6.4 Tangent Lines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A **tangent line** to a circle is a line that intersects the circle at exactly one point, called the **point of tangency**.

"Exactly one point" is the whole definition. A line meeting a circle twice cuts off a chord; a line meeting it not at all misses entirely; the tangent is the single borderline case between them.

## Tangents and radii

**Theorem 12-1:** If a line is tangent to a circle, then it is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.

**Converse of Theorem 12-1:** If a line in the plane of a circle is perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint on the circle, then the line is tangent to the circle.

Together these give a test in both directions: a line touching a circle at a point is tangent there *if and only if* it meets the radius to that point at a right angle.

The practical consequence is that a tangent problem is almost always a right-triangle problem. Draw the radius to the point of tangency and a right angle appears, which puts the Pythagorean theorem and the trigonometric ratios of chapter 8 immediately in reach.

Note the phrase "at its endpoint on the circle" in the converse. Perpendicularity to a radius somewhere in the interior of the circle proves nothing; the right angle must occur at the circle itself.

## Two tangents from an external point

**Theorem 12-3:** Two segments tangent to a circle from a point outside the circle are congruent.

From a point outside a circle there are exactly two tangent lines, and this theorem says the two touching distances are equal. The figure it produces — external point, two points of tangency, and the centre — is symmetric about the line joining the external point to the centre, which is why the two tangent segments come out the same length.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Tangent line to a circle** | A line that intersects the circle at exactly one point |
| **Point of tangency** | The single point at which a tangent meets the circle |
| **Theorem 12-1** | If a line is tangent to a circle, then it is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency |
| **Converse of Theorem 12-1** | If a line in the plane of a circle is perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint on the circle, then the line is tangent to the circle |
| **Theorem 12-3** | Two segments tangent to a circle from a point outside the circle are congruent |

# 6.5 Angle Measures and Segment Lengths

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Sections 6.1 and 6.3 covered the two special vertex positions: the centre, where an angle equals its arc, and the circle itself, where an angle is half its arc. This section handles every remaining position — strictly inside the circle, and strictly outside it.

## Angles formed by two intersecting lines

**Theorem 12-11:** The measure of an angle formed by two lines that intersect **inside** a circle is half the sum of the measures of the intercepted arcs.

$$m\angle 1 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(m\overset{\frown}{AB} + m\overset{\frown}{CD}\right)$$

The measure of an angle formed by two lines that intersect **outside** a circle is half the difference of the measures of the intercepted arcs.

$$m\angle 1 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(m\overset{\frown}{AB} - m\overset{\frown}{CD}\right)$$

Two lines crossing a circle always intercept two arcs, and the vertex position decides which operation applies.

| Vertex position | Rule |
|---|---|
| At the centre (6.1) | Angle equals the arc |
| On the circle (6.3) | Half of one arc |
| Inside the circle | Half the **sum** of the two arcs |
| Outside the circle | Half the **difference** of the two arcs |

Read down that table and the behaviour is consistent: the further the vertex moves from the centre, the smaller the angle it subtends becomes, from the whole arc, through half of it, down to half a difference that shrinks towards zero as the vertex travels away.

For the outside case the subtraction must be taken in the right order — the farther (larger) arc minus the nearer (smaller) one, so that the result is positive.

## Segment lengths

**Theorem 12-12:** For a given point and circle, the product of the lengths of the two segments from the point to the circle is constant along any line through the point and circle.

Any line drawn through the point meets the circle in two places, giving two segment lengths measured from the point. Their product does not depend on which line was drawn. That is what makes the theorem useful: draw a second line through the same point, and the product it produces must equal the first, which yields an equation in the unknown length.

$$a \cdot b = c \cdot d$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Theorem 12-11** | The measure of an angle formed by two lines that intersect inside a circle is half the sum of the measures of the intercepted arcs; if they intersect outside a circle, it is half the difference |
| **Theorem 12-12** | For a given point and circle, the product of the lengths of the two segments from the point to the circle is constant along any line through the point and circle |

# 6.6 Areas of Circles and Sectors

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Area of a circle

**Theorem 10-11 (Area of a Circle):**

$$A = \pi r^2$$

The area depends on the square of the radius, whereas the circumference of 6.1 depends on the radius itself. Doubling a circle's radius therefore doubles the distance round it but quadruples the space inside it.

## Area of a sector

A sector is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the "slice" cut off by a central angle.

**Theorem 10-12 (Area of a Sector of a Circle):**

$$\text{Area of sector } AOB = \frac{m\overset{\frown}{AB}}{360} \cdot \pi r^2$$

The structure is identical to the arc length formula of 6.1: work out what fraction of the full circle the central angle represents, then take that fraction of the whole. The only difference is what is being divided up — the circumference for arc length, the area for a sector.

| Quantity | Whole circle | Portion cut off by arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Distance round | $2\pi r$ | $\dfrac{m\overset{\frown}{AB}}{360}\cdot 2\pi r$ |
| Region enclosed | $\pi r^2$ | $\dfrac{m\overset{\frown}{AB}}{360}\cdot \pi r^2$ |

Because both come from the same ratio, a common error is to answer one when the question asked for the other. Check the units: an arc length is a distance, a sector area is a square measure.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Area of a Circle (Th 10-11)** | $A = \pi r^2$ |
| **Sector** | The region of a circle bounded by two radii and the arc between them |
| **Area of a Sector (Th 10-12)** | The ratio of the arc's measure to $360$, multiplied by the area of the circle |

markdown:
# 8.1 The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The theorem

**Theorem 8-1 (Pythagorean Theorem):** In a right triangle, the sum of the squares of the lengths of the legs is equal to the square of the length of the hypotenuse.

$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$

Here $a$ and $b$ are the legs and $c$ is the hypotenuse. The letters are not interchangeable: $c$ must be the hypotenuse, which is the side opposite the right angle and always the longest of the three.

## The converse, and what it classifies

**Theorem 8-2 (Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem):** If the square of the length of one side of a triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides, that is $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, then the triangle is a right triangle.

Theorem 8-1 goes from a right angle to an equation; Theorem 8-2 goes from the equation back to a right angle. This is what makes the relation a *test* — three measured lengths can be checked for a right angle without ever measuring an angle.

**Theorem 8-3:** If the square of the length of one side of a triangle is greater than the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides, that is $a^2 + b^2 < c^2$, then the triangle is an obtuse triangle.

Taken together with the classification steps of 3.4, the three cases cover every triangle:

| Comparison | Triangle |
|---|---|
| $a^2 + b^2 > c^2$ | Acute |
| $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ | Right |
| $a^2 + b^2 < c^2$ | Obtuse |

As always, $c$ must be the longest side before the comparison is made.

## Pythagorean triples

A **Pythagorean triple** is a set of nonzero three numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ that satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

These are worth recognising on sight, because spotting one turns a calculation into a lookup. It is better to memorise them.

| $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 5 |
| 5 | 12 | 13 |
| 8 | 15 | 17 |
| 7 | 24 | 25 |
| 9 | 40 | 41 |
| 11 | 60 | 61 |
| 12 | 35 | 37 |
| 13 | 84 | 85 |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Pythagorean Theorem (Th 8-1)** | In a right triangle, the sum of the squares of the lengths of the legs is equal to the square of the length of the hypotenuse: $a^2+b^2=c^2$ |
| **Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem (Th 8-2)** | If $a^2+b^2=c^2$ for the three sides of a triangle, then the triangle is a right triangle |
| **Theorem 8-3** | If the square of one side is greater than the sum of the squares of the other two, that is $a^2+b^2<c^2$, then the triangle is obtuse |
| **Pythagorean triple** | A set of nonzero three numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ that satisfy $a^2+b^2=c^2$ |

# 8.2 Special Right Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two right triangles turn up so often that their side ratios are worth knowing outright. In both cases the angles are fixed, so the shape is fixed, so the sides are locked into a constant ratio no matter how large the triangle is drawn — and one known side gives the other two without any calculation beyond multiplying or dividing.

## The 45°-45°-90° triangle

**Theorem 8-5 (45°-45°-90° Triangle Theorem):** In a 45°-45°-90° triangle, both legs are congruent and the length of the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.

The 3 sides are in the ratio

$$1 : 1 : \sqrt{2}$$

So if a leg is $x$, the hypotenuse is $x\sqrt{2}$; if the hypotenuse is $x$, each leg is $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The two legs are congruent because the two acute angles are equal, and the $\sqrt{2}$ is just the Pythagorean theorem of 8.1 applied to that case: $x^2 + x^2 = 2x^2$, whose square root is $x\sqrt{2}$.

## The 30°-60°-90° triangle

**Theorem 8-6 (30°-60°-90° Triangle Theorem):** In a 30°-60°-90° triangle, the length of the hypotenuse is twice the length of the shorter leg. The length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times the length of the shorter leg.

The 3 sides are in the ratio

$$1 : 2 : \sqrt{3}$$

reading shorter leg, hypotenuse, longer leg.

| Side | Length if the shorter leg is $x$ |
|---|---|
| Shorter leg (opposite the 30° angle) | $x$ |
| Longer leg (opposite the 60° angle) | $x\sqrt{3}$ |
| Hypotenuse (opposite the right angle) | $2x$ |

Everything is expressed in terms of the **shorter** leg, so a problem that gives the hypotenuse or the longer leg has to be worked back to the shorter leg first. Matching the sides to the angles is what prevents the two legs from being swapped: the larger angle always faces the longer side, so the $\sqrt{3}$ leg belongs to the 60° angle.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **45°-45°-90° Triangle Theorem (Th 8-5)** | In a 45°-45°-90° triangle, both legs are congruent and the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg; the sides are in ratio $1:1:\sqrt{2}$ |
| **30°-60°-90° Triangle Theorem (Th 8-6)** | In a 30°-60°-90° triangle, the hypotenuse is twice the shorter leg and the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times the shorter leg; the sides are in ratio $1:2:\sqrt{3}$ |

# 8.3 The Tangent Ratio

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Naming the sides

Before any ratio can be written down, the sides of a right triangle have to be named relative to the angle being used.

The **adjacent legs** are the two sides of a right triangle that are connected to the right angle — sides $a$ and $b$ in a triangle with hypotenuse $c$.

The **opposite leg** is the side of the triangle that is across from a given acute angle. So $a$ is the opposite leg of angle $A$, which leaves $b$ as the leg adjacent to $A$.

Because "opposite" and "adjacent" are defined relative to a chosen acute angle, the same two legs exchange roles when you switch to the other acute angle. Only the hypotenuse keeps its identity.

## The tangent ratio

The **tangent ratio** is the ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the adjacent side, relative to a given acute angle in a right triangle.

$$\tan A = \frac{a}{b} = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$$

The essential point is that the tangent ratio depends on the measure of the angle rather than on the size of the sides. Enlarging the triangle multiplies $a$ and $b$ by the same factor, which cancels in the ratio. This is what makes the tangent a property of the *angle*, and therefore something that can be tabulated once and used on any triangle.

Rearranging the definition gives the two ways it is used to find a missing length:

$$a = \tan(m\angle A) \cdot b, \qquad b = \frac{a}{\tan(m\angle A)}$$

That is, multiply by the tangent ratio to go from the adjacent leg to the opposite leg, and divide by it to go back the other way.

## The symbols $\tan$ and $\tan^{-1}$

$\tan$ is the symbol used to find the tangent ratio of an angle from the measure of that angle. For example,

$$\tan(30^\circ) = 0.577$$

$\tan^{-1}$ is the symbol used to find the measure of an angle from the tangent ratio of that angle. It is the converse of $\tan$:

$$\tan^{-1}(0.577) = 30^\circ$$

Because $\tan$ and $\tan^{-1}$ are converse versions of each other, nothing happens to the value if you apply one and then the other:

$$\tan^{-1}\left(\tan(30^\circ)\right) = 30^\circ$$

Which one you need depends on what is missing. An unknown side calls for $\tan$, since the angle is known; an unknown angle calls for $\tan^{-1}$, since the sides are known.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Adjacent legs** | The two sides of a right triangle that are connected to the right angle |
| **Opposite leg** | The side of the triangle that is across from a given acute angle |
| **Tangent ratio** | The ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the adjacent side relative to a given acute angle in a right triangle |
| **$\tan$** | The symbol to find the tangent ratio of one angle from the measure of that angle |
| **$\tan^{-1}$** | The symbol to find the measure of one angle from the tangent ratio of that angle; the converse version of $\tan$ |

# 8.4 Sine and Cosine Ratios

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The tangent ratio of 8.3 compares the two legs to each other and never involves the hypotenuse. The two ratios in this section bring the hypotenuse in, which is what allows a problem giving the hypotenuse to be solved at all.

## The two ratios

The **sine ratio** is the ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the hypotenuse, relative to a given acute angle in a right triangle. For angle $A$ in a triangle with legs $a$, $b$ and hypotenuse $c$, where $a$ is opposite $A$:

$$\sin A = \frac{a}{c} = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$

The **cosine ratio** is the ratio of the length of the adjacent side to the length of the hypotenuse, relative to a given acute angle in a right triangle.

$$\cos A = \frac{b}{c} = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$

| Ratio | Numerator | Denominator |
|---|---|---|
| $\sin A$ | Opposite | Hypotenuse |
| $\cos A$ | Adjacent | Hypotenuse |
| $\tan A$ | Opposite | Adjacent |

Between the three, every pairing of two sides is covered, so whichever two sides a problem supplies, one of the ratios connects them to the angle.

## The symbols

$\sin$ is the symbol used to find the sine ratio of an angle from the measure of that angle; $\cos$ does the same for the cosine ratio.

$$\sin(30^\circ) = 0.5, \qquad \cos(30^\circ) = 0.866$$

$\sin^{-1}$ finds the measure of an angle from its sine ratio, and $\cos^{-1}$ finds it from the cosine ratio. Each is the converse version of the function it undoes.

$$\sin^{-1}(0.5) = 30^\circ, \qquad \cos^{-1}(0.866) = 30^\circ$$

As with the tangent, the direction of the problem selects the symbol: use $\sin$ or $\cos$ when the angle is known and a side is wanted, and $\sin^{-1}$ or $\cos^{-1}$ when the sides are known and the angle is wanted.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sine ratio** | The ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the hypotenuse relative to a given acute angle in a right triangle |
| **Cosine ratio** | The ratio of the length of the adjacent side to the length of the hypotenuse relative to a given acute angle in a right triangle |
| **$\sin$** | The symbol to find the sine ratio of one angle from the measure of that angle |
| **$\cos$** | The symbol to find the cosine ratio of one angle from the measure of that angle |
| **$\sin^{-1}$** | The symbol to find the measure of one angle from its sine ratio; the converse version of $\sin$ |
| **$\cos^{-1}$** | The symbol to find the measure of one angle from its cosine ratio; the converse version of $\cos$ |

# 8.5 Angles of Elevation and Depression

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The two angles

The trigonometric ratios of 8.3 and 8.4 are applied to real situations through two named angles, both measured from a horizontal line.

The **angle of elevation** is the angle above the horizontal when looking up at an object.

The **angle of depression** is the angle below the horizontal when looking down at an object.

## Setting up the triangle

Both definitions are stated relative to the horizontal, and that is the detail on which these problems turn. The horizontal line of sight is one side of the right triangle, the vertical height is the other, and the actual line of sight to the object is the hypotenuse. Once the figure is drawn that way, the problem is an ordinary right-triangle problem and any of $\sin$, $\cos$ or $\tan$ can be used.

The common error is to measure the angle from the vertical, or to place it inside the triangle at the wrong vertex. If the angle given is the one at the observer's eye between the horizontal and the line of sight, it is the angle of elevation or depression; anything else has to be converted before use.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Angle of elevation** | The angle above the horizontal when looking up at an object |
| **Angle of depression** | The angle below the horizontal when looking down at an object |

# 8.6 Solving Right Triangles and Areas of Polygons

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Solving a right triangle

Collecting the three ratios of 8.3 and 8.4 in one place:

$$\sin X = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \cos X = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \tan X = \frac{\sin X}{\cos X} = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$$

The middle equality is worth checking, because it explains why only two of the three ratios are independent. Dividing sine by cosine cancels the hypotenuse:

$$\frac{\sin X}{\cos X} = \frac{\text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{adjacent}/\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \tan X$$

## Height from a side and an angle

In $\triangle ABC$, the height dropped to a side can be written straight from the sine ratio:

$$H = b\sin A = a\sin B$$

The height is a leg of the right triangle formed by the altitude, and the side it is cut from acts as the hypotenuse — so the height is that side multiplied by the sine of the angle between them. Both expressions describe the same height, which is why the two forms agree.

## The area of a triangle

Substituting that height into the usual area rule turns a base-and-height formula into one that needs only two sides and the angle between them:

$$\text{Area} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{base} \times \text{height} = \tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C = \tfrac{1}{2}ac\sin B = \tfrac{1}{2}bc\sin A$$

In each version the angle named is the one *included* between the two sides used. Choosing the angle that is not between them is the standard mistake here.

## Areas of parallelograms and triangles

$$\text{Area of a rectangle} = \text{base} \times \text{height}$$

When all three sides of a triangle are known but no angle is, the area can be found without any trigonometry at all by **Heron's formula**. Let

$$s = \tfrac{1}{2}(a+b+c)$$

be half the perimeter. Then

$$\text{Area} = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$$

## Areas of trapezoids, rhombuses, and kites

$$\text{Area of a trapezoid} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{base}_1 + \text{base}_2)\times\text{height}$$

$$\text{Area of a rhombus or kite} = \tfrac{1}{2}d_1 d_2$$

The trapezoid formula uses the two parallel sides and the perpendicular distance between them; the rhombus and kite formula uses the two diagonals. Note that a trapezoid with equal bases is a parallelogram, and the formula then collapses to base $\times$ height, as it should.

## Areas and perimeters of regular polygons

A regular $n$-gon can be cut from its centre into $n$ congruent triangles, one on each side. Each has the side length as its base and the **apothem** $a$ — the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side — as its height. Adding the $n$ triangles gives

$$\text{Area} = n\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\times\text{side}\times\text{apothem}\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}ap$$

where $p$ is the perimeter. The second form follows from the first because the $n$ equal sides total $p = n \times \text{side}$, which is also how the perimeter of any regular polygon is found.

For an equilateral triangle of side $s$ there is a shortcut:

$$\text{Area} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2$$

## Trigonometry and areas

The same decomposition can be done with radii instead of an apothem. Joining the centre to each vertex of a regular $n$-gon produces $n$ congruent triangles, each with two sides of length $r$ from the centre and an included angle

$$X = \frac{360^\circ}{n}$$

since the $n$ angles at the centre share the full turn equally. Applying $\text{Area} = \tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ to one triangle and multiplying by $n$:

$$\text{Area} = \tfrac{1}{2}nr^2\sin X, \qquad X = \frac{360^\circ}{n}$$

This is the version to reach for when the distance from the centre to a vertex is known rather than the side length or the apothem.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Height of a triangle** | $H = b\sin A = a\sin B$ |
| **Area of a triangle** | $\tfrac12\,\text{base}\times\text{height} = \tfrac12 ab\sin C = \tfrac12 ac\sin B = \tfrac12 bc\sin A$ |
| **Area of a rectangle** | Base $\times$ height |
| **Heron's formula** | With $s=\tfrac12(a+b+c)$, the area is $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ |
| **Area of a trapezoid** | $\tfrac12(\text{base}_1+\text{base}_2)\times\text{height}$ |
| **Area of a rhombus or kite** | $\tfrac12 d_1 d_2$, half the product of the diagonals |
| **Apothem** | The perpendicular distance from the centre of a regular polygon to a side |
| **Area of a regular $n$-gon** | $n\left(\tfrac12\times\text{side}\times\text{apothem}\right)=\tfrac12 ap$ |
| **Perimeter of a regular $n$-gon** | $p = n \times \text{side}$ |
| **Area of an equilateral triangle** | $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$ |
| **Trigonometric area of a regular $n$-gon** | $\tfrac12 nr^2\sin X$, where $X = \dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$ |

# 9.1 Translations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A **translation**, or slide, is an **isometry** — a transformation that preserves distances — that moves all points of a figure the same distance in the same direction.

Two conditions are doing the work here, and both are needed. *The same distance* rules out stretching part of the figure; *the same direction* rules out turning it. Between them they mean a translated figure is identical to the original in every respect except position: same size, same shape, same orientation.

The word *isometry* is the general term for a transformation that preserves distances, and it is the property the rest of this chapter keeps returning to. A translation is one; so are the reflections and rotations of 9.2 and 9.3. The dilations of 9.5 are not, which is exactly what sets them apart.

## Compositions

A **composition of translations** is the result of applying two or more translations in sequence.

Because each translation shifts every point by the same amount, applying one and then another shifts every point by the total of the two shifts — which is itself the same distance in the same direction for every point. So a composition of translations is again a translation, and a sequence of slides can always be replaced by a single one.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Translation (slide)** | An isometry that moves all points of a figure the same distance in the same direction |
| **Isometry** | A transformation that preserves distances |
| **Composition of translations** | The result of applying two or more translations in sequence |

# 9.2 Reflections

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A **reflection** is an isometry in which a figure and its image have opposite orientation.

Like a translation, a reflection preserves distances, so the image is the same size and shape as the original. The difference is the reversal: reading round the original figure clockwise corresponds to reading round the image anticlockwise. That flip is what no translation can produce, however far it slides the figure.

## How to draw a reflection

1. Draw lines perpendicular to the reflection line, passing through the points of the figure.
2. Locate each image point on its perpendicular, on the far side of the reflection line and the same distance from it — this is what makes the reflection an isometry.
3. Connect the reflected points.

The perpendicular step is the one to get right. Measuring the distance to the reflection line along any other direction gives a point that is not the mirror image.

## Reflection across $y = x$

In the coordinate plane, reflecting across the line $y = x$ swaps the two coordinates:

$$(x,\, y) \rightarrow (y,\, x)$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Reflection** | An isometry in which a figure and its image have opposite orientation |
| **Reflection across $y=x$** | $(x, y) \rightarrow (y, x)$ |

# 9.3 Rotations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A **rotation** is a transformation that turns a figure around a fixed point by a specified angle and direction.

Three pieces of information are therefore needed to specify a rotation completely: the fixed point, the angle, and the direction. Leave any one out and the image is not determined.

The **center of rotation** is the fixed point about which a figure is rotated. Every point on the figure moves along a circular path around this point during rotation — which is what keeps each point's distance from the centre unchanged.

The **angle of rotation** is the measure, in degrees or radians, by which a figure is turned around the center of rotation. It determines how far the figure rotates.

**Clockwise** rotation is rotation in the same direction as the movement of a clock's hands ($\curvearrowright$); **counterclockwise** is the opposite direction ($\curvearrowleft$). Mathematically, clockwise is a negative angle and counterclockwise a positive one.

## How to draw a rotation

1. Locate the center of rotation.
2. Turn each point by the angle of rotation, clockwise or counterclockwise — take it as counterclockwise if the direction is not mentioned, since that is the positive direction.
3. Connect the points to complete the image.

## How to find the center of rotation

Given a figure and its image, the centre can be recovered.

1. Select two pairs of points (original and rotated).
2. Draw two segments connecting original and rotated points.
3. Construct a perpendicular bisector of each segment.
4. The intersection point of the two perpendicular bisectors is the center of rotation.

The perpendicular bisectors work because every point travels on a circle centred at the centre of rotation, so the centre is equidistant from a point and its image — and the set of points equidistant from two points is precisely their perpendicular bisector. One bisector narrows the centre down to a line; a second pins it to a single point.

## Rotation in the coordinate plane

$$90^\circ \text{ counterclockwise:} \qquad (x,\, y) \rightarrow (-y,\, x)$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Rotation** | A transformation that turns a figure around a fixed point by a specified angle and direction |
| **Center of rotation** | The fixed point about which a figure is rotated; every point moves along a circular path around it |
| **Angle of rotation** | The measure, in degrees or radians, by which a figure is turned around the center of rotation |
| **Clockwise** | Rotation in the same direction as a clock's hands; a negative angle |
| **Counterclockwise** | Rotation opposite to a clock's hands; a positive angle |
| **$90^\circ$ counterclockwise rule** | $(x, y) \rightarrow (-y, x)$ |

# 9.4 Symmetry

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What symmetry means

**Symmetry** refers to a figure that can be mapped onto itself by a transformation — a reflection or a rotation.

The transformations of 9.2 and 9.3 have so far been applied to move a figure somewhere new. Symmetry is the special case where the figure lands exactly back on top of itself, so the two types of transformation give two types of symmetry.

## Types of symmetry

**Line symmetry**, also called **reflectional symmetry**, means a figure can be reflected over a line to map onto itself. That line is a line of symmetry.

**Rotational symmetry** means a figure can be rotated about a point onto itself through some angle less than a full turn.

For a regular $n$-gon, both kinds are present and both are governed by $n$: it has $n$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of

$$\frac{360^\circ}{n}$$

A pentagon has $n = 5$, so it has $5$ lines of symmetry and $72^\circ$ rotational symmetry, since $360 \div 5 = 72$.

An isosceles trapezoid has 1 line of symmetry.

## Recognising symmetry in objects

A ping pong paddle has rotational symmetry.

The capital letters make a compact set of examples, and they show that the two kinds of symmetry are independent — a figure can have one without the other.

| Letter | Lines of symmetry | Rotational symmetry |
|---|---|---|
| V | 1 | No |
| A | 1 | No |
| H | 2 | — |
| I | 2 | — |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Symmetry** | A figure that can be mapped onto itself by a transformation (reflection or rotation) |
| **Line (reflectional) symmetry** | A figure can be reflected over a line to map onto itself |
| **Rotational symmetry** | A figure can be rotated onto itself; a regular $n$-gon has rotational symmetry of $360^\circ/n$ |
| **Lines of symmetry of a regular $n$-gon** | $n$ |

# 9.5 Dilations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

A **dilation** is a transformation that changes the size of a figure — an enlargement or a reduction — with a **center** and a **scale factor**.

This is the one transformation in the chapter that is not an isometry. Translations, reflections and rotations all preserve distances; a dilation deliberately does not, which is why it produces a figure similar to the original rather than congruent to it.

As with a rotation, two pieces of information are required. The centre fixes the point everything moves towards or away from, and the scale factor $s$ fixes how far. A scale factor greater than $1$ enlarges the figure; a scale factor between $0$ and $1$ reduces it.

## Dilation rules

For a dilation with centre at the origin $O(0,0)$ and scale factor $s$:

$$(x,\, y) \rightarrow (sx,\, sy)$$

For a dilation with centre $(h, k)$ and scale factor $s$:

$$(x,\, y) \rightarrow \big(h + s(x-h),\, k + s(y-k)\big)$$

The general rule is the origin rule with two extra steps built in. The quantities $x - h$ and $y - k$ measure the point's displacement from the centre; multiplying by $s$ scales that displacement; adding $h$ and $k$ back puts the result in position relative to the centre again. Setting $h = k = 0$ collapses the second rule to the first, as it should.

Note that the centre of a dilation is the one point that does not move: substituting $x = h$ and $y = k$ returns $(h, k)$ whatever the scale factor.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dilation** | A transformation that changes the size of a figure (enlargement or reduction) with a center and a scale factor |
| **Dilation about the origin** | For centre $O(0,0)$ and scale factor $s$: $(x,y) \rightarrow (sx, sy)$ |
| **Dilation about $(h,k)$** | For centre $(h,k)$ and scale factor $s$: $(x,y) \rightarrow (h+s(x-h),\, k+s(y-k))$ |

# 11.1 Space Figures and Cross Sections

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Polyhedra and their parts

A **polyhedron** is a three-dimensional shape. It is described by three kinds of part, each one dimension lower than the last.

A **face** is one of the flat surfaces of the polyhedron. An **edge** is a segment that is formed by the intersection of two faces. A **vertex** is a point where three or more edges meet.

Notice how the three definitions chain together: faces meet to give edges, and edges meet to give vertices. That chaining is why the three counts cannot vary independently, which is the content of Euler's formula below.

## Cross sections

A **cross section** is the shape formed by the intersection of a solid and a plane. You can think of a cross section as a very thin slice of the solid.

The same solid gives different cross sections depending on how the plane cuts it, so a cross-section question is always really a question about the orientation of the cutting plane.

## Euler's formula

The numbers of faces $F$, vertices $V$, and edges $E$ of a polyhedron are related by

$$F + V = E + 2$$

In two dimensions, Euler's formula reduces to

$$F + V = E + 1$$

where $F$ is the number of regions formed by $V$ vertices linked by $E$ segments.

The two-dimensional version is the same statement applied to a flat figure rather than a solid, with "regions" playing the part of faces. Losing a dimension costs exactly one from the constant on the right.

The formula is a check as much as a tool: count any two of $F$, $V$ and $E$ on a solid and the third is fixed.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polyhedron** | A three-dimensional shape |
| **Face** | One of the flat surfaces of a polyhedron |
| **Edge** | A segment that is formed by the intersection of two faces |
| **Vertex** | A point where three or more edges meet |
| **Cross section** | The shape formed by a solid and a plane; a very thin slice of the solid |
| **Euler's formula** | $F + V = E + 2$ for a polyhedron; $F + V = E + 1$ in two dimensions |

# 11.2 Surface Areas of Prisms and Cylinders

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Prisms

A **prism** is a polyhedron with at least two congruent parallel faces, called the **bases**. The other faces are the **lateral faces**. A prism is named by the shape of its base — a triangular prism has triangular bases, a hexagonal prism hexagonal ones.

An **altitude** of a prism is a perpendicular segment that joins the planes of the bases, and the **height** $h$ of the prism is the length of an altitude. Because the bases are parallel, every altitude has the same length, so the height is well defined.

## Lateral area and surface area

The **lateral area** of a prism is the sum of the areas of the lateral faces. The **surface area** is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the two bases.

Keeping the two apart matters, because a question asking how much material wraps *around* a solid wants the lateral area, while one asking for the total outside surface wants the surface area.

**Theorem 11-1 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Prism):** The lateral area of a right prism is the product of the circumference of the base and the height. The surface area is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the bases.

$$L.A. = Ch, \qquad S.A. = Ch + 2B$$

Here $C$ is the distance round the base and $B$ is the area of one base — hence the factor of $2$, since a prism has two.

## Cylinders

A **cylinder** has two congruent parallel bases, which are circles.

Unrolling the curved face results in a rectangle. That rectangle's height is the height of the cylinder, and its width is the distance around the base, so its area is the product of the circumference of the base and the height. This is why the cylinder obeys the same formula as the prism.

**Theorem 11-2 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Cylinder):** The lateral area of a right cylinder is the product of the circumference of the base and the height. The surface area is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the two bases.

$$L.A. = Ch, \qquad S.A. = Ch + 2B = Ch + 2\pi r^2$$

The final form simply substitutes the area of a circle for $B$.

An **altitude** of a cylinder, as for a prism, is a perpendicular segment joining the planes of the bases, and the **height** is its length.

| Solid | Lateral area | Surface area |
|---|---|---|
| Right prism | $Ch$ | $Ch + 2B$ |
| Right cylinder | $Ch$ | $Ch + 2B = Ch + 2\pi r^2$ |

The identical structure is not a coincidence. Both solids are a base swept straight upwards through a height, and unrolling the side of either gives a rectangle of width $C$ and height $h$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Prism** | A polyhedron with at least two congruent parallel faces, called the bases; the other faces are the lateral faces. Named by the shape of its base |
| **Lateral area** | The sum of the areas of the lateral faces |
| **Surface area** | The sum of the lateral area and the area of the two bases |
| **Cylinder** | A solid with two congruent parallel bases, which are circles |
| **Altitude** | A perpendicular segment that joins the planes of the bases |
| **Height ($h$)** | The length of an altitude |
| **Theorem 11-1** | For a right prism, $L.A. = Ch$ and $S.A. = Ch + 2B$ |
| **Theorem 11-2** | For a right cylinder, $L.A. = Ch$ and $S.A. = Ch + 2B = Ch + 2\pi r^2$ |

# 11.3 Surface Areas of Pyramids and Cones

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Pyramids

A **pyramid** is a polyhedron in which one face, the base, can be any polygon, and the other faces — the **lateral faces** — are the triangular sides that meet at a common vertex, the **vertex of the pyramid**. As with a prism, a pyramid is named by the shape of its base.

Two different lengths have to be kept apart.

The **altitude** is the perpendicular segment from the vertex of the pyramid to the plane of the base, and the length of the altitude is the **height** $h$. The **slant height** $\ell$ is the length of the altitude of a lateral face.

So the height runs through the inside of the solid, and the slant height runs along the surface of a triangular face. The slant height is always the longer of the two, and confusing them is the most common error in these problems.

A **regular pyramid** is a pyramid whose base is a regular polygon and whose lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles. That condition is what makes a single slant height meaningful — in an irregular pyramid, each face would have its own.

## Cones

The base of a **cone** is a circle. In a right cone, the altitude is a perpendicular segment from the vertex to the center of the base, and the **height** $h$ is the length of the altitude. The **slant height** $\ell$ is the distance from the vertex to a point on the circumference of the base.

## The formulas

**Theorem 11-3 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Regular Pyramid):**

$$L.A. = \tfrac{1}{2}C\ell, \qquad S.A. = L.A. + B$$

**Theorem 11-4 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Cone):**

$$L.A. = \pi r\ell, \qquad S.A. = L.A. + \pi r^2$$

The two agree with each other. A cone's base has circumference $C = 2\pi r$, so $\tfrac{1}{2}C\ell = \tfrac{1}{2}(2\pi r)\ell = \pi r\ell$ — the cone formula is the pyramid formula with a circular base. Likewise $B = \pi r^2$ turns the pyramid's $S.A. = L.A. + B$ into the cone's.

| Solid | Lateral area | Surface area |
|---|---|---|
| Regular pyramid | $\tfrac12 C\ell$ | $\tfrac12 C\ell + B$ |
| Cone | $\pi r \ell$ | $\pi r\ell + \pi r^2$ |

Note that only **one** base area is added here, against the two of 11.2. A pyramid or cone has a single base; the rest of it tapers to a point.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Pyramid** | A polyhedron in which one face (the base) can be any polygon and the other faces (the lateral faces) are triangular sides that meet at a common vertex |
| **Vertex of the pyramid** | The common point at which the lateral faces meet |
| **Altitude (pyramid)** | The perpendicular segment from the vertex of the pyramid to the plane of the base |
| **Height ($h$)** | The length of the altitude |
| **Slant height ($\ell$)** | For a pyramid, the length of the altitude of a lateral face; for a cone, the distance from the vertex to a point on the circumference of the base |
| **Regular pyramid** | A pyramid whose base is a regular polygon and whose lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles |
| **Cone** | A solid whose base is a circle; in a right cone the altitude runs from the vertex to the center of the base |
| **Theorem 11-3** | For a regular pyramid, $L.A. = \tfrac12 C\ell$ and $S.A. = L.A. + B$ |
| **Theorem 11-4** | For a cone, $L.A. = \pi r\ell$ and $S.A. = L.A. + \pi r^2$ |

# 11.4 Volumes of Prisms and Cylinders

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Volume

**Volume** is the measure of the amount of 3-dimensional space occupied by a solid object, expressed in cubic units such as $\text{cm}^3$, $\text{m}^3$ or $\text{in}^3$. It quantifies the capacity of the object, or how much a container can hold.

The cubic units are the immediate contrast with 11.2 and 11.3, where surface area was measured in square units. Checking the units of an answer is the quickest way to catch a volume formula used where a surface-area formula was wanted.

## Cavalieri's principle

**Theorem 11-5 (Cavalieri's Principle):** If two space figures have the same height and the same cross-sectional area at every level, then they have the same volume.

This is the theorem that makes the rest of the chapter's volume formulas possible. It says volume depends only on how much cross section there is at each level, not on where that cross section sits. A prism sheared over so that it leans has the same base area at every height as the upright one, and therefore the same volume — so the formulas below hold whether the solid is upright or oblique.

The two conditions must both be met. Equal heights alone, or equal cross sections at a single level, prove nothing.

## The formulas

**Theorem 11-6 (Volume of a Prism):**

$$V = Bh$$

**Theorem 11-7 (Volume of a Cylinder):**

$$V = Bh = \pi r^2 h$$

$B$ is the area of the base and $h$ is the height. Both formulas are the same statement — stack the base straight up through a height $h$ and every level contributes the same area $B$ — and the cylinder version simply substitutes $\pi r^2$ for the area of its circular base.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Volume** | The measure of the amount of 3-dimensional space occupied by a solid object, expressed in cubic units; it quantifies capacity, or how much a container can hold |
| **Cavalieri's Principle (Th 11-5)** | If two space figures have the same height and the same cross-sectional area at every level, then they have the same volume |
| **Volume of a Prism (Th 11-6)** | $V = Bh$ |
| **Volume of a Cylinder (Th 11-7)** | $V = Bh = \pi r^2 h$ |

# 11.5 Volumes of Pyramids and Cones

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The formulas

**Theorem 11-8 (Volume of a Pyramid):**

$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}Bh$$

**Theorem 11-9 (Volume of a Cone):**

$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}Bh$$

The two theorems give the same expression, exactly as the surface-area theorems of 11.3 did. What differs is the base area $B$ substituted into it: any polygon for a pyramid, and a circle for a cone, so that a cone's volume works out as $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.

## The factor of one third

Set these against the prism and cylinder of 11.4:

| Solid | Volume |
|---|---|
| Prism | $Bh$ |
| Cylinder | $Bh$ |
| Pyramid | $\tfrac13 Bh$ |
| Cone | $\tfrac13 Bh$ |

A pyramid or a cone occupies one third of the prism or cylinder built on the same base with the same height. The reason is visible in the shape: a prism holds its full cross-sectional area $B$ all the way up, whereas a pyramid's cross section shrinks from $B$ at the base to nothing at the vertex.

The height $h$ is still the length of the altitude — the perpendicular distance from the vertex to the plane of the base, as defined in 11.3. It is not the slant height, and substituting $\ell$ for $h$ here is the standard error.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Volume of a Pyramid (Th 11-8)** | $V = \tfrac13 Bh$ |
| **Volume of a Cone (Th 11-9)** | $V = \tfrac13 Bh$ |

# 11.6 Surface Areas and Volumes of Spheres

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The sphere and its parts

A **sphere** is the set of all points in three-dimensional space equidistant from a fixed point called the **center**.

This is the three-dimensional counterpart of a circle, and the vocabulary carries across unchanged. A **radius** is a segment that has one endpoint at the center and the other endpoint on the sphere. A **diameter** is a segment passing through the center with endpoints on the sphere.

A **great circle** is the largest possible circle of the sphere, and it contains the center of the sphere. A great circle divides a sphere into two hemispheres.

The great circle is the largest because any other plane cutting the sphere misses the centre and so slices off a smaller circle. Its radius is the sphere's own radius $r$, which is why $\pi r^2$ keeps appearing in the formulas below.

## Surface area

**Theorem 11-10 (Surface Area of a Sphere):**

$$S.A. = 4\pi r^2 = \pi d^2$$

The two forms are equal because $d = 2r$, so $\pi d^2 = \pi(2r)^2 = 4\pi r^2$.

Read the first form as four great circles: the surface of a sphere has the same area as four circles of radius $r$.

## Volume

**Theorem 11-11 (Volume of a Sphere):**

$$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$

As always, surface area goes as $r^2$ and volume as $r^3$. Doubling a sphere's radius multiplies its surface area by $4$ and its volume by $8$ — the special case of the similar-solids result in 11.7.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sphere** | The set of all points in three-dimensional space equidistant from a fixed point called the center |
| **Radius** | A segment that has one endpoint at the center and the other endpoint on the sphere |
| **Diameter** | A segment passing through the center with endpoints on the sphere |
| **Great circle** | The largest possible circle of the sphere, containing the center; it divides a sphere into two hemispheres |
| **Surface Area of a Sphere (Th 11-10)** | $S.A. = 4\pi r^2 = \pi d^2$ |
| **Volume of a Sphere (Th 11-11)** | $V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3$ |

# 11.7 Areas and Volumes of Similar Solids

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The theorem

**Theorem 11-12 (Areas and Volumes of Similar Solids):** If the similarity ratio of two similar solids is $a : b$, then

$$\frac{SA_1}{SA_2} = \frac{a^2}{b^2}, \qquad \frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{a^3}{b^3}$$

## Reading the exponents

The similarity ratio $a : b$ is a ratio of *lengths* — corresponding edges, radii, heights, slant heights. The exponents record how many lengths are multiplied together to produce each quantity.

| Quantity | Built from | Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Length | One dimension | $a : b$ |
| Surface area | Two dimensions | $a^2 : b^2$ |
| Volume | Three dimensions | $a^3 : b^3$ |

Every surface-area formula in this chapter is a product of two lengths — $Ch$, $\pi r\ell$, $4\pi r^2$ — so scaling all lengths by a factor multiplies the area by that factor twice over. Every volume formula is a product of three — $Bh$, $\tfrac13 Bh$, $\tfrac43\pi r^3$ — so the factor applies three times.

## Using it

The direction of the calculation is what catches people out. Going from a length ratio to an area or volume ratio means squaring or cubing; going the other way, from a known volume ratio back to the scale of the solids, means taking a cube root.

So two similar solids in the ratio $2 : 1$ do not have twice the surface area — they have four times, and eight times the volume.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Similarity ratio** | The ratio $a : b$ of corresponding lengths in two similar solids |
| **Areas and Volumes of Similar Solids (Th 11-12)** | If the similarity ratio of two similar solids is $a:b$, then $\dfrac{SA_1}{SA_2}=\dfrac{a^2}{b^2}$ and $\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}=\dfrac{a^3}{b^3}$ |

# 12 Coordinate Geometry: Points, Lines, and Circles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Coordinate geometry basics

The **rectangular** or **Cartesian coordinate system** locates every point in the plane by a pair of numbers. The **x-axis** is a horizontal number line, and the y-axis the vertical one crossing it.

Points are written as **ordered pairs** $(x, y)$. The x-coordinate, also called the **abscissa**, is the distance from the y-axis; the y-coordinate is the distance from the x-axis.

Any set $S$ of ordered pairs $(x, y)$ can therefore be represented by points in the plane, which is what allows a geometric figure to be described by an equation and an equation to be drawn as a figure.

## Forms of linear equations

A straight line can be written in four ways, and choosing the right one for the information given saves most of the algebra.

| Form | Equation | Use it when you know |
|---|---|---|
| **General form** | $Ax + By = C$ | Any line, including vertical ones |
| **Slope-intercept form** | $y = mx + k$ | The slope $m$ and the y-intercept $k$ |
| **Point-slope form** | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ | The slope and any one point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the line |
| **Intercept form** | $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$ | The x-intercept $a$ and the y-intercept $b$ |

## Finding intercepts

An intercept is where the line crosses an axis, and on each axis the other coordinate is zero. That single observation is the whole method.

**Example.** For $2x + 3y = 15$:

y-intercept — set $x = 0$:

$$3y = 15 \implies y = 5$$

So the y-intercept is $(0, 5)$.

x-intercept — set $y = 0$:

$$2x = 15 \implies x = 7.5$$

So the x-intercept is $(7.5, 0)$.

## Distance and midpoint

For points $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$:

$$AB = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$$

$$M = \left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$$

The distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem of 8.1 applied to the right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical gaps between the two points. The midpoint formula averages the coordinates separately, because the midpoint is halfway across in each direction independently.

## Slopes of lines

For points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$:

$$m = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$$

Horizontal lines have slope $m = 0$: the y-coordinates are equal, so the numerator vanishes. Vertical lines have no defined slope, because the denominator vanishes instead — which is why a vertical line cannot be written as $y = mx + k$ and must be given as $x = \text{constant}$.

**Parallel lines** have the same slope, $m_1 = m_2$. **Perpendicular lines** have slopes whose product is $-1$, that is $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

## Circles in the coordinate plane

A circle with center $(h, k)$ and radius $r$ has the standard equation

$$(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$$

This is the distance formula in disguise: the left-hand side is the squared distance from $(x, y)$ to the centre, and setting it equal to $r^2$ says exactly that the point lies $r$ from the centre.

A line is **tangent** to a circle if it intersects it at exactly one point.

## Proofs using coordinate geometry

Placing a figure on axes turns a geometric claim into an algebraic one, provable with the distance, midpoint and slope formulas above.

**Midsegment Theorem (Trapezoid):** The midsegment of a trapezoid is parallel to the bases and its length is the average of the lengths of the bases.

$$\text{midsegment} = \frac{b_1 + b_2}{2}$$

The two conclusions are proved by two different tools: parallelism by the slope formula, and length by the distance formula.

## Practice questions

**1. The line with x-intercept $-3$ and y-intercept $8$.**

Intercept form with $a = -3$ and $b = 8$:

$$\frac{x}{-3} + \frac{y}{8} = 1$$

**2. The line with x-intercept $-2$ and through $(3, 7)$.**

An x-intercept of $-2$ is the point $(-2, 0)$, so

$$m = \frac{7-0}{3-(-2)} = \frac{7}{5}$$

Point-slope form through $(3,7)$:

$$y - 7 = \frac{7}{5}(x-3)$$

**3. The line through $(8, 5)$ and perpendicular to $y = 4$.**

$y = 4$ is horizontal, so a perpendicular line is vertical, and every point on it shares the x-coordinate of $(8,5)$:

$$x = 8$$

**4. The line through $(9, 2)$ and the origin.**

$$m = \frac{2-0}{9-0} = \frac{2}{9}$$

The line passes through the origin, so its y-intercept is $0$:

$$y = \frac{2x}{9}$$

**5. A quadrilateral has vertices $(-4,4)$, $(-6,0)$, $(-4,-4)$, $(-2,0)$. Name the type of quadrilateral and find its area.**

Each side, by the distance formula, has length $\sqrt{2^2+4^2} = \sqrt{20}$, so all four sides are equal and the quadrilateral is a **rhombus**.

Its diagonals run from $(-4,4)$ to $(-4,-4)$, of length $8$, and from $(-6,0)$ to $(-2,0)$, of length $4$. Using the rhombus area formula of 8.6:

$$A = \tfrac{1}{2}d_1 d_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(8)(4) = 16$$

**6. $ABCD$ is a square with vertices $A(0,0)$ and $B(5,3)$. Find the coordinates of $C$ and $D$.**

Side $AB$ is the displacement $(5, 3)$. Side $AD$ must be perpendicular to it and the same length, so it is $(-3, 5)$ or $(3, -5)$, and there are two squares.

Taking $(-3,5)$: $D = (-3, 5)$ and $C = B + (-3,5) = (5-3,\ 3+5) = (2, 8)$.

Taking $(3,-5)$: $D = (3, -5)$ and $C = B + (3,-5) = (8, -2)$.

**7. $\triangle ABC$ has vertices $A(-2,-1)$, $B(0,7)$ and $C(8,3)$. Find the circumcenter $Q$.**

The circumcentre is the point equidistant from all three vertices, so write $Q = (x, y)$ and set the squared distances equal using the distance formula.

From $QA^2 = QB^2$:

$$(x+2)^2 + (y+1)^2 = x^2 + (y-7)^2$$
$$4x + 2y + 5 = -14y + 49 \implies x + 4y = 11$$

From $QB^2 = QC^2$:

$$x^2 + (y-7)^2 = (x-8)^2 + (y-3)^2$$
$$-14y + 49 = -16x - 6y + 73 \implies 2x - y = 3$$

Substituting $y = 2x - 3$ into $x + 4y = 11$ gives $9x = 23$, so

$$Q = \left(\frac{23}{9},\ \frac{19}{9}\right)$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular (Cartesian) coordinate system** | The system locating points by an ordered pair of distances from two perpendicular number lines |
| **x-axis** | The horizontal number line |
| **Ordered pair** | A point written as $(x, y)$ |
| **Abscissa** | The x-coordinate; the distance from the y-axis |
| **General form** | $Ax + By = C$ |
| **Slope-intercept form** | $y = mx + k$, where $m$ is the slope |
| **Point-slope form** | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$, where $(x_1, y_1)$ is a point on the line |
| **Intercept form** | $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$, where $a$ is the x-intercept and $b$ is the y-intercept |
| **Distance formula** | $AB = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$ |
| **Midpoint formula** | $M = \left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$ |
| **Slope formula** | $m = \dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$; horizontal lines have $m = 0$ |
| **Parallel lines** | Lines with the same slope, $m_1 = m_2$ |
| **Perpendicular lines** | Lines whose slopes satisfy $m_1m_2 = -1$ |
| **Standard equation of a circle** | $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$, with center $(h,k)$ and radius $r$ |
| **Tangent to a circle** | A line that intersects the circle at exactly one point |
| **Midsegment Theorem (Trapezoid)** | The midsegment of a trapezoid is parallel to the bases and its length is the average of the lengths of the bases |

# 13 Statistics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Structured and unstructured data

**Unstructured data** are easy to read and contain great information, but they are usually given in natural language. They can vary greatly in length, style, and content, which makes them difficult to analyse. This is the kind of data most common in daily life.

**Structured data** are any data that are organised in a predefined manner, typically in a table format with rows and columns — a **data table**.

The contrast explains why the rest of this lesson is about tables. Analysis needs values that can be counted and compared, and a predefined structure is what guarantees that the same kind of information appears in the same place for every case. Unstructured data have to be turned into structured data before any of the displays below can be built.

## Variables

**Variables** are the characteristics recorded about each individual. In a data table, each row is an individual and each column is a variable.

Two types are distinguished, and the type decides which displays and summaries are legitimate.

| Type | What it records |
|---|---|
| **Categorical variables** | Related to the category of what is measured |
| **Quantitative variables** | Related to the quantity of what is measured |

Gender, for instance, is categorical: it sorts individuals into groups rather than measuring an amount.

## How to display data

A **frequency table** lists the categories of a variable together with the count in each. A **relative frequency table** does the same but displays percentages instead of the actual numbers, which makes groups of different sizes comparable.

A **bar chart** displays the distribution of a categorical variable, showing the counts for each category.

A **pie chart** shows the whole group of cases as a circle, where each slice is proportional to the fraction of the whole in that category. The choice between the two follows from what the reader is meant to see: a bar chart compares categories against each other, a pie chart shows each category as a share of the whole.

The **area principle** governs both: the area occupied by a part of the graph should correspond to the magnitude of the value it represents. This is the rule that a display is judged against, because the eye reads area rather than any label. A bar drawn twice as wide as its neighbour, or a picture scaled in two dimensions to show a doubling, breaks the principle and misleads even when its numbers are correct.

## Analysing two variables together

A **contingency table**, also called a **crosstabulation**, shows how the individuals are distributed along each variable, contingent on the value of the other variable.

Three terms describe its parts:

- A **cell** gives the count for a combination of values of the two variables.
- In the margins of a contingency table, the frequency distribution of one of the variables is called its **marginal distribution**.
- **Conditional distributions** show the distribution of one variable for just those cases that satisfy a condition on another variable.

The marginal distribution ignores the second variable altogether, while a conditional distribution restricts attention to one of its values. Comparing conditional distributions with each other, or with the marginal distribution, is how a relationship between the two variables is detected: if the conditional distributions all look alike, knowing one variable tells you nothing about the other.

A **segmented bar chart** displays exactly that comparison. Each bar is a whole and divides proportionally into segments corresponding to the percentage in each group, so the bars stand for conditional distributions and can be read against one another at a glance.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unstructured data** | Data that are easy to read and contain great information but are usually given in natural language, varying greatly in length, style and content, which makes them difficult to analyse |
| **Structured data** | Any data that are organised in a predefined manner, typically in a table format with rows and columns |
| **Data table** | A table of structured data |
| **Variables** | The characteristics recorded about each individual |
| **Categorical variables** | Variables related to the category of what is measured |
| **Quantitative variables** | Variables related to the quantity of what is measured |
| **Frequency table** | A table giving the count in each category |
| **Relative frequency table** | A table displaying percentages instead of the actual numbers |
| **Bar chart** | A display of the distribution of a categorical variable, showing the counts for each category |
| **Pie chart** | A display of the whole group of cases as a circle, where each slice is proportional to the fraction of the whole in the category |
| **Area principle** | The area occupied by a part of the graph should correspond to the magnitude of the value it represents |
| **Contingency table (crosstabulation)** | A table showing how the individuals are distributed along each variable, contingent on the value of the other variable |
| **Cell** | The count for a combination of values of the two variables |
| **Marginal distribution** | The frequency distribution of one of the variables, given in the margins of a contingency table |
| **Conditional distribution** | The distribution of one variable for just those cases that satisfy a condition on another variable |
| **Segmented bar chart** | A chart in which each bar is a whole, divided proportionally into segments corresponding to the percentage in each group |
